front: State the relationship between plasma sodium concentration and plasma osmolarity in a normal clinical state.
back:
• Plasma Na+ is a primary indicator of osmolarity.
• Na+ and associated anions (Cl-) account for >90% of ECF solute.
• Plasma osmolarity ≈ 2.1 × [Na+].

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: The primary extracellular cation responsible for maintaining the osmotic equilibrium between the intracellular and extracellular fluid compartments is [___].
back:
• Sodium (Na+)
• Accounts for over 90% of ECF solutes
• Directs water movement across cell membranes

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: A patient with a bronchogenic tumor presents with lethargy and a plasma sodium of 115 mEq/L. Identify the primary pathophysiological effect on brain cells.
back:
• Intracellular edema (brain cell swelling)
• Occurs as water moves from hypotonic ECF into the hypertonic ICF
• Can lead to seizures, coma, or brain herniation

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: Explain the role of Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) deficiency in the development of hypernatremia-dehydration.
back:
• Inability to conserve water (Central Diabetes Insipidus)
• Kidneys excrete large volumes of dilute urine
• Increases ECF osmolarity, drawing water out of cells and shrinking them

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: Contrast the effect on Intracellular Fluid (ICF) volume in hyponatremia caused by adrenal insufficiency versus hypernatremia caused by primary aldosteronism.
back:
• Adrenal Insufficiency: ICF volume increases (cellular swelling)
• Primary Aldosteronism: ICF volume decreases (cellular shrinkage)
• Driven by the osmotic gradient created by sodium concentration changes

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: Identify the direct effect of infusing hypertonic 3% NaCl on the steady-state volumes of the ECF and ICF.
back:
• ECF volume increases (greater than volume infused)
• ICF volume decreases
• Osmolarity increases equally in both compartments

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: In the adaptation to chronic hyponatremia, brain cells mitigate swelling by transporting organic solutes and [___] from the ICF to the ECF.
back:
• Potassium (K+) and Sodium (Na+)
• Also involves solutes like glutamate
• Reduces the osmotic gradient to prevent excessive edema

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: A patient with excessive vomiting presents with hyponatremia and signs of dehydration. Describe the resulting changes in ECF and ICF volumes.
back:
• ECF volume decreases (loss of sodium and water)
• ICF volume increases (water moves into cells due to low ECF sodium)
• This is hyponatremia-dehydration

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: Explain why rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia with hypertonic saline can lead to osmotic demyelination syndrome.
back:
• Rapid ECF osmolarity increase outpaces the cell's ability to recapture lost solutes
• Causes sudden, severe shrinkage of neurons
• Leads to loss of the myelin sheath and permanent nerve damage

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: Contrast the changes in ECF volume and plasma osmolarity in Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH (SIADH) versus simple dehydration from sweating.
back:
• SIADH: ECF volume increases; Plasma osmolarity decreases
• Sweating: ECF volume decreases; Plasma osmolarity increases
• SIADH causes cell swelling; Sweating causes cell shrinkage

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: Identify the hormone deficiency in Addison's disease that specifically impairs the kidney's ability to reabsorb sodium, leading to hyponatremia.
back:
• Aldosterone
• Deficiency causes sodium wasting and potassium retention
• Results in decreased ECF volume and increased ICF volume

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: A rapid reduction in plasma sodium concentration can lead to dangerous brain swelling and potential [___].
back:
• Herniation
• Brain cell edema
• Permanent neurological injury
• Seizures or coma

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: A patient with a bronchogenic tumor presents with lethargy and disorientation. Labs reveal serum Na+ of 115 mEq/L and increased extracellular fluid volume. Identify the underlying pathophysiology.
back:
• SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH)
• Excess water reabsorption by kidney tubules
• Hyponatremia-overhydration
• Intracellular edema (ICF expansion)

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: Explain the role of the brain's organic solutes (e.g., glutamate) during the adaptation to chronic hyponatremia.
back:
• Solutes are transported out of neurons
• Attenuates osmotic water flow into cells
• Reduces brain swelling/edema
• Makes neurons vulnerable to injury if sodium is corrected too rapidly

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: Contrast the effects of Addison’s disease and Primary Aldosteronism on Extracellular Fluid (ECF) and Intracellular Fluid (ICF) volumes.
back:
• Addison’s: ↓ECF volume (sodium loss), ↑ICF volume (osmotic shift into cells)
• Aldosteronism: ↑ECF volume (sodium retention), ↓ICF volume (osmotic shift out of cells)

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: Identify the primary mechanism of cell volume change during severe hypernatremia (>158 mmol/L).
back:
• Hyperosmotic ECF creates osmotic gradient
• Water flows out of cells into ECF
• Resultant cell shrinkage (crenation)
• Common in hypothalamic lesions or Diabetes Insipidus

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: In patients with Central Diabetes Insipidus, hypernatremia occurs due to a lack of [___].
back:
• Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH)
• Leads to large volumes of dilute urine
• Results in ECF dehydration and increased Na+ concentration

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: A 35-year-old female presents with hypernatremia, hypertension, and hypokalemia. Imaging shows an adrenal cortical tumor. Describe the fluid compartment status.
back:
• Increased ECF volume (Hypernatremia-overhydration)
• Decreased ICF volume (Cell shrinkage)
• Diagnosis: Conn's Syndrome (Primary Aldosteronism)

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: How does the kidney maintain plasma sodium concentration during excessive salt intake in a healthy individual?
back:
• Thirst stimulation increases water intake
• Osmoreceptor-ADH system reabsorbs water
• Kidney increases Na+ excretion (pressure natriuresis)
• Dilutes excess sodium to maintain normonatremia

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: Contrast the cause and effect of Nephrogenic vs. Central Diabetes Insipidus on sodium balance.
back:
• Central: Lack of ADH secretion
• Nephrogenic: Kidney inability to respond to ADH
• Both: Cause hypernatremia-dehydration (↓ECF volume, ↓ICF volume)

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: State the average normal plasma sodium concentration and its contribution to total ECF osmolarity.
back:
• Normal Na+: ~142 mEq/L (Range 140–145)
• Contribution: Na+ and associated anions (Cl-, HCO3-) account for >90% of ECF solute

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: In patients with [___], a primary deficiency in aldosterone impairs renal sodium reabsorption, resulting in hyponatremia and decreased extracellular fluid volume.
back:
• Addison disease (adrenal insufficiency)
• Causes sodium wasting and water loss
• Leads to hyponatremia-dehydration and hyperkalemia

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: A 65-year-old male with a bronchogenic tumor presents with confusion and a plasma sodium of 115 mEq/L. If this chronic condition is corrected at a rate exceeding 12 mmol/L per 24 hours, what neurological risk is most significant?
back:
• Osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis)
• Occurs as brain cells fail to rapidly recapture solutes lost during adaptation
• Leads to irreversible myelin sheath damage

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: Explain the role of the osmotic gradient in the development of neurological symptoms during acute hyponatremia.
back:
• Low extracellular sodium creates a gradient favoring water entry into cells
• Brain cells swell (intracellular edema)
• Increased intracranial pressure causes headache, seizures, and herniation

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: Contrast the effects of hyponatremia-dehydration (e.g., adrenal insufficiency) versus hyponatremia-overhydration (e.g., SIADH) on extracellular fluid (ECF) and intracellular fluid (ICF) volumes.
back:
• Hyponatremia-Dehydration: Decreased ECF; Increased ICF
• Hyponatremia-Overhydration: Increased ECF; Increased ICF
• Both cause cell swelling due to low plasma osmolarity

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: In Central Diabetes Insipidus, identify the hormonal defect and its direct impact on plasma sodium concentration.
back:
• Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) deficiency
• Inability to conserve water leads to large volumes of dilute urine
• Results in hypernatremia-dehydration as plasma becomes concentrated

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: The primary clinical finding in hypernatremia regardless of the cause is cellular [___] due to the movement of water out of the cells.
back:
• Shrinkage (intracellular dehydration)
• Hyperosmotic ECF pulls water from the ICF
• Symptoms include intense thirst and altered mental status

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: A patient presents with hypernatremia and an increased ECF volume. This presentation is most consistent with which underlying endocrinopathy?
back:
• Primary Aldosteronism (Conn syndrome) or Cushing disease
• Excess sodium retention by the kidneys
• Secondary water retention follows, expanding ECF volume

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: How do brain cells adapt to chronic hypernatremia to prevent excessive shrinkage?
back:
• Intracellular concentration of sodium and other solutes is increased
• Mechanisms activate to pull water back into the cells
• Protects cell volume against the hyperosmotic ECF

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: Contrast the primary causes of hypernatremia-dehydration versus hypernatremia-overhydration.
back:
• Dehydration: Pure water loss (Diabetes Insipidus, excessive sweating)
• Overhydration: Excessive sodium addition (primary aldosteronism)
• Both increase plasma sodium but have opposite effects on ECF volume

category: Explain the causes of hypo & hypernatremia and their effects on Composition of body fluid compartments
front: Identify the primary solute that accounts for over 90% of the effective osmolarity in the extracellular fluid.
back:
• Sodium (and its associated anions, mainly chloride)
• Plasma sodium is the most reliable indicator of plasma osmolarity
• Normal range is approximately 142 mEq/L

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: A solution with an osmolarity exactly equal to that of normal cell fluid, regardless of whether the solute can permeate the membrane, is termed [___].
back:
• Isosmotic
• Refers to total solute concentration
• Does not account for solute permeability or effect on cell volume.

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: A patient is accidentally infused with a 3.0% NaCl solution. Describe the resulting fluid shift between the intracellular (ICF) and extracellular (ECF) compartments.
back:
• ECF osmolarity increases (Hyperosmotic)
• Water moves from ICF to ECF via osmosis
• Result: Cell shrinkage and increased ECF volume.

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Explain why a solution containing a highly permeant solute like urea might be isosmotic to a cell but not isotonic.
back:
• Isosmotic refers to total solute concentration (equal to cell).
• Isotonic requires equal concentrations of *impermeant* solutes.
• Urea eventually equilibrates across membranes, failing to prevent osmotic water movement.

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Contrast the defining criteria for a hyperosmotic solution versus a hypertonic solution.
back:
• Hyperosmotic: Total osmolarity > normal ECF (300 mOsm/L).
• Hypertonic: Higher concentration of *impermeant* solutes than cell fluid; always causes cell shrinkage.

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Predict the immediate effect on cell volume when a tissue is bathed in a hypo-osmotic solution of impermeant solutes.
back:
• Water diffuses into the cell (higher internal osmolarity).
• The cell swells.
• Diffusion continues until intracellular and extracellular osmolarities equalize.

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: While osmolality is expressed as osmoles per kilogram of water, [___] is the term for concentration expressed as osmoles per liter of solution.
back:
• Osmolarity
• Used synonymously with osmolality in dilute body fluids.
• Standard unit for clinical calculations.

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: A dehydrated patient receives an infusion of 5% glucose. Describe how this initially isosmotic fluid becomes effectively hypotonic in the body.
back:
• Glucose is rapidly transported into cells and metabolized.
• Only pure water remains in the ECF.
• This reduces ECF osmolarity, allowing water to enter cells to correct dehydration.

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Describe the transient vs. steady-state effect of adding a hyperosmotic urea solution to the extracellular fluid.
back:
• Transient: Water initially moves out of cells due to urea concentration gradient.
• Steady-state: Urea permeates the cell membrane until concentrations equalize; water moves back, resulting in no change in volume.

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Distinguish between iso-osmotic and hypo-osmotic fluids based on their respective solute concentrations relative to normal plasma.
back:
• Iso-osmotic: Solute concentration equals normal plasma (approx. 280-300 mOsm/L).
• Hypo-osmotic: Solute concentration is lower than normal plasma.

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: State the approximate time required to achieve total osmotic equilibrium throughout the body after a person drinks a significant volume of water.
back:
• Approximately 30 minutes.
• Water moves across cell membranes in seconds/minutes locally.
• Body-wide equilibrium requires transport via blood and distribution through all tissues.

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: A solution with an osmolarity significantly lower than the normal 282 mOsm/L of intracellular fluid is classified as [___].
back:
• Hypo-osmotic fluid
• Initially decreases ECF osmolarity
• Results in water diffusion into cells until equilibrium is reached

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: A 30-year-old male is infused with 5% glucose solution to treat dehydration. Describe the initial osmolarity of this fluid relative to the plasma and its effect on red blood cells.
back:
• Isosmotic (~300 mOsm/L)
• Prevents red blood cell lysis or shrinkage
• Becomes hypotonic after glucose metabolism, providing free water

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Explain the role of solute permeability in determining why a 300 mOsm/L urea solution is isosmotic but not isotonic.
back:
• Urea is a highly permeant solute
• It crosses cell membranes, abolishing the osmotic gradient
• Water follows urea into the cell, causing cell swelling

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Contrast hyper-osmotic fluids with hypertonic fluids regarding their definition and primary effect on cell volume.
back:
• Hyper-osmotic: Higher total solute concentration than normal ECF (>300 mOsm/L)
• Hypertonic: Higher concentration of non-permeating solutes only
• Effect: Hypertonic fluids always cause cell shrinkage

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Specify the characteristic osmolarity of a 0.9% sodium chloride solution and its classification in clinical medicine.
back:
• Osmolarity: ~308 mOsm/L (actual activity ~286 mOsm/L)
• Classification: Isosmotic and Isotonic
• Does not cause shifts in cell volume

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Solutions that have an osmolarity higher than the normal extracellular fluid, regardless of whether the solute permeates the cell membrane, are termed [___].
back:
• Hyperosmotic fluids
• Cause transient fluid shifts if solutes are permeant
• Lead to steady-state shrinkage if solutes are non-permeant

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: A patient is accidentally infused with a highly concentrated salt solution (>0.9% NaCl). Categorize this fluid's osmolarity and predict the immediate effect on intracellular fluid volume.
back:
• Hyper-osmotic fluid
• Hypertonic
• Effect: Rapid osmosis of water out of cells causing intracellular dehydration

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Describe the mechanism by which isosmotic equilibrium is rapidly attained between intracellular and extracellular compartments after drinking a large volume of water.
back:
• Rapid water movement across highly permeable cell membranes
• Occurs within seconds to minutes locally
• Whole-body equilibrium takes ~30 minutes due to distribution time

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Distinguish between iso-osmotic and isotonic solutions based on their reference criteria.
back:
• Iso-osmotic: Based on the total number of osmoles per liter of solution
• Isotonic: Based on whether the solution causes a change in cell volume
• Isotonicity depends specifically on non-permeating solutes

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
coreConcept: Van't Hoff's Law and Osmotic Pressure
front: State the approximate potential osmotic pressure exerted across a cell membrane by a concentration gradient of 1 mOsm/L of an impermeant solute.
back:
• ~19.3 mm Hg
• Illustrates the massive force generated by small osmolarity differences
• Explains why cell volume changes so rapidly with hyper/hypo-osmotic fluids

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: The volume of a body fluid compartment is calculated by dividing the total mass of the injected indicator by its final [___] in the compartment.
back:
● Concentration
● Based on the conservation of mass principle ($Volume = Mass / Concentration$)
● Assumes even distribution and no loss of indicator.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: A medical researcher needs to determine a patient's total body water (TBW). Which high-yield substances can be utilized as indicators?
back:
● Radioactive water (Tritium, $^3H_2O$)
● Heavy water (Deuterium, $^2H_2O$)
● Antipyrine (highly lipid-soluble, penetrates all membranes).

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: Explain the biological mechanism of the Indicator-Dilution Principle for measuring body fluid volumes.
back:
● An indicator mass is injected into a compartment.
● It disperses evenly throughout the fluid.
● The total mass remains constant ($V_1C_1 = V_2C_2$).
● Volume is determined by analyzing the extent of dilution.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: Contrast the measurement methods for Extracellular Fluid (ECF) volume versus Intracellular Fluid (ICF) volume.
back:
● ECF: Measured directly using substances that stay outside cells (Inulin, $^{22}Na$, thiosulfate).
● ICF: Cannot be measured directly.
● ICF Calculation: Total Body Water minus ECF volume.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: Enlist the specific substances used to estimate the Extracellular Fluid (ECF) volume.
back:
● Inulin
● Radioactive Sodium or Chloride
● Radioactive Iothalamate
● Thiosulfate ion.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: [___] is a diagnostic dye used to measure plasma volume because it binds avidly to plasma proteins.
back:
● Evans Blue Dye (T-1824)
● Alternatives include $^{125}I$-albumin.
● It remains in the vascular system rather than entering the interstitium.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: In a clinical study, a subject's plasma volume is 3L and hematocrit is 0.40. Calculate the total blood volume.
back:
● Formula: $Plasma Volume / (1 - Hematocrit)$
● Calculation: $3 / (1 - 0.40) = 5L$
● Alternative: Use $^{51}Cr$-labeled red blood cells for direct measurement.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: Describe the three mandatory functional requirements for an ideal indicator used in the dilution method.
back:
● Disperses evenly throughout the targeted compartment.
● Stays exclusively in the compartment being measured.
● Is not metabolized or excreted (or loss must be correctable).

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: Contrast the determination of Plasma Volume (PV) and Interstitial Fluid (ISF) volume.
back:
● PV: Measured directly using $^{125}I$-albumin or Evans blue dye.
● ISF: Cannot be measured directly.
● ISF Calculation: Extracellular Fluid volume minus Plasma Volume.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: How is the total blood volume measured directly using radioactive isotopes?
back:
● Red blood cells are labeled with Radioactive Chromium ($^{51}Cr$).
● Labeled cells are injected into the circulation.
● Radioactivity of a mixed blood sample is measured.
● Calculation uses the standard dilution principle.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: The volume of a body fluid compartment is measured using the indicator-dilution principle, which is based on the [___] principle.
back:
• Conservation of mass
• Total mass of substance after dispersion equals total mass injected
• Formula: Volume B = (Volume A × Concentration A) / Concentration B

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: A researcher needs to assess changes in a patient's total body hydration status. List the specific indicators that can be used to measure Total Body Water (TBW).
back:
• Radioactive water (Tritium, 3H2O)
• Heavy water (Deuterium, 2H2O)
• Antipyrine (highly lipid-soluble, penetrates all cell membranes)

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: Explain the essential criteria a substance must meet to be an ideal indicator for measuring the volume of a specific body fluid compartment.
back:
• Disperses evenly throughout the targeted compartment
• Stays only in the compartment being measured
• Is not metabolized or excreted (or loss must be corrected for)

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: Contrast the properties of indicators used to measure Extracellular Fluid (ECF) volume versus those used for Plasma Volume (PV).
back:
• ECF indicators (Inulin, 22Na): Must cross capillary membranes but cannot penetrate cell membranes.
• PV indicators (Evans Blue, 125I-albumin): Must stay within the vascular system, typically by binding to plasma proteins.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: Outline the indirect steps required to determine a patient's Intracellular Fluid (ICF) volume.
back:
• ICF cannot be measured directly
• Step 1: Measure Total Body Water (TBW) using tritium
• Step 2: Measure Extracellular Fluid (ECF) volume using inulin
• Step 3: Calculate ICF = TBW - ECF

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: To determine the volume of the interstitial fluid (ISF) compartment, one must subtract the [___] from the total extracellular fluid (ECF) volume.
back:
• Plasma Volume (PV)
• Equation: ISF = ECF - PV
• ISF is typically 3/4 of the total ECF volume

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: A patient with anemia has a measured plasma volume of 3 Liters and a hematocrit of 0.20. Determine the total blood volume.
back:
• Total Blood Volume = Plasma Volume / (1 - Hematocrit)
• Calculation: 3 / (1 - 0.2) = 3.75 Liters

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: How is radioactive chromium (51Cr) utilized to directly measure total blood volume rather than just plasma volume?
back:
• 51Cr binds tightly to red blood cells (RBCs)
• Labeled RBCs are injected and allowed to mix
• Dilution of radioactivity in a whole blood sample reveals total volume

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: Distinguish between the volumes measured by Inulin versus Antipyrine.
back:
• Inulin: Measures ECF volume only (remains extracellular).
• Antipyrine: Measures TBW (penetrates all cells due to lipid solubility).

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
coreConcept: Clinical Significance of Blood Volume Measurement
front: Why is the direct measurement of blood volume particularly critical for cardiovascular management?
back:
• Essential for controlling cardiovascular dynamics
• Guides fluid replacement in hemorrhage or shock
• Helps differentiate between absolute and relative polycythemia

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Solutions possessi ng an osmol arity identical to the cell (~282 mOsm/L), irre spective of whether the solutes can pe netrate the cell me mbrane, are defined as [___].
back:
● Isos motic
● Based on total solute concentration
● Contrasts with isotonicity, which only considers impermeant solutes

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: A solution of urea is measured at 400 mOsm/L. Despite urea's ability to eventually diffuse across cell membranes and equilibrate, the solution is initially classified as [___].
back:
● Hyperosmotic
● Osmolarity accounts for all solutes initially present
● Because urea is permeant, the fluid is hyperosmotic but eventually behaves as hypotonic

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Explain the fundamental mechanism that allows a fluid to be isosmotic yet hypotonic simultaneously.
back:
● Osmolarity includes total solutes (permeant + impermeant)
● Tonicity only includes impermeant solutes
● If solutes permeate the cell, they exert no long-term effective osmotic pressure, causing water to enter and cells to swell

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Contrast the clinical outcome of infusing a hyperosmotic permeant solution versus a hyperosmotic impermeant solution on intracellular fluid (ICF) volume.
back:
● Permeant (e.g., Urea): Causes transient cell shrinkage followed by volume restoration as solutes equilibrate
● Impermeant (e.g., NaCl): Causes sustained cell shrinkage (hypertonicity) as water moves out to balance the gradient

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Identify the standard reference point used to categorize a solution as hypo-osmotic in human physiology.
back:
● Normal extracellular fluid osmolarity
● Approximately 282–300 mOsm/L
● Any solution with a total solute concentration below this range is hypo-osmotic

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: A solution with a lower total concentration of solutes compared to the normal extracellular fluid is termed [___].
back:
● Hypo-osmotic
● Characterized by lower osmotic pressure
● Usually results in water movement into cells (hypotonic effect)

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: A patient is accidentally administered a large volume of pure water intravenously. Categorize this fluid's osmotic status and the resulting effect on red blood cells.
back:
● Status: Severely hypo-osmotic
● Effect: Rapid osmosis into cells leading to swelling and hemolysis
● Pure water lacks solutes to balance intracellular osmotic pressure

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Describe the physiological utility of 5% glucose being isosmotic during clinical administration for dehydration.
back:
● Prevents red blood cell swelling/lysis during initial infusion
● Glucose is eventually transported into cells and metabolized
● Leaves solute-free water to correct extracellular fluid hyperosmolarity

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Contrast the parameters used to calculate osmolarity (osmoticity) versus those used for tonicity.
back:
● Osmolarity: Total osmoles per liter of solution (permeant and impermeant)
● Tonicity: Effective osmotic pressure determined only by impermeant solutes that force water movement across membranes

category: Describe difference between iso-osmotic, hyper- osmotic, hypo-osmotic fluids
front: Define the term 'Hyperosmotic' as it relates to the renal medullary interstitium during water conservation.
back:
● Total solute concentration exceeds 300 mOsm/L
● Reaches up to 1200-1400 mOsm/L in the inner medulla
● Created by the countercurrent multiplier to facilitate water reabsorption

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: In ischemic tissues, intracellular edema occurs because the depression of metabolic systems prevents the [___] pump from maintaining ionic gradients, leading to sodium accumulation and osmotic water inflow.
back:
• Na+/K+ ATPase pump
• Inhibition causes Na+ to leak in and stay in
• Osmotic pressure draws water into cells

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: A 5-year-old child presents with periorbital edema and 'frothy' urine. Laboratory findings reveal severe proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia. Identify the primary Starling force alteration causing this extracellular edema.
back:
• Decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure (πc)
• Results from massive loss of albumin in urine
• Seen in Nephrotic Syndrome

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
coreConcept: Hormonal Regulation of Edema in Heart Failure
front: Explain the role of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) in the progression of extracellular edema during heart failure.
back:
• Reduced cardiac output lowers renal blood flow
• Stimulates Renin release and Angiotensin II formation
• Causes renal salt and water retention, expanding extracellular volume

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
coreConcept: Gel vs. Free Fluid Interstitial Dynamics
front: Contrast the physical state of interstitial fluid in normal conditions versus pitting edema.
back:
• Normal: Fluid is bound in a 'proteoglycan gel' (gel form) with minimal free water
• Pitting: Fluid exceeds gel capacity, forming 'free fluid' channels that flow when pressed

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: State the primary reason why acute, severe hyponatremia (<115 mmol/L) can lead to rapid neurological deterioration and herniation.
back:
• Osmotic shift of water from ECF to ICF
• Causes rapid brain cell swelling (intracellular edema)
• Rigid skull restricts expansion, leading to compression

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Lymphedema is characterized by a failure to remove [___] from the interstitium, which raises the interstitial colloid osmotic pressure and draws more fluid out of capillaries.
back:
• Plasma proteins
• Blockage prevents protein return to circulation
• Example: Filarial infections or post-mastectomy

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: A patient with liver cirrhosis presents with ascites. Beyond decreased albumin synthesis, identify the specific hemodynamic pressure change in the portal system contributing to this localized edema.
back:
• Increased portal capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc)
• Caused by liver fibrosis compressing portal drainage
• Leads to fluid transudation into the abdominal cavity

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Describe the physiological 'washdown' of interstitial protein as a safety factor against edema development.
back:
• Increased filtration increases lymph flow
• Lymphatics remove proteins faster than they are filtered
• Lowers interstitial colloid osmotic pressure, reducing net filtration force

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Contrast the clinical manifestation of left-sided heart failure with that of right-sided heart failure regarding edema location.
back:
• Left-sided: High pulmonary vascular pressures cause pulmonary edema
• Right-sided: High systemic venous pressures cause peripheral edema (legs/sacrum)

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: List the three major safety factors and their specific numerical contributions that prevent the interstitium from accumulating fluid until capillary pressure doubles.
back:
• Low tissue compliance (negative pressure): 3 mmHg
• Increased lymph flow: 7 mmHg
• Protein washdown: 7 mmHg
• Total: 17 mmHg

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: In tissues where blood flow is severely reduced, the failure of the [___] leads to intracellular sodium accumulation and subsequent osmotic cellular swelling.
back:
• Na+-K+ ATPase pump (Sodium-potassium pump)
• Failure results from ATP depletion during ischemia
• Leads to intracellular edema and potential cell death

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: A child presents with generalized edema and frothy urine. Labs show heavy proteinuria and plasma protein <2.5 g/dl. Identify the primary physiological cause of this extracellular edema.
back:
• Decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure
• Excessive filtration exceeds lymphatic return capacity
• Characteristic of Nephrotic Syndrome

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Explain the role of cell membrane permeability in the development of intracellular edema during inflammation.
back:
• Inflammation increases cell membrane permeability
• Allows sodium and other ions to leak into the cell
• Water follows ions osmotically, causing cellular swelling

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Contrast the physical state of the interstitium in 'Pitting Edema' versus 'Non-pitting Edema'.
back:
• Pitting: Excess free fluid in the interstitium that can be displaced by pressure.
• Non-pitting: Occurs when cells swell (intracellular) or fluid is clotted with fibrinogen in the interstitium.

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: List the three conditions specifically noted for causing intracellular swelling.
back:
• Hyponatremia (osmotic shift)
• Depression of metabolic systems (pump failure)
• Lack of adequate nutrition to cells (ischemia)

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Lymphedema caused by the nematode [___] leads to severe elephantiasis by blocking the return of proteins and fluid to the circulation.
back:
• Wuchereria bancrofti
• Causes extreme elevation of interstitial colloid osmotic pressure
• Results in massive localized extracellular edema

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: A patient with liver cirrhosis presents with massive ascites. Explain the two-fold mechanism contributing to this localized extracellular fluid accumulation.
back:
• Decreased albumin synthesis (lowers plasma colloid osmotic pressure)
• Portal venous hypertension (increases gastrointestinal capillary hydrostatic pressure)

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Explain how left-sided heart failure triggers life-threatening pulmonary edema without initial right-sided involvement.
back:
• Weakened left ventricle causes blood buildup in pulmonary veins
• Drastic rise in pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure
• Filtration rate into lungs exceeds lymphatic drainage capacity

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Contrast the effect of hyponatremia versus hypernatremia on neuronal volume.
back:
• Hyponatremia: Low ECF osmolarity forces water into neurons (Cell Swelling/Edema)
• Hypernatremia: High ECF osmolarity draws water out of neurons (Cell Shrinkage)

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: State the three major 'Safety Factors' that normally prevent the development of severe extracellular edema.
back:
• Low compliance of interstitium (negative pressure range)
• Increased lymph flow (up to 50-fold)
• Washdown of interstitial fluid proteins (lowers interstitial colloid osmotic pressure)

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Intracellular edema can occur during [___], which creates an osmotic gradient that drives water from the extracellular fluid into the cells.
back:
* Hyponatremia (decreased plasma sodium concentration).
* This leads to cell swelling and is particularly dangerous in brain cells.

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: A 55-year-old male with a history of acute limb ischemia develops severe localized swelling in the affected leg. What is the underlying pathophysiology of this intracellular edema?
back:
* Decreased blood flow leads to lack of oxygen and nutrients.
* Failure of Na+-K+ ATPase pumps due to ATP depletion.
* Intracellular Na+ accumulation causes osmotic water entry.

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Explain the role of 'interstitial protein washdown' as a physiological safety factor against the development of extracellular edema.
back:
* Increased lymph flow removes proteins from the interstitium.
* This lowers interstitial colloid osmotic pressure.
* Reduced osmotic pull decreases net capillary filtration.

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Contrast the physical state of the interstitium in pitting edema versus non-pitting edema.
back:
* Pitting: Accumulation of 'free fluid' that exceeds the capacity of the proteoglycan gel.
* Non-pitting: Occurs when tissue cells swell (intracellular) or fluid is clotted with fibrinogen in the interstitium.

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Enumerate the three primary Starling force alterations that lead to excessive capillary filtration and extracellular edema.
back:
* Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc).
* Decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure (pi-c).
* Increased capillary filtration coefficient (Kf) due to permeability.

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: In nephrotic syndrome, the primary cause of generalized extracellular edema is the loss of [___] in the urine, which reduces plasma oncotic pressure.
back:
* Plasma proteins (specifically albumin).
* This shifts the Starling balance toward filtration into the interstitium.

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: A patient with long-standing liver cirrhosis presents with massive abdominal swelling (ascites). Which two specific hemodynamic changes contribute to this extracellular fluid accumulation?
back:
* Decreased albumin synthesis (lowers colloid osmotic pressure).
* Portal hypertension (increases capillary hydrostatic pressure in abdominal viscera).

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: How does right-sided heart failure cause peripheral extracellular edema compared to the mechanism of pulmonary edema in left-sided heart failure?
back:
* Right-sided: Increases systemic venous and capillary hydrostatic pressure.
* Left-sided: Increases pulmonary venous and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, leading to fluid in lungs.

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Distinguish between the mechanism of edema caused by burns versus that caused by histamine release in allergic reactions.
back:
* Burns: Both increased capillary permeability and loss of proteins from denuded skin.
* Histamine: Primarily increases capillary permeability by dilating arterioles and opening endothelial gaps.

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Which parasitic infection is a major cause of lymphedema and elephantiasis in tropical regions by obstructing lymphatic drainage?
back:
* Filarial nematodes (e.g., Wuchereria bancrofti).
* These worms live in lymph nodes and block the return of fluid and proteins.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: The fundamental technique used to measure the volume of a body fluid compartment by analyzing the dilution of a known mass of indicator is the [___] principle.
back:
• Indicator-dilution principle.
• Based on the conservation of mass.
• Volume = Total Mass / Final Concentration.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: A medical researcher requires a marker to measure the total body water in a study participant. Which isotopes or lipid-soluble substances are specifically used for this measurement?
back:
• Radioactive water (Tritium, 3H2O).
• Heavy water (Deuterium, 2H2O).
• Antipyrine (highly lipid-soluble; penetrates all compartments).

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: Explain the three properties an indicator must possess to provide an accurate measurement of a specific body fluid compartment.
back:
• Indicator must disperse evenly throughout the target compartment.
• It must be confined strictly to the compartment being measured.
• It must not be metabolized or excreted during the measurement period.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: Contrast the dispersal characteristics required for indicators used to measure Extracellular Fluid (ECF) volume versus those used for Plasma Volume (PV).
back:
• ECF Indicators (Inulin, 22Na): Must cross capillary membranes but remain excluded from cells.
• PV Indicators (Evans Blue, 125I-albumin): Must remain within the vascular system and not leak into the interstitium.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: Specify the calculation used to determine the Intracellular Fluid (ICF) volume when direct indicator measurement is impossible.
back:
• Subtract the measured Extracellular Fluid (ECF) volume from the Total Body Water (TBW).
• ICF = TBW - ECF.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: To determine plasma volume, a clinician can use serum albumin labeled with radioactive iodine or a specific dye that binds avidly to plasma proteins known as [___].
back:
• Evans blue dye.
• Also known as T-1824.
• Binds to albumin to remain in the vascular space.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: A patient is found to have a plasma volume of 3 Liters and a measured hematocrit of 0.40. Calculate the total blood volume for this patient.
back:
• Blood Volume = Plasma Volume / (1 - Hematocrit).
• 3 / (1 - 0.40) = 5 Liters.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: Describe the mechanism of the direct isotope method for measuring total blood volume without relying on the hematocrit calculation.
back:
• Red blood cells are labeled with Radioactive Chromium (51Cr).
• Labeled cells are injected and allowed to equilibrate in the circulation.
• Final blood radioactivity is analyzed to calculate total volume.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: Distinguish between the indirect methods used to calculate Interstitial Fluid (ISF) volume and Intracellular Fluid (ICF) volume.
back:
• ISF Volume = Extracellular Fluid (ECF) volume minus Plasma Volume.
• ICF Volume = Total Body Water (TBW) minus ECF volume.

category: Enlist the methods to measure body fluids volumes
front: Enlist three specific substances used as indicators to define the 'sodium space' or 'inulin space' in the extracellular compartment.
back:
• Inulin.
• Radioactive Sodium (22Na).
• Thiosulfate ion or Radioactive Iothalamate.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: The total estimated safety factor against edema formation in peripheral tissues, which allows capillary pressure to rise significantly before marked fluid accumulation occurs, is [___] mmHg.
back:
• 17 mmHg.
• Calculated as the sum of 3 mmHg (low compliance), 7 mmHg (lymph flow), and 7 mmHg (protein washdown).

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: A patient with mild heart failure does not show signs of edema despite a slight increase in capillary pressure. This physiological resilience is due to the interstitium existing in a [___] state, preventing free fluid flow.
back:
• Gel state.
• Fluid is bound in a proteoglycan meshwork.
• Maintains low compliance in the negative pressure range.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Explain the role of 'washdown' of interstitial fluid protein concentration as a safety factor against edema.
back:
• Increased filtration increases lymph flow.
• Lymph removes proteins faster than they can leak out of capillaries.
• This lowers interstitial colloid osmotic pressure, reducing the net filtration force.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Contrast the compliance of the interstitium when interstitial fluid pressure is in the negative range versus the positive range.
back:
• Negative Range: Low compliance; small volume changes cause large pressure rises (3 mmHg safety factor).
• Positive Range: High compliance; large amounts of free fluid accumulate easily.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Identify the primary mechanism through which the lymphatic system provides a safety factor of approximately 7 mmHg against edema.
back:
• Increased lymph flow (10- to 50-fold).
• Returns excess filtered fluid and leaked proteins to the circulation, preventing positive pressure buildup.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: The safety factor against edema provided by the low compliance of the interstitium when pressure is in the sub-atmospheric range is [___] mmHg.
back:
• 3 mmHg.
• Represents the increase required to shift pressure from -3 mmHg (normal) to 0 mmHg (positive).

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: A researcher notes that when a patient's interstitial fluid pressure exceeds 0 mmHg, 'pitting' edema occurs. Explain the physical change in the interstitium that allows this to happen.
back:
• Pressure becomes positive, causing high compliance.
• Proteoglycan filaments are pushed apart.
• Fluid accumulates as 'free fluid' rather than bound gel.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Describe how the proteoglycan filaments specifically prevent edema through their function as a 'spacer' and 'brush pile'.
back:
• Act as elastic resistance to compression.
• Prevent fluid from flowing too easily through tissues (prevents gravitation of fluid to lower limbs during standing).

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Contrast the physical state of interstitial fluid in pitting edema versus non-pitting edema.
back:
• Pitting: Free fluid accumulates in the interstitium (positive pressure range).
• Non-pitting: Occurs when tissue cells swell (intracellular) or fluid in interstitium is clotted with fibrinogen.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Specify the normal interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure in loose subcutaneous tissue that acts as a baseline suction.
back:
• -3 mmHg (sub-atmospheric).
• This negative pressure keeps the tissues held together and maintains the low-compliance safety range.

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Intracellular swelling occurs when tissue [___] reduces oxygen delivery, causing failure of ionic pumps and subsequent accumulation of sodium inside the cell.
back:
* **Ischemia** (or decreased blood flow)
* Leads to Na+/K+ ATPase pump failure
* Results in osmotic water entry into the cell

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: A 5-year-old child presents with facial puffiness, generalized edema, and massive proteinuria. Identify the primary Starling force alteration driving this extracellular fluid accumulation.
back:
* **Decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure**
* Caused by loss of albumin in urine (Nephrotic syndrome)
* Reduces the force that pulls fluid back into capillaries

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Explain the role of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) in the development of extracellular edema during heart failure.
back:
* Reduced arterial pressure triggers renin release
* Increased Angiotensin II and Aldosterone promote salt and water retention
* This expands extracellular volume, further raising capillary hydrostatic pressure

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Contrast the physical nature of 'pitting edema' with 'non-pitting edema' regarding the interstitial fluid.
back:
* **Pitting**: Excess 'free fluid' in the interstitium that moves upon pressure
* **Non-pitting**: Swelling of tissue cells (intracellular) or fluid clotted with fibrinogen

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Identify the specific mechanism by which lymphatic obstruction, such as in filariasis, leads to extracellular edema.
back:
* Failure to return leaked proteins to blood
* Raises interstitial colloid osmotic pressure
* Draws water out of capillaries into the tissue spaces

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: In the Starling equation, an increase in the [___] is the primary cause of localized extracellular edema during acute inflammation or allergic reactions.
back:
* **Capillary permeability** (or Filtration Coefficient $K_f$)
* Mediated by histamine or toxins
* Allows proteins and water to leak into the interstitium

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: A chronic alcoholic presents with ascites and esophageal varices. List the two primary Starling force changes contributing to this localized extracellular edema.
back:
* **Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure** (Portal hypertension)
* **Decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure** (Failure of liver to synthesize albumin)

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Describe how acute hyponatremia leads to life-threatening brain edema.
back:
* Decreased extracellular osmolarity creates a gradient
* Water moves from extracellular fluid into brain cells via osmosis
* Causes intracellular swelling (edema) and potential herniation

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Distinguish the primary triggers of intracellular edema from those of extracellular edema.
back:
* **Intracellular**: Metabolic depression (pump failure), membrane inflammation, or hyponatremia
* **Extracellular**: Increased capillary filtration or lymphatic blockage

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Enumerate the three major safety factors that normally prevent the accumulation of fluid in the interstitium.
back:
* **Low tissue compliance** in the negative pressure range
* **Increased lymph flow** (10-50 fold increase)
* **Washdown of interstitial proteins**

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: The primary safety factor preventing edema when interstitial fluid pressure remains in the negative range is the [___] of the interstitium.
back:
• Low compliance
• Small volume increases cause large pressure rises
• This opposes further capillary filtration
• Provides a ~3 mm Hg safety factor

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: A patient presents with swelling where thumb pressure leaves a temporary indentation. This 'pitting' occurs because the interstitial fluid has transitioned from [___] to [___].
back:
• Gel form (bound to proteoglycans)
• Free fluid (liquid) form
• Occurs when interstitial pressure becomes positive
• Safety factor is lost as compliance increases

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Explain the role of the lymphatic system as a safety factor against excessive interstitial fluid accumulation.
back:
• Increases flow 10- to 50-fold
• Carries away excess filtered fluid and proteins
• Prevents interstitial pressure from reaching the positive range
• Provides a ~7 mm Hg safety factor

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Contrast the compliance of the renal/subcutaneous interstitium in the negative pressure range versus the positive pressure range.
back:
• Negative Range: Low compliance; resists fluid accumulation
• Positive Range: High compliance; allows massive 'free fluid' accumulation
• Transition point: ~0 mm Hg (atmospheric pressure)

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Calculate the total theoretical safety factor (in mm Hg) that prevents edema in peripheral tissues.
back:
• Total: ~17 mm Hg
• Components: 3 mmHg (low compliance) + 7 mmHg (lymph flow) + 7 mmHg (protein washdown)

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: During increased capillary filtration, the interstitial fluid protein concentration decreases via a process known as [___].
back:
• Washdown (or Washout) of proteins
• Caused by lymphatics removing proteins faster than capillaries leak them
• Decreases interstitial colloid osmotic pressure ($π_{if}$)
• Provides a ~7 mm Hg safety factor

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: A patient with early heart failure experiences a rise in mean capillary pressure from 17 to 25 mm Hg. Why might they still show no clinical signs of edema?
back:
• Total safety factor is ~17 mm Hg
• Capillary pressure must rise above ~34 mm Hg to cause marked edema
• Compensatory lymph flow and protein washdown are active

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Describe how proteoglycan filaments (interstitial gel) prevent the rapid flow of fluid to lower body parts upon standing.
back:
• Fluid is trapped in a 'brush-pile' meshwork
• Prevents free fluid movement via elastic resistance
• Keeps fluid evenly distributed between cells
• Only fails when pressure becomes positive

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Contrast the 'pitting' feature of interstitial edema with 'non-pitting' edema caused by intracellular swelling.
back:
• Pitting: Excess free fluid pushes aside proteoglycans
• Non-pitting: Fluid is inside cells or clotted by fibrinogen
• Non-pitting often implies more severe tissue damage or inflammation

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Identify the safety factor that specifically reduces the net filtration force across the capillary membrane by altering $π_{if}$.
back:
• Washdown of interstitial fluid proteins
• Lower $π_{if}$ reduces the 'pull' of fluid out of capillaries
• Increases the effectiveness of other safety mechanisms

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: In states of tissue ischemia, the failure of the [___] leads to intracellular sodium accumulation and subsequent osmotic cellular swelling.
back:
• Na+-K+ ATPase pump
• Absence of ATP/nutrients prevents sodium extrusion
• Common prelude to tissue death

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: A 4-year-old child presents with generalized pitting edema and frothy urine. Labs show severe hypoalbuminemia (<2.5 g/dl). Identify the primary physiological cause of this extracellular edema.
back:
• Decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure
• Result of urinary protein loss (Nephrotic Syndrome)
• Leads to excessive capillary filtration

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Explain the role of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) in the progression of extracellular edema during heart failure.
back:
• Reduced GFR and arterial pressure stimulate renin release
• Angiotensin II and Aldosterone promote renal Na+ and H2O retention
• This increases blood volume and capillary hydrostatic pressure

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Contrast the physiological mechanism of 'pitting edema' found in cardiac failure with 'non-pitting edema' seen in lymphedema or inflammation.
back:
• Pitting: Excess free fluid in interstitium exceeding gel compliance
• Non-pitting: Fluid bound in proteoglycan meshwork or clotted with fibrinogen
• Intracellular swelling also presents as non-pitting

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Identify the two general categories of abnormalities that result in extracellular edema.
back:
• Abnormal leakage of fluid from plasma to interstitium (excess filtration)
• Failure of lymphatics to return fluid/protein from interstitium (Lymphedema)

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: The total safety factor preventing edema in peripheral tissues, which allows capillary pressure to nearly double before marked swelling occurs, is approximately [___] mm Hg.
back:
• 17 mm Hg
• Components: Low tissue compliance (3), Lymph flow (7), and Protein washdown (7)

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: A patient with liver cirrhosis presents with massive ascites. How does portal hypertension specifically contribute to this localized extracellular edema?
back:
• Increases capillary hydrostatic pressure in the intestinal/mesenteric bed
• Fibrosis compresses portal venous drainage
• Causes fluid transudation into the abdominal cavity

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Describe the 'washdown of interstitial fluid protein' mechanism as a defense against edema.
back:
• Increased filtration raises lymph flow
• Lymphatics remove proteins faster than they can leak out
• Lowered interstitial colloid osmotic pressure reduces net filtration forces

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Contrast the primary anatomical site of edema in Left-sided Heart Failure versus Right-sided Heart Failure.
back:
• Left-sided: Pulmonary edema (high pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure)
• Right-sided: Peripheral/Systemic edema (venous congestion in body tissues)

category: Enumerate causes of Intracellular and extracellular edema Integrate with Medicine
front: Identify three specific conditions that promote intracellular swelling (intracellular edema).
back:
• Hyponatremia (osmotic shift into cells)
• Depressed metabolic systems/ischemia (ionic pump failure)
• Inflammation (increased membrane permeability to ions)

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: The total safety factor that must be overcome before significant interstitial edema occurs is approximately [___] mm Hg.
back:
• 17 mm Hg
• This is the sum of low tissue compliance (3 mmHg), increased lymph flow (7 mmHg), and protein washdown (7 mmHg).

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: A 50-year-old patient with early heart failure experiences a 10 mm Hg rise in peripheral capillary hydrostatic pressure but shows no clinical swelling. Identify the underlying physiological concept preventing fluid accumulation in this case.
back:
• Safety factors against edema
• These mechanisms provide a cumulative 17 mm Hg buffer against increased filtration forces before edema becomes manifest.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Explain the role of 'washdown of interstitial fluid protein' in preventing edema formation.
back:
• Increased filtration raises interstitial pressure, boosting lymph flow
• Lymph removes proteins faster than they filter through capillaries
• This reduces interstitial colloid osmotic pressure, decreasing the net filtration force.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Contrast the compliance of the interstitium in the negative pressure range versus the positive pressure range.
back:
• Negative range: Low compliance (small volume changes cause large pressure rises, opposing filtration)
• Positive range: High compliance (large fluid volumes accumulate with minimal pressure increase; safety factor is lost).

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Identify the magnitude of the safety factor provided specifically by the increase in lymph flow.
back:
• Approximately 7 mm Hg
• This results from the 10- to 50-fold increase in lymphatic drainage that occurs when fluid begins to accumulate.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: In normal tissues with negative interstitial pressure, fluid is held primarily in a [___] form by proteoglycan filaments, ensuring low compliance.
back:
• Gel
• This state prevents fluid from flowing easily and maintains the safety factor by resisting volume expansion.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: A patient undergoes a radical mastectomy with extensive lymph node removal and develops severe lymphedema. Which specific safety factor was compromised by this procedure?
back:
• Increased lymph flow
• Removal of vessels prevents the 10-50 fold drainage increase that normally provides a 7 mm Hg safety buffer.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: How does the 'low compliance' of the interstitium in the negative pressure range technically function as a safety factor?
back:
• Interstitial pressure is normally -3 mmHg (suction)
• Any volume increase causes pressure to rise toward 0 rapidly
• This rising hydrostatic pressure directly opposes further capillary filtration.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Contrast the physiological consequences of fluid accumulation in the 'gel' state versus the 'free fluid' state.
back:
• Gel state: Fluid is bound to proteoglycans; occurs in negative pressure range; prevents pitting
• Free fluid state: Occurs in positive pressure range; pushes filaments apart; results in pitting edema.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: List the three major safety factors that prevent the development of edema.
back:
• 1. Low interstitial compliance (in the negative pressure range)
• 2. Increased lymph flow (10-50 fold increase)
• 3. Washdown of interstitial proteins (reduces interstitial colloid pressure).

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: The total safety factor that must be overcome before significant extracellular edema develops is approximately [___] mm Hg.
back:
• 17 mm Hg.
• Comprised of: Low compliance (3 mmHg), Lymph flow (7 mmHg), and Protein washdown (7 mmHg).

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: A patient's capillary hydrostatic pressure rises from 17 to 30 mm Hg, yet no clinical edema is observed. Explain the primary tissue-level defense mechanism involved.
back:
• Low compliance of the interstitium.
• In the negative pressure range, small volume changes cause large pressure increases.
• This opposes further filtration into the tissues.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Explain the role of the 'protein washdown' mechanism in preventing interstitial fluid accumulation.
back:
• Increased lymph flow carries away proteins faster than they can leak from capillaries.
• Reduces interstitial colloid osmotic pressure.
• Decreases the net filtration force, favoring reabsorption.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Contrast the underlying physical cause of pitting edema with that of non-pitting edema.
back:
• Pitting: Accumulation of mobile 'free fluid' that pushes proteoglycan filaments apart.
• Non-pitting: Occurs when cells swell (intracellular) or fluid clots with fibrinogen.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: How do proteoglycan filaments specifically prevent fluid from pooling in the lower extremities when a person stands?
back:
• Act as a spacer and meshwork brush pile.
• Prevent fluid from flowing easily through tissue spaces.
• Trap fluid in a 'gel' form with high resistance to compression.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: The safety factor against edema provided by the ability of lymph flow to increase 10- to 50-fold is calculated to be [___] mm Hg.
back:
• 7 mm Hg.
• Lymphatics return leaked proteins and fluid back to the circulation.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: A 40-year-old male with a Wuchereria bancrofti infection presents with elephantiasis. Which specific safety factor against edema is primarily compromised?
back:
• Increased lymph flow safety factor.
• Blockage of lymph nodes prevents the return of proteins and fluid.
• Causes a rise in interstitial colloid osmotic pressure.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Explain why the interstitium becomes highly compliant once the interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure enters the positive range.
back:
• 'Free fluid' accumulates and pushes proteoglycan filaments apart.
• The elastic resistance of the gel is overcome.
• Large volumes of fluid can enter with minimal further pressure rise.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Distinguish between the interstitial 'low compliance' and 'high compliance' ranges in terms of fluid pressure values.
back:
• Low compliance: Negative pressure range (typically -3 to 0 mm Hg).
• High compliance: Positive pressure range (>0 mm Hg).

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: State the average normal interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure in loose subcutaneous tissue that provides initial safety 'suction'.
back:
• -3 mm Hg.
• This negative pressure helps hold tissues together and provides a 3 mmHg buffer before positive pressure edema begins.

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: The kidney facilitates long-term regulation of arterial pressure primarily by adjusting the excretion of [___] and water.
back:
• Sodium (Na+)
• Achieved via the pressure natriuresis and pressure diuresis mechanisms
• Regulated by the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: A patient with end-stage renal disease presents with a hematocrit of 22%. The primary hormonal deficiency causing this condition is [___].
back:
• Erythropoietin (EPO)
• Secreted by renal interstitial cells in response to hypoxia
• Stimulates RBC production by hematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: Explain the role of the kidney in activating vitamin D and its subsequent effect on calcium homeostasis.
back:
• Hydroxylates 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 at the '1' position
• Forms 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (Calcitriol)
• Essential for calcium deposition in bone and intestinal absorption

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: Contrast the renal handling of urea with that of creatinine regarding their utility as markers for Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR).
back:
• Creatinine: Freely filtered, not reabsorbed; provides a more accurate estimate of GFR
• Urea: Freely filtered but significantly reabsorbed (approx. 50%); influenced by protein intake and hydration

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: Identify the specific metabolic process used by the kidneys to add glucose to the blood during periods of prolonged starvation.
back:
• Gluconeogenesis
• Synthesizes glucose from amino acids and other precursors
• Renal capacity for this pathway rivals that of the liver during fasting

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: The kidneys are the sole route for eliminating non-volatile acids produced by protein metabolism, specifically [___] and phosphoric acid.
back:
• Sulfuric acid
• Secreted as H+ ions into the tubular lumen
• Excretion involves urinary buffers like ammonia and phosphate

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: A 60-year-old male with chronic renal failure presents with spontaneous fractures. This condition results from the failure of the kidney to excrete [___].
back:
• Phosphate (HPO4 2-)
• Retention causes secondary hyperparathyroidism
• High PTH leads to calcium mobilization from bones and subsequent demineralization

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: Describe the physiological mechanism triggered by the kidneys to regulate body fluid osmolality during a water deficit.
back:
• Secretion of Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH/Vasopressin)
• Increases water permeability in distal and collecting tubules
• Results in the excretion of a small volume of hyperosmotic urine

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: Contrast the renal short-term and long-term mechanisms for regulating systemic arterial pressure.
back:
• Short-term: Secretion of renin leading to the formation of vasoactive Angiotensin II
• Long-term: Adjustment of sodium and water excretion via pressure natriuresis

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: List the four primary metabolic waste products that are almost exclusively eliminated from the body via the kidneys.
back:
• Urea (from amino acids)
• Creatinine (from muscle)
• Uric Acid (from nucleic acids)
• Bilirubin (from hemoglobin breakdown)

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: The kidneys help maintain calcium and phosphate homeostasis by converting vitamin D into its active form, [___], through hydroxylation at the number 1 position.
back:
• Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3)
• Essential for intestinal calcium absorption
• Facilitates normal calcium deposition in bones

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: A patient with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on maintenance hemodialysis presents with a normocytic, normochromic anemia. What is the primary hormonal deficiency causing this condition?
back:
• Erythropoietin (EPO) deficiency
• EPO is secreted by renal cells in response to hypoxia
• It stimulates red blood cell production in bone marrow

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: Explain the dual mechanism by which the kidneys participate in arterial pressure regulation.
back:
• Long-term: Adjusting sodium and water excretion (pressure natriuresis)
• Short-term: Secretion of renin, leading to the formation of the vasoconstrictor Angiotensin II

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: Contrast the kidney's role in gluconeogenesis during prolonged fasting versus its metabolic waste removal function.
back:
• Gluconeogenesis: Synthesizes glucose from amino acids (rivals liver capacity)
• Waste Excretion: Eliminates urea (protein metabolism), creatinine (muscle), and uric acid (nucleic acids)

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: Identify the nonvolatile acids that are uniquely eliminated from the body through renal excretion rather than respiratory expiration.
back:
• Sulfuric acid and Phosphoric acid
• Generated via protein metabolism
• These cannot be converted to CO2 for lung excretion

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: The kidneys regulate body fluid osmolality and electrolyte concentrations primarily by matching [___] to [___] precisely.
back:
• Intake (ingestion/metabolic production)
• Output (excretion/metabolic consumption)
• Maintains stable internal environment for cellular activity

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: A patient presents with unintended ingestion of a lipid-soluble pesticide. How do the kidneys manage the excretion of such foreign chemicals and toxins?
back:
• Primarily by filtering the plasma
• Active secretion from peritubular capillaries into the tubules
• Poor tubular reabsorption ensures toxins remain in the filtrate

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: Describe how the kidney's high glomerular filtration rate (GFR) serves as a critical mechanism for waste management.
back:
• Allows entire plasma volume (3L) to be processed ~60 times/day
• Enables rapid removal of poorly reabsorbed wastes (urea, creatinine)
• Permits precise, rapid control of fluid volume/composition

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: Contrast the renal handling of metabolic wastes like creatinine with nutritional substances like glucose.
back:
• Creatinine: Freely filtered but not reabsorbed; 100% excreted
• Glucose: Freely filtered but 100% reabsorbed via secondary active transport in healthy kidneys

category: Explain the functions of the kidney
front: List the four primary sources of metabolic waste products eliminated by the kidneys.
back:
• Urea: Amino acid metabolism
• Creatinine: Muscle creatine
• Uric Acid: Nucleic acid metabolism
• Bilirubin: Hemoglobin breakdown

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: The total safety factor that must be overcome before significant edema develops in peripheral tissues is approximately [___] mm Hg.
back:
• 17 mm Hg
• Consists of: Low tissue compliance (3 mmHg), lymph flow (7 mmHg), and protein washdown (7 mmHg).

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: A patient presents with 'pitting edema' in the ankles. This clinical sign indicates that the interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure has transitioned from its normal negative range into the [___].
back:
• Positive pressure range
• This causes 'free fluid' to accumulate outside the proteoglycan gel, which flows easily when pressure is applied.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Describe the physiological 'washdown' of interstitial proteins as a safety factor against edema.
back:
• Increased filtration raises interstitial pressure, boosting lymph flow.
• Lymphatics remove proteins faster than they leak from capillaries.
• This lowers interstitial colloid osmotic pressure, reducing the net filtration force.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: A patient with severe inflammation has non-pitting edema, whereas a patient with heart failure has pitting edema. Contrast the underlying interstitial characteristics of these two states.
back:
• Pitting: High 'free fluid' in the interstitium due to positive hydrostatic pressure.
• Non-pitting: Occurs when cells swell (intracellular) or when interstitial fluid is clotted with fibrinogen.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Identify the numerical contribution of increased lymph flow to the body's total safety factor against edema.
back:
• 7 mm Hg
• This is achieved by the ability of lymphatics to increase flow 10- to 50-fold when fluid begins to accumulate.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: In normal loose subcutaneous tissue, the interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure averages about [___] mm Hg, creating a 'suction' that holds tissues together.
back:
• -3 mm Hg
• As long as pressure is negative, tissue compliance remains very low, preventing fluid accumulation.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: A researcher observes that a subject's capillary hydrostatic pressure rises by 10 mm Hg, yet no edema occurs. Explain which concept prevents fluid accumulation in this instance.
back:
• The 17 mmHg total safety factor buffer.
• Edema only occurs when the rise in pressure exceeds the combined safety factors of the interstitium and lymphatics.

category: Describe safety factors that prevent edema
front: Explain the specific role of the 'interstitial gel' (proteoglycan meshwork) in preventing edema during brief changes in posture.
back:
• Traps water to prevent it from flowing easily through tissues.
• Offers elastic resistance to compression.
