• Uninhibited: Brain/cord injury (inhibitory tract destruction), causing hyperactive reflex incontinence.

category: Write the causes, pathophysiology, and features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder
front: Name the two specific central nervous system regions where damage most commonly results in an uninhibited neurogenic bladder.
back:
• Brain stem
• Spinal cord (partial damage/interruption of descending inhibitory tracts).

category: Write the causes, pathophysiology, and features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder
front: The abnormality of micturition characterized by frequent and uncontrolled voiding due to a loss of inhibitory signals from the brain is [___].
back:
• Uninhibited neurogenic bladder
• Caused by partial damage to the spinal cord or brain stem
• Results in hyper-excitable sacral micturition centers.

category: Write the causes, pathophysiology, and features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder
coreConcept: Clinical Presentation of Uninhibited Neurogenic Bladder
front: A 50-year-old patient with a history of a brain stem lesion presents with frequent, uncontrollable urination. He reports that even minimal fluid intake triggers an immediate, forceful urge to void. Diagnosis?
back:
• Uninhibited neurogenic bladder
• Interruption of inhibitory pathways allows facilitative signals to dominate
• Small urine volumes trigger full micturition reflexes.

category: Write the causes, pathophysiology, and features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder
front: Explain the neurophysiological state of the sacral micturition centers in a patient with an uninhibited neurogenic bladder.
back:
• Highly excitable state
• Constant stimulation by facilitative impulses moving down the spinal cord
• Lack of normal inhibitory modulation from higher brain centers.

category: Write the causes, pathophysiology, and features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder
front: Contrast the micturition pattern of an uninhibited neurogenic bladder with that of an automatic bladder following recovery from spinal shock.
back:
• Uninhibited: Frequent, uncontrollable urination; inhibitory signals partially lost.
• Automatic: Periodic, unannounced voiding; higher brain control is totally absent (complete cord transection).

category: Write the causes, pathophysiology, and features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder
front: Identify the specific neurological defect responsible for the pathophysiology of uninhibited neurogenic bladder.
back:
• Partial damage to the spinal cord or brain stem
• Selective interruption of inhibitory pathways
• Spares the facilitative pathways to the sacral centers.

category: Write the causes, pathophysiology, and features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder
front: In uninhibited neurogenic bladder, even a small quantity of urine elicits an uncontrollable [___] because of hyper-excitable sacral centers.
back:
• Micturition reflex
• Result of continuous facilitative impulses
• Causes frequent urination and loss of voluntary suppression.

category: Write the causes, pathophysiology, and features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder
front: A patient with partial spinal cord compression cannot voluntarily delay urination once the urge begins. Which mechanism explains this lack of control?
back:
• Loss of inhibitory brain stem/cortical signals
• Hyper-reflexic micturition contractions
• Inability of higher centers to suppress the sacral reflex arc.

category: Write the causes, pathophysiology, and features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder
front: How does the threshold for the micturition reflex change in a patient with uninhibited neurogenic bladder?
back:
• The threshold is significantly lowered
• Very low intravesical volumes trigger the self-regenerative reflex
• Results in low-capacity, high-frequency voiding.

category: Write the causes, pathophysiology, and features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder
front: Contrast the status of the sensory nerves in uninhibited neurogenic bladder versus atonic (tabetic) bladder.
back:
• Uninhibited: Sensory nerves are intact; trigger reflex hyper-excitability.
• Atonic: Sensory nerves are destroyed; bladder fills to capacity and overflows (no reflex).

category: Write the causes, pathophysiology, and features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder
front: List the three primary features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder.
back:
• Frequent urination
• Uncontrolled/involuntary micturition
• Triggered by small urine volumes.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: The net urinary excretion rate of any substance is mathematically represented by the formula: Excretion = [___] − Reabsorption + Secretion.
back:
• Glomerular Filtration
• Represents the initial step where protein-free fluid enters Bowman's capsule from the glomerular capillaries.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: A 5-year-old child presents with massive generalized edema and heavy proteinuria. Electron microscopy reveals flattening of podocyte foot processes. Identify the specific step of urine formation that is primarily compromised.
back:
• Glomerular Filtration
• Loss of the size and charge-selective barrier (podocyte effacement) allows plasma proteins like albumin to leak into the filtrate.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: Explain how the sodium-potassium ATPase pump on the basolateral membrane carries out the reabsorption of glucose in the proximal tubule.
back:
• Establishes a low intracellular Na+ concentration.
• Creates a gradient for Na+ to enter the cell via luminal SGLT proteins.
• Provides the energy to co-transport glucose against its concentration gradient.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: Contrast the physiological objectives of "Tubular Reabsorption" versus "Tubular Secretion" in the process of urine formation.
back:
• Reabsorption: Conserves vital substances (glucose, water, electrolytes) by moving them from filtrate back into peritubular blood.
• Secretion: Rapidly clears waste and toxins (H+, K+, drugs) from blood into the tubular lumen.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: List the three sequential renal processes that ensure a substance like para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) is cleared from the blood at a rate nearly equal to total renal plasma flow.
back:
• Glomerular Filtration (approximately 20% filtered).
• Tubular Secretion (remaining PAH moved from peritubular capillaries to lumen).
• Absence of Reabsorption.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: In the first step of urine formation, the specific ratio of glomerular filtration rate (GFR) to renal plasma flow (RPF) is termed the [___].
back:
• Filtration Fraction
• Indicates the percentage of plasma passing through the kidney that becomes glomerular filtrate (normally about 0.2).

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: A patient with chronic kidney disease presents with a serum potassium of 7.0 mEq/L. Which step of urine formation is specifically upregulated by aldosterone in the principal cells to address this hyperkalemia?
back:
• Tubular Secretion
• Aldosterone increases Na+/K+ ATPase activity and luminal K+ permeability (ROMK channels) to move K+ into the tubular fluid.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: Describe how the physical forces in peritubular capillaries facilitate the final stage of "Tubular Reabsorption."
back:
• High colloid osmotic pressure and low hydrostatic pressure create a net reabsorptive force (10 mmHg).
• This force drives bulk flow of water and solutes from the renal interstitium back into the blood.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: Contrast the filterability of small electrolytes like sodium with large molecules like albumin during the initial step of urine formation.
back:
• Sodium/Glucose: Freely filtered (Filterability = 1.0).
• Albumin: Heavily restricted (Filterability ≈ 0.005) due to large molecular size and negative electrostatic repulsion by basement membrane proteoglycans.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: Name the enzyme in the proximal tubular cells required to generate H+ for secretion and HCO3- for reabsorption.
back:
• Carbonic Anhydrase
• Catalyzes the reaction of CO2 and H2O to form H2CO3, which then dissociates into H+ and HCO3-.

category: Discuss the causes, pathophysiology, and features of automatic bladder
coreConcept: Neuro-anatomical site of automatic bladder lesions
front: In the development of an automatic bladder, spinal cord damage occurs [___] the sacral region, leaving the sacral cord segments (S2-S3) intact.
back:
• Above.
• Micturition reflexes can still occur but lack voluntary brain control.
• Typically follows recovery from the initial state of spinal shock.

category: Discuss the causes, pathophysiology, and features of automatic bladder
coreConcept: Initial Spinal Shock in Bladder Dysfunction
front: A patient sustains a mid-thoracic spinal cord injury. During the first few weeks, micturition reflexes are completely absent despite intact sacral segments. Identify this state and its pathophysiology.
back:
• Spinal shock.
• Caused by the sudden loss of facilitative impulses from the brain stem and cerebrum.
• Results in suppression of the autonomic spinal cord micturition reflex.

category: Discuss the causes, pathophysiology, and features of automatic bladder
front: Explain the role of bladder stretch receptors in the emptying mechanism of a patient with a fully developed automatic bladder.
back:
• Stretch receptors sense bladder wall tension and send signals to sacral segments.
• This initiates a self-regenerative micturition reflex.
• The bladder empties automatically without higher brain facilitation or inhibition.

category: Discuss the causes, pathophysiology, and features of automatic bladder
coreConcept: Upper vs. Lower Motor Neuron Bladder Lesions
front: Contrast the physiological status of the micturition reflex arc in 'automatic bladder' versus 'tabetic bladder' (atonic bladder).
back:
• Automatic: Reflex arc is fully intact but isolated from the brain.
• Tabetic: Sensory limb of the reflex arc is destroyed (e.g., syphilis).
• Automatic empties periodically; Tabetic results in overflow incontinence.

category: Discuss the causes, pathophysiology, and features of automatic bladder
front: Identify the primary clinical management objective for the bladder during the transition from spinal shock to the automatic bladder state.
back:
• Periodic catheterization.
• Essential to prevent bladder injury caused by overstretching.
• Protects the bladder wall until reflex excitability eventually returns.

category: Discuss the causes, pathophysiology, and features of automatic bladder
front: The automatic bladder is characterized by the return of [___] micturition reflexes that are no longer subject to voluntary cerebral control.
back:
• Spontaneous (or typical).
• Occurs once spinal shock subsides.
• Reflexes become periodic but remain unannounced/involuntary.

category: Discuss the causes, pathophysiology, and features of automatic bladder
coreConcept: Loss of Cerebral Control in Automatic Bladder
front: A 25-year-old male with a history of cervical spine fracture presents with periodic, involuntary voiding without any sensation of bladder fullness. What is the status of his higher brain centers regarding micturition?
back:
• Completely disconnected from the sacral reflex centers.
• Higher centers can no longer inhibit or facilitate the micturition reflex.
• The external sphincter cannot be voluntarily constricted to prevent voiding.

category: Discuss the causes, pathophysiology, and features of automatic bladder
coreConcept: Temporal Progression of Spinal Bladder Injuries
front: Describe how the micturition reflex changes during the weeks following a supra-sacral spinal cord injury.
back:
• Initially suppressed due to spinal shock.
• Excitability gradually increases over days to weeks.
• Eventually returns to full function, though isolated from cerebral coordination.

category: Discuss the causes, pathophysiology, and features of automatic bladder
front: Contrast the 'uninhibited neurogenic bladder' with the 'automatic bladder' in terms of the underlying neurological lesion.
back:
• Automatic: Complete supra-sacral cord transection; no brain-cord communication.
• Uninhibited: Partial cord/brainstem damage; loss of inhibitory signals only.
• Uninhibited involves hyper-excitable sacral centers and frequent, uncontrollable voiding.

category: Discuss the causes, pathophysiology, and features of automatic bladder
front: Following recovery from spinal shock, what determines when an automatic bladder will empty?
back:
• Intravesical pressure reaching the threshold level.
• Sufficient stretch receptor stimulation to trigger the local spinal reflex.
• It is purely pressure-dependent and lacks voluntary abdominal facilitation.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: Urine formation begins with [___], where protein-free fluid moves from the glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule.
back:
• Glomerular Filtration
• Filters ~180 L/day
• Excludes plasma proteins and cells due to size and negative charge.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: A 55-year-old diabetic patient presents with glucose in the urine (glycosuria). This occurs because the filtered load of glucose exceeds the capacity of which specific step in urine formation?
back:
• Tubular Reabsorption
• The transport maximum (Tm) of SGLT proteins is exceeded
• Excess glucose remains in the tubule and acts as an osmotic diuretic.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: Explain the role of the basolateral Na+-K+ ATPase pump in the tubular reabsorption step of urine formation.
back:
• Pumps Na+ out of the cell to create low intracellular Na+
• Establishes a negative intracellular potential (-70 mV)
• Provides the primary electrochemical gradient for Na+ and solute entry from the lumen.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: Contrast the direction of solute movement between the tubular reabsorption and tubular secretion steps of urine formation.
back:
• Reabsorption: From tubular lumen into peritubular capillaries (reclaims solutes)
• Secretion: From peritubular capillaries into the tubular lumen (adds to urine).

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: Enlist the three primary renal processes that determine the final rate of urinary excretion for any substance.
back:
• Glomerular filtration
• Tubular reabsorption
• Tubular secretion.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: In the proximal tubule, the reabsorption of organic nutrients like glucose and amino acids is coupled with sodium via [___].
back:
• Secondary Active Transport (Co-transport)
• Driven by the Na+ concentration gradient
• Extremely efficient, reclaiming virtually all filtered nutrients.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: A patient is given Para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) to estimate renal plasma flow. Identify the urine formation step that ensures nearly 90% of PAH is cleared from the blood even if it wasn't initially filtered.
back:
• Tubular Secretion
• Rapidly moves PAH from peritubular capillaries into the lumen
• Primary mechanism for clearing toxins and organic acids.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: Describe how the proximal tubule maintains isosmotic fluid while reabsorbing 65% of the filtered load.
back:
• High water permeability via Aquaporin-1 channels
• Water reabsorption follows Na+ reabsorption by osmosis
• Resulting osmolarity remains ~300 mOsm/L.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: Contrast the selectivity of glomerular filtration with that of tubular reabsorption.
back:
• Filtration: Relatively non-selective (filters everything except proteins/cells)
• Reabsorption: Highly selective (reclaims glucose but leaves urea).

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: State the mathematical relationship used to calculate the final urinary excretion rate of a substance.
back:
• Excretion = Filtration - Reabsorption + Secretion
• Filtration = GFR × Plasma concentration
• Reabsorption and secretion vary per substance.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: The urinary excretion rate of a substance is determined by the physiological formula: [___] − Tubular Reabsorption + Tubular Secretion.
back: Glomerular Filtration. This initial step involves the bulk movement of protein-free plasma from glomerular capillaries into Bowman’s capsule.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: A lab report indicates that a specific metabolic waste product has a renal clearance equal to the GFR. Identify the net involvement of tubular reabsorption and secretion for this substance.
back: Zero net reabsorption and secretion. The substance is handled solely by Glomerular Filtration, meaning the total filtered load is excreted (e.g., Creatinine).

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: Explain the role of 'Tubular Reabsorption' in the renal handling of nutritional substances like glucose and amino acids.
back: Complete Reabsorption. These substances are freely filtered but are entirely transported from the tubular lumen back into the peritubular capillaries, primarily in the proximal tubule.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: Contrast the movement direction and primary physiological goal of 'Tubular Reabsorption' versus 'Tubular Secretion'.
back:
• Reabsorption: Lumen to Peritubular Blood; conserves water and essential electrolytes.
• Secretion: Peritubular Blood to Lumen; aids rapid clearance of H+, K+, and metabolic toxins.

category: Enlist the steps of urine formation
front: Enlist the three primary physiological steps that result in the formation and final excretion of urine.
back:
1. Glomerular Filtration: Production of filtrate from plasma.
2. Tubular Reabsorption: Recovery of solutes/water into blood.
3. Tubular Secretion: Transport of additional wastes into the tubule.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: The final layer of the glomerular filtration barrier consists of specialized epithelial cells called [___], which possess long foot processes that encircle the outer surface of the capillaries.
back:
• Podocytes
• Their foot processes (pedicels) are separated by gaps called slit pores
• These pores provide the final restriction to protein filtration and are coated with negative charges.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: A 6-year-old child presents with severe generalized edema and heavy albuminuria. Electron microscopy reveals podocyte foot process effacement. Identify the underlying pathophysiology regarding the glomerular membrane.
back:
• Minimal-change nephropathy
• Loss of negative charges on the glomerular basement membrane
• Increased permeability to lower-molecular-weight proteins, specifically albumin.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: Explain how the glomerular capillary membrane prevents the filtration of plasma albumin despite albumin's molecular diameter (6 nm) being smaller than the membrane's pores (8 nm).
back:
• Electrostatic repulsion
• The endothelium, basement membrane, and podocytes are richly endowed with fixed negative charges
• These charges repel negatively charged plasma proteins like albumin.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: Contrast the hydrostatic pressures of the glomerular capillaries with those of the peritubular capillaries and the resulting primary functional difference.
back:
• Glomerular: High (~60 mmHg), favoring rapid fluid filtration
• Peritubular: Low (~13 mmHg), favoring rapid fluid reabsorption
• The difference is regulated by adjusting resistance in the efferent arterioles.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: State the normal value for net filtration pressure in the glomerular capillaries and the three primary forces used to calculate it.
back:
• Normal value: +10 mmHg
• Calculated as: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure (60) minus Bowman's capsule pressure (18) minus Glomerular colloid osmotic pressure (32).

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: The innermost layer of the glomerular capillary membrane is the endothelium, which is perforated by thousands of small holes called [___] that are richly endowed with fixed negative charges.
back:
• Fenestrae
• They allow rapid filtration of water and small solutes
• They hinder the passage of large plasma proteins.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: A patient develops an acute ureteral obstruction due to a calcium stone. Describe the immediate effect on the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and the specific physical force responsible.
back:
• GFR decreases
• Obstruction increases Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure ($P_B$)
• This increased pressure opposes filtration across the glomerular membrane.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: Describe the biphasic effect of efferent arteriolar constriction on the Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR).
back:
• Moderate constriction: Increases GFR by raising glomerular hydrostatic pressure
• Severe constriction (>3x normal): Decreases GFR
• At high resistance, the rise in colloid osmotic pressure outweighs the rise in hydrostatic pressure.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: Distinguish between cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons based on their loop of Henle anatomy and vascular supply.
back:
• Cortical: Short loops of Henle; supplied by peritubular capillaries
• Juxtamedullary: Long loops dipping deep into medulla; supplied by specialized vasa recta capillaries.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: Define the capillary filtration coefficient ($K_f$) and identify the two physical properties of the glomerular membrane that determine its value.
back:
• $K_f$ is the product of glomerular permeability and filtering surface area
• It is normally ~12.5 ml/min/mmHg
• Chronic hypertension decreases $K_f$ by thickening the membrane or reducing surface area.

category: Write the causes, pathophysiology, and features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder
front: Uninhibited neurogenic bladder results from partial damage to the spinal cord or brain stem that specifically interrupts descending [___] signals.
back:
• Inhibitory
• Allows facilitative impulses to keep sacral centers hyper-excitable
• Results in frequent, uncontrollable micturition triggered by small urine volumes.

category: Write the causes, pathophysiology, and features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder
coreConcept: Clinical Features of Uninhibited Neurogenic Bladder
front: A patient recovering from a stroke involving the brain stem develops frequent, uncontrollable micturition triggered by minimal bladder filling. Identify the specific neurogenic diagnosis.
back:
• Uninhibited neurogenic bladder
• Pathophysiology: Interruption of descending inhibitory signals from the brain
• Key Feature: Loss of conscious suppression of the micturition reflex.

category: Write the causes, pathophysiology, and features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder
front: Describe the mechanism by which the sacral micturition centers become hyper-excitable in an uninhibited neurogenic bladder.
back:
• Interruption of brain-derived inhibitory pathways due to partial cord/brainstem damage
• Facilitative impulses pass continually down the spinal cord to sacral centers
• Lowered threshold: even small urine quantities elicit an uncontrollable reflex.

category: Write the causes, pathophysiology, and features of uninhibited neurogenic bladder
front: Contrast the clinical micturition pattern of an automatic bladder with that of an uninhibited neurogenic bladder.
back:
• Automatic Bladder: Periodic, unannounced voiding caused by complete suprasacral cord transection.
• Uninhibited Bladder: Frequent, uncontrollable voiding caused by partial loss of inhibitory signals.
• Uninhibited phenotype is characterized by extreme hyper-excitability of the sacral centers.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: The glomerular capillary basement membrane prevents the filtration of plasma proteins primarily through a meshwork of collagen and [___] fibrillae that carry strong negative charges.
back:
• Proteoglycan
• These fixed negative charges exert electrostatic repulsion against negatively charged proteins like albumin.
• It is the middle layer of the three-part filtration barrier.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: A 5-year-old male presents with severe generalized edema and heavy proteinuria. Electron microscopy reveals flattening and detachment of podocyte foot processes. Identify the most likely diagnosis and the specific protein lost.
back:
• Minimal-change nephropathy
• Albumin
• Podocyte effacement leads to increased permeability to lower molecular weight proteins.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: Explain the role of the podocyte slit pores in the glomerular filtration process.
back:
• Podocytes encircle capillaries with pedicels (foot processes).
• Pedicels are separated by gaps called slit pores.
• These pores provide the final restriction to protein filtration while permitting rapid water and solute flux.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: Contrast the filterability of polycationic dextrans with polyanionic dextrans of equal molecular radius at the glomerular capillary membrane.
back:
• Polycationic (positive) dextrans are filtered much more readily.
• Polyanionic (negative) dextrans are restricted by electrostatic repulsion from membrane proteoglycans.
• Neutral dextrans exhibit intermediate filterability.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: Describe the structural feature of the glomerular capillary endothelium that allows it to filter several hundred times more water than a standard capillary.
back:
• Thousands of small holes called fenestrae.
• Though fenestrae are relatively large, endothelial proteins are richly endowed with fixed negative charges to hinder proteins.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: The layer of the glomerular capillary membrane characterized by long foot-like processes and pedicels is the [___].
back:
• Epithelium (Podocytes).
• Pedicels encircle the outer capillary surface.
• Gaps between pedicels are called slit pores.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: A 5-year-old patient presents with generalized edema and massive albuminuria. Electron microscopy reveals podocyte effacement (flattened foot processes). Identify the primary physiological defect.
back:
• Minimal-Change Nephropathy.
• Loss of fixed negative charges on the glomerular membrane.
• Increased permeability to polyanionic plasma proteins.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: Explain the role of the glomerular basement membrane proteoglycans in restricting the filtration of plasma albumin.
back:
• Provide fixed negative electrical charges.
• Exert electrostatic repulsion against negatively charged molecules.
• Prevent albumin (anion) filtration despite its small size.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: Contrast the filterability of neutral dextrans with polyanionic dextrans of the same effective molecular radius (e.g., 34 Å).
back:
• Neutral dextrans: Filtered more readily.
• Polyanionic dextrans: Filtered significantly less easily.
• Difference is due to repulsion by anionic glomerular charges.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: Identify the primary physical force in the glomerular capillaries that is subject to physiological regulation via changes in arteriolar resistance.
back:
• Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (PG).
• Regulated by afferent and efferent arteriolar resistances.
• Higher PG increases GFR; lower PG decreases GFR.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: The product of the hydraulic conductivity and the filtering surface area of the glomerular capillaries is termed the [___].
back:
• Capillary Filtration Coefficient (Kf).
• Normally 400 times higher than most other capillaries.
• Reduced in diabetes or chronic uncontrolled hypertension.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: A patient with a large ureteral stone presents with flank pain and oliguria. Which Starling force increases acutely to cause a reduction in the Glomerular Filtration Rate?
back:
• Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure (PB).
• Obstruction raises pressure upstream in the nephron.
• Increased PB directly opposes glomerular filtration.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: Explain why severe efferent arteriolar constriction (more than 3-fold) leads to a paradoxical decrease in the Glomerular Filtration Rate.
back:
• Drastic reduction in renal blood flow occurs.
• Causes steep rise in glomerular colloid osmotic pressure (πG).
• Rising πG overrides the increase in hydrostatic pressure.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: Contrast the anatomical location and primary filtration function of endothelial fenestrae versus epithelial slit pores.
back:
• Fenestrae: Endothelial holes; exclude cells and large proteins.
• Slit Pores: Gaps between podocyte pedicels; provide final protein barrier.
• Both layers contribute fixed negative charges to the barrier.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy and functions of glomerular capillary membrane
front: State the three specific layers that compose the glomerular capillary membrane.
back:
• Capillary endothelium (perforated by fenestrae).
• Basement membrane (collagen-proteoglycan meshwork).
• Epithelium (podocytes with foot processes).

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
coreConcept: Podocyte Effacement in Minimal Change Nephropathy
front: In minimal change nephropathy, the characteristic ultrastructural finding observed under electron microscopy is the diffuse flattening and spreading of podocyte foot processes, a condition known as [___].
back:
• Podocyte effacement.
• Involves loss of the normal interdigitating architecture.
• Leads to the loss of the filtration barrier's integrity, specifically for plasma proteins.

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
coreConcept: Diagnosis and Charge Selectivity in MCN
front: A 5-year-old child presents with massive generalized edema and heavy proteinuria. Light microscopy shows normal glomeruli, but electron microscopy reveals podocyte foot process effacement. Identify the likely diagnosis and the specific filtration barrier component lost.
back:
• Diagnosis: Minimal Change Nephropathy (MCN).
• Component Lost: Negative charge (anionic) barrier.
• Results in selective proteinuria, primarily involving albumin.

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: Explain the mechanism by which minimal change nephropathy (MCN) specifically increases glomerular permeability to negatively charged plasma proteins like albumin.
back:
• T-cell derived cytokines injure podocytes.
• This leads to the depletion of heparan sulfate (negative charges) from the basement membrane.
• Loss of electrostatic repulsion allows albumin to pass through the filtration slits.

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
coreConcept: Microscopic Findings in Minimal Change Nephropathy
front: Contrast the glomerular appearance in Minimal Change Nephropathy (MCN) when viewed under Light Microscopy (LM) versus Electron Microscopy (EM).
back:
• Light Microscopy: Glomeruli appear histologically normal (hence 'minimal change').
• Electron Microscopy: Shows diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes and detachment from the basement membrane.
• Clinical Correlation: EM is essential for definitive diagnosis.

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: Identify the primary immunological trigger responsible for the podocyte damage and subsequent albuminuria in minimal change nephropathy.
back:
• Abnormal T-cell secretion of cytokines.
• These circulating factors directly injure podocyte foot processes.
• The damage specifically disrupts the polyanionic charge barrier of the glomerular capillary wall.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: Glomerular filtrate is characterized as an ultrafiltrate of plasma that is essentially protein-free and devoid of cellular elements, containing concentrations of salts and organic molecules similar to [___].
back:
• Plasma.
• Exceptions include substances bound to proteins (e.g., calcium, fatty acids).
• The filtration barrier restricts cells and large macromolecules.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: A 5-year-old child presents with generalized edema and heavy proteinuria. While light microscopy appears normal, electron microscopy shows podocyte foot process effacement. Identify the underlying defect in filtrate composition and the specific protein lost.
back:
• Minimal Change Nephropathy.
• Defect: Loss of fixed negative charges on the glomerular filtration barrier.
• Result: Increased permeability to albumin (albuminuria).

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: Explain why the concentration of calcium in the glomerular filtrate is approximately only 50-60% of the total plasma calcium concentration.
back:
• Only ionized and complexed calcium are freely filtered.
• Roughly 40-50% of plasma calcium is bound to large plasma proteins (albumin).
• Protein-bound substances cannot cross the filtration barrier.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: Contrast the filterability of neutral dextrans versus polyanionic dextrans of an equal molecular radius (e.g., 32 Å) across the glomerular membrane.
back:
• Neutral dextrans are filtered more readily.
• Polyanionic (negative) dextrans are electrostatically repelled.
• Negative charges on the basement membrane and podocytes restrict anionic passage.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: Define the relationship between molecular weight and filtrate entry for molecules ranging from 5,000 to 70,000 Daltons.
back:
• Entry is inversely related to molecular weight/size.
• Small molecules (e.g., inulin, 5.5 kDa) are freely filtered (1.0 ratio).
• Large molecules (e.g., albumin, 69 kDa) are restricted (0.005 ratio).

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: The primary component of the glomerular basement membrane that provides the critical negative charge barrier to restrict large anions is the [___] meshwork.
back:
• Proteoglycan fibrillae (rich in fixed negative charges).
• Collagen fibrillae provide structural support.
• Together they hinder filtration of plasma proteins.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: A patient presents with chronic uncontrolled hypertension. Renal biopsy shows significant thickening of the glomerular basement membrane. State the impact on the filtration coefficient ($K_f$) and the resulting filtrate volume.
back:
• $K_f$ decreases due to increased membrane thickness and reduced surface area.
• Decreased $K_f$ leads to a direct reduction in Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR).

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: Describe the specific functional role of podocyte slit pores in determining the protein composition of the filtrate.
back:
• Podocytes encircle capillaries with pedicels separated by slit pores.
• Epithelial cells carry negative charges to repel albumin.
• Slit pores provide the final mechanical restriction for large macromolecules.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: Contrast the composition of the filtrate in the Bowman's space versus the plasma regarding the presence of non-esterified fatty acids.
back:
• Plasma: High concentration (mostly bound to albumin).
• Filtrate: Virtually absent.
• Reason: Albumin-bound substances are not filtered by the glomerular capillaries.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: Identify the three distinct anatomical layers of the glomerular capillary membrane that a solute must traverse to become part of the filtrate.
back:
1. Fenestrated capillary endothelium.
2. Glomerular basement membrane.
3. Epithelial layer (podocytes).

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: In minimal change nephropathy, the primary ultrastructural hallmark seen on electron microscopy is the effacement of [___].
back:
• Podocyte foot processes.
• Processes become flattened or detached from the basement membrane.
• This leads to a loss of the glomerular filtration barrier integrity.

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: A 4-year-old child presents with sudden onset generalized edema and massive proteinuria. Light microscopy of the renal biopsy appears normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
back:
• Minimal Change Nephropathy (MCD).
• Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.
• Characterized by selective proteinuria (albuminuria).

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: Describe how the loss of negative electrical charges in the glomerular membrane contributes to albuminuria in minimal change nephropathy.
back:
• Loss of polyanionic charges (proteoglycans) on the basement membrane.
• Reduction of electrostatic repulsion.
• Negatively charged albumin is allowed to filter through the pores more easily.

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: Contrast the glomerular appearance of Minimal Change Nephropathy with Post-streptococcal Glomerulonephritis regarding light microscopy (LM) and the nature of urinary sediment.
back:
• MCN: Normal/near-normal LM; Massive proteinuria (selective).
• PSGN: Proliferative/inflammatory LM; Hematuria and RBC casts.
• MCN is a non-inflammatory podocyte injury; PSGN is immune-complex mediated.

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: Identify the immune-mediated triggers believed to initiate the podocyte injury in minimal change nephropathy.
back:
• T-cell dysfunction.
• Abnormal secretion of cytokines (permeability factors).
• These factors injure podocytes directly, leading to the loss of foot processes.

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: Severe generalized edema in nephrotic syndrome is primarily driven by a decrease in plasma [___] osmotic pressure.
back:
• Colloid (or oncotic).
• Caused by excessive urinary loss of albumin.
• Leads to fluid shift from vascular space to interstitium.

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: A child with minimal change nephropathy has a plasma albumin level of 1.5 g/dl. Explain the secondary renal response to the resulting decreased effective circulating volume.
back:
• Activation of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS).
• Increased ADH secretion.
• Kidneys retain salt and water, which paradoxically exacerbates the interstitial edema.

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: Explain the physiological sequence from podocyte injury to the clinical finding of 'frothy' urine in minimal change disease.
back:
• Podocyte effacement removes the size/charge barrier.
• Large-scale leakage of albumin into the tubular fluid.
• Albumin lowers surface tension in urine, creating characteristic foam/froth.

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: Contrast 'Selective Proteinuria' in minimal change disease with 'Non-selective Proteinuria' in advanced chronic glomerulonephritis.
back:
• Selective: Loss is primarily low molecular weight albumin.
• Non-selective: Larger proteins (globulins) also pass through.
• Selective proteinuria suggests the charge barrier is lost while the basement membrane structure remains intact.

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: Name the specific water channel found in the proximal tubule that facilitates the rapid water reabsorption often coupled with sodium.
back:
• Aquaporin-1 (AQP-1).
• Present in both luminal and basolateral membranes.
• Essential for maintaining isosmotic fluid reabsorption in the early nephron.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: The glomerular filtrate is essentially [___]-free and devoid of cellular elements such as red blood cells, maintaining an electrolyte profile similar to plasma.
back:
• Protein-free.
• Contains salts and small organic molecules.
• Concentration of solutes is nearly identical to plasma (excluding protein-bound ions).

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: A 5-year-old child presents with generalized edema and heavy proteinuria. If the filtration barrier looks normal under a light microscope but shows podocyte effacement on electron microscopy, the primary defect involves the loss of [___].
back:
• Negative electrical charges.
• Proteoglycans in the basement membrane/podocytes.
• Electrostatic repulsion of albumin is lost, causing proteinuria.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: Explain the role of fixed negative charges within the glomerular basement membrane regarding the filtration of plasma proteins.
back:
• Proteoglycans exert electrostatic repulsion.
• They specifically hinder large anions like albumin.
• This makes negatively charged molecules less filterable than neutral or positive molecules.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: Contrast the filterability of plasma sodium with that of plasma calcium and fatty acids within the initial filtrate.
back:
• Sodium: Freely filtered; concentration in filtrate equals plasma.
• Calcium/Fatty Acids: Partially protein-bound.
• Only the free, non-bound portion enters the glomerular filtrate.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: Identify the quantitative relationship expressed as the filtration fraction in a healthy adult.
back:
• Filtration Fraction = GFR / Renal Plasma Flow.
• Averages approximately 0.2 (20%).
• Represents the percentage of plasma that becomes glomerular filtrate.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: The innermost layer of the glomerular filtration barrier, the capillary [___], is perforated by thousands of small holes called fenestrae to allow rapid solute movement.
back:
• Endothelium.
• Contains fenestrations (pores).
• Endothelial proteins are richly endowed with fixed negative charges.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: A research study injects a polysaccharide with a molecular weight of 5,500 into a subject and determines its filterability is 1.0. Identify this substance and its concentration in Bowman’s space.
back:
• Inulin.
• Filtered as freely as water.
• Concentration in Bowman's space is identical to plasma concentration.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: Describe how the podocyte layer contributes to the size-selectivity of the glomerular filtration barrier.
back:
• Pedicels (foot processes) encircle capillaries.
• Separated by gaps called slit pores.
• Provides a final physical barrier to large molecules and proteins.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: Contrast the glomerular capillary membrane with standard systemic capillaries regarding their anatomical layers.
back:
• Glomerular: 3 layers (Endothelium, Basement membrane, Podocytes).
• Systemic: 2 layers (Endothelium, Basement membrane).
• Glomerular barrier filters several hundred times more water/solutes.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: State the concentration profile of salts and small organic molecules in the initial glomerular filtrate relative to plasma.
back:
• Concentrations are essentially identical.
• Includes sodium, glucose, and amino acids.
• Reflects the non-selective filtration of small, non-bound solutes.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: The Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is determined mathematically by the product of the capillary filtration coefficient ($K_f$) and the [___].
back:
• Net filtration pressure.
• Sum of hydrostatic and colloid osmotic forces.
• $Net Pressure = P_G - P_B - \pi_G + \pi_B$.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: A 45-year-old male presents with severe renal colic. Imaging confirms a large ureteral stone causing urinary tract obstruction and hydronephrosis. Identify the primary force alteration that decreases his GFR.
back:
• Increased Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure ($P_B$).
• Increased pressure opposes filtration.
• Normal $P_B$ is ~18 mmHg.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: Explain the role of the macula densa in the tubuloglomerular feedback mechanism when a decrease in arterial pressure causes GFR to fall.
back:
• Senses decreased NaCl delivery to distal tubule.
• Triggers afferent arteriolar dilation.
• Stimulates renin release to increase Angiotensin II (efferent constriction).

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: Contrast the biphasic effects of efferent arteriolar constriction on GFR.
back:
• Moderate constriction: Increases GFR by raising glomerular hydrostatic pressure ($P_G$).
• Severe constriction (>3-fold): Decreases GFR due to rising colloid osmotic pressure (Donnan effect).

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: The proportion of renal plasma flow that is filtered through the glomerular capillaries, typically averaging 20%, is defined as [___].
back:
• Filtration Fraction (FF).
• Calculated as $GFR / Renal Plasma Flow (RPF)$.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: A substance is used to measure GFR if it is freely filtered at the glomerulus but is neither [___] nor [___] by the renal tubules.
back:
• Reabsorbed.
• Secreted.
• Primary example: Inulin.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: A patient with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus presents with hyperglycemia. Explain why the subsequent increase in proximal glucose reabsorption leads to an elevated GFR.
back:
• Glucose is co-transported with Na+.
• Increased reabsorption decreases NaCl at macula densa.
• Triggers tubuloglomerular feedback to dilate afferent arterioles.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: How does Angiotensin II maintain GFR during physiological states of volume depletion or low sodium diet?
back:
• Preferentially constricts efferent arterioles.
• Increases glomerular hydrostatic pressure ($P_G$).
• Offsets the tendency for GFR to fall due to reduced renal perfusion.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: Distinguish between the effects of mild versus strong sympathetic nervous system activation on GFR.
back:
• Mild/Moderate: Minimal effect due to autoregulation.
• Strong (e.g., hemorrhage/defense reaction): Constricts renal arterioles, significantly decreasing renal blood flow and GFR.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: What is the average GFR value for a healthy 70-kg adult male?
back:
• 125 ml/min.
• 180 L/day.
• Represents 20% of renal plasma flow.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is defined as the volume of fluid filtered from the glomerular capillaries into [___] per unit of time.
back:
• Bowman’s capsule.
• It represents the first step in urine formation.
• Normal value is approximately 125 ml/min (180 L/day).

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: A patient with a large kidney stone obstructing the ureter presents with decreased urine output. Explain the specific hemodynamic change in GFR.
back:
• Obstruction causes urine back-up into the renal pelvis.
• Increases Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure (Pb).
• Increased Pb opposes filtration, leading to a significant decrease in GFR.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: Explain the role of the Macula densa in the tubuloglomerular feedback mechanism when GFR falls.
back:
• Senses decreased NaCl delivery to distal tubules.
• Triggers dilation of the afferent arteriole.
• Increases renin release, producing Angiotensin II which constricts the efferent arteriole.
• Both actions restore glomerular hydrostatic pressure and GFR.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: Contrast the effect on GFR of isolated afferent arteriolar constriction versus moderate efferent arteriolar constriction.
back:
• Afferent Constriction: Decreases glomerular hydrostatic pressure and GFR.
• Moderate Efferent Constriction: Increases glomerular hydrostatic pressure and GFR.
• Severe Efferent Constriction: Eventually decreases GFR due to rising colloid osmotic pressure.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: How do non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) acutely reduce GFR in patients with low blood volume?
back:
• NSAIDs block vasodilatory prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2).
• Leads to unopposed afferent arteriolar constriction.
• Decreases glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, reducing filtration.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: To estimate GFR clinically, [___] clearance is used because it is an endogenous byproduct of muscle metabolism and is not reabsorbed by the tubules.
back:
• Creatinine.
• It is filtered and slightly secreted, providing a practical estimate.
• Serum levels are inversely proportional to GFR.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: A patient consumes a high-protein meal. Explain the physiological increase in GFR that follows ingestion.
back:
• Amino acids increase proximal sodium reabsorption (co-transport).
• Decreased NaCl delivery to the Macula Densa.
• Dilation of afferent arterioles via feedback.
• Increases renal blood flow and GFR to excrete waste.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: Describe the specific mechanism by which Angiotensin II preserves GFR during states of renal hypoperfusion.
back:
• Preferentially constricts efferent arterioles.
• Increases glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pg).
• Maintains filtration despite reduced total renal blood flow.
• Prevents excessive drop in GFR during hypotension.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: Contrast the use of inulin versus creatinine as markers for GFR measurement.
back:
• Inulin: Gold standard; freely filtered, not reabsorbed or secreted; requires IV infusion.
• Creatinine: Endogenous; slightly overestimates GFR (~10-20%) because it is filtered and secreted.

category: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
front: State the relationship between GFR, Renal Plasma Flow (RPF), and the Filtration Fraction.
back:
• Filtration Fraction = GFR / RPF.
• Reprents the portion of plasma filtered into the tubules.
• Normal value is roughly 0.20 (one-fifth of plasma).

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: In minimal change nephropathy, the characteristic ultrastructural finding observed under an electron microscope is [___].
back:
• Podocyte effacement
• Flattening of foot processes
• Detachment from the glomerular basement membrane

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: A 4-year-old child presents with generalized pitting edema and massive proteinuria. Light microscopy of a renal biopsy is unremarkable. Identify the underlying pathophysiology.
back:
• Minimal change nephropathy
• Cytokine-mediated injury to podocytes
• Increased glomerular permeability to albumin

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: Explain the role of cytokines secreted by abnormal T-cells in the development of minimal change nephropathy.
back:
• Directly injure glomerular podocytes
• Cause effacement of foot processes
• Disrupt the negative charge barrier
• Lead to selective proteinuria (albuminuria)

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: Contrast the glomerular appearance of a patient with minimal change nephropathy under light microscopy versus electron microscopy.
back:
• Light Microscopy: Glomeruli appear normal/unremarkable
• Electron Microscopy: Reveals flattened podocyte foot processes
• Clinical Significance: MCN is the primary cause of childhood nephrotic syndrome

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: Identify the primary mechanism by which the glomerular capillary wall restricts the filtration of the plasma protein albumin.
back:
• Electrostatic repulsion
• Fixed negative charges on proteoglycans
• Basement membrane and podocyte barrier
• Size-selective restriction by slit pores

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: The condition known as [___] occurs when podocyte injury in minimal change disease allows proteins to leak into the urine.
back:
• Proteinuria or Albuminuria
• Results from increased glomerular permeability
• Characteristic of nephrotic syndrome

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: A patient with minimal change nephropathy presents with severe edema and a plasma protein level below 2 g/dl. Describe the Starling force change causing this edema.
back:
• Decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure
• Caused by excessive urinary loss of albumin
• Leads to fluid transudation into interstitial spaces

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: Explain the biological mechanism that determines why polyanionic dextrans are filtered less easily than neutral dextrans of identical molecular size.
back:
• Electrostatic repulsion from the filtration barrier
• Negative charges on endothelium and podocytes
• Hinders passage of negatively charged molecules (like albumin)

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: Contrast the physiological cycle of sodium retention in the nephrotic syndrome versus a normal healthy state.
back:
• Nephrotic: Low plasma volume triggers RAAS and sympathetic activity
• Normal: Sodium excretion matches intake precisely
• Result: Massive fluid retention and edema in nephrotic states

category: Explain the minimal change nephropathy and increase permeability to plasma protein
front: Enlist the three major anatomical layers that constitute the filtration barrier of the glomerular capillary membrane.
back:
• Fenestrated capillary endothelium
• Glomerular basement membrane (collagen/proteoglycans)
• Epithelial podocytes (with foot processes/slit pores)

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: The product of the glomerular capillary permeability and the filtering surface area is known as the [___].
back:
• Glomerular filtration coefficient (Kf)
• Diseases like chronic hypertension reduce Kf by decreasing surface area or increasing membrane thickness.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: A 45-year-old male with recurrent kidney stones presents with intense flank pain and oliguria. Imaging shows a stone lodged in the ureter. GFR is reduced in this patient primarily due to an increase in [___].
back:
• Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure (PB)
• Increased PB opposes filtration, potentially causing hydronephrosis if the obstruction is not relieved.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: Explain the role of the plasma colloid osmotic pressure (πG) along the length of the glomerular capillary.
back:
• Increases by ~20% from afferent to efferent end
• Caused by filtration of water into Bowman's space, concentrating the non-filtered proteins
• Opposes glomerular filtration.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: Contrast the filtration characteristics of neutral dextrans versus polyanionic dextrans of identical molecular radii (e.g., 34 Å).
back:
• Polyanionic dextrans: Lower filterability due to electrostatic repulsion from negative charges (proteoglycans) on the basement membrane.
• Neutral dextrans: Higher filterability as they are only size-restricted.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: Identify the three physiological variables that determine Glomerular Hydrostatic Pressure (PG).
back:
• Arterial pressure
• Afferent arteriolar resistance (RA)
• Efferent arteriolar resistance (RE)

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: In minimal-change nephropathy, the loss of negative charges on the filtration barrier results in significant [___].
back:
• Proteinuria (specifically Albuminuria)
• Caused by podocyte effacement and loss of the electrical barrier to anionic proteins.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: A hypertensive patient with renal artery stenosis is prescribed an ACE inhibitor, resulting in a sudden drop in GFR. Identify the underlying mechanism.
back:
• Blockade of Angiotensin II prevents its preferential constriction of efferent arterioles
• This reduces Glomerular Hydrostatic Pressure (PG), crashing the GFR in low-perfusion states.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
coreConcept: Biphasic Effect of Efferent Arteriolar Resistance
front: Describe the biphasic effect of efferent arteriolar constriction on Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR).
back:
• Moderate constriction: Increases PG, slightly increasing GFR.
• Severe constriction (>3-fold): Markedly reduces renal blood flow, causing a massive rise in colloid osmotic pressure that decreases GFR.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
coreConcept: Autacoid and Nervous Control of GFR
front: Distinguish between the effects of sympathetic nervous system activation and Nitric Oxide (NO) on renal hemodynamics.
back:
• Sympathetic activation: Increases RA and RE, decreasing renal blood flow and GFR (occurs in hemorrhage).
• Nitric Oxide: Basal vasodilator that decreases renal resistance and increases GFR.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: Specify the approximate normal value for net filtration pressure in a healthy human glomerulus.
back:
• +10 mmHg
• Calculated as PG (60) minus PB (18) minus πG (32).

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: The Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is mathematically defined as the product of the net filtration pressure and the [___].
back:
● Capillary filtration coefficient (Kf)
● Kf represents the product of capillary permeability and effective filtration surface area
● Diseases like diabetes or chronic hypertension reduce GFR by lowering Kf.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: A 50-year-old patient presents with acute urinary retention due to a large kidney stone obstructing the ureter. Identify the specific Starling force that increases and opposes filtration in this scenario.
back:
● Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure (Pb)
● Obstruction increases pressure upstream in the capsule
● This increased Pb opposes the glomerular hydrostatic pressure, leading to decreased GFR.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: Explain the biphasic effect of increasing efferent arteriolar resistance on the GFR.
back:
● Modest constriction increases GFR by raising glomerular hydrostatic pressure (Pg)
● Severe constriction (over 3-fold) decreases GFR
● Severe resistance reduces renal blood flow, causing a rapid rise in colloid osmotic pressure (πg) that opposes filtration.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: Contrast the physiological consequences of isolated afferent arteriolar constriction versus isolated efferent arteriolar constriction on Glomerular Hydrostatic Pressure (Pg).
back:
● Afferent constriction: Decreases Pg because it restricts blood flow into the glomerulus
● Efferent constriction: Increases Pg because it creates a 'backlog' of pressure within the glomerular capillaries.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: List the three primary variables that physiologically regulate Glomerular Hydrostatic Pressure (Pg).
back:
● Arterial pressure (Pg is buffered by autoregulation)
● Afferent arteriolar resistance
● Efferent arteriolar resistance

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: In conditions of severe dehydration, a rise in the systemic plasma protein concentration leads to a decrease in GFR primarily by increasing the [___].
back:
● Glomerular capillary colloid osmotic pressure (πg)
● Increased πg exerts an inward 'pulling' force that opposes the filtration of fluid into Bowman's capsule.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: A patient is started on an ACE inhibitor which prevents the formation of Angiotensin II. Predict the effect on GFR in a patient with renal artery stenosis and explain the underlying change in Starling forces.
back:
● GFR decreases significantly
● Loss of Angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction lowers glomerular hydrostatic pressure (Pg)
● Pg falls below the threshold required to maintain filtration in the stenosed kidney.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: Describe the two-fold tubuloglomerular feedback mechanism triggered by a decrease in sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa.
back:
● Afferent Dilation: Decreases resistance to raise glomerular hydrostatic pressure
● Renin Release: Increases Angiotensin II, which constricts efferent arterioles to raise glomerular hydrostatic pressure
● Both actions act to return GFR toward normal.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: The glomerular filtrate is essentially protein-free and devoid of cellular elements such as [___].
back:
• Red blood cells (RBCs).
• Large protein molecules (e.g., albumin).
• Most calcium and fatty acids (those bound to plasma proteins).

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: A 5-year-old child presents with massive edema and heavy albuminuria. Electron microscopy shows podocyte effacement. The underlying mechanism for the presence of albumin in the filtrate is [___].
back:
• Loss of fixed negative charges (proteoglycans) on the glomerular basement membrane.
• Reduced electrostatic repulsion allows anionic proteins like albumin to cross the barrier.
• Often seen in Minimal Change Disease.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: Explain the role of the podocyte slit pores in maintaining the specific composition of the filtrate.
back:
• Podocytes encircle the capillaries with foot processes (pedicels).
• Pedicels are separated by slit pores (~8 nm wide).
• These pores, coated with negative charges, provide a final mechanical and electrostatic barrier to restrict large proteins.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: A patient with nephrotic syndrome has altered filtrate composition. Contrast the filterability of albumin in a healthy kidney versus one with lost glomerular negative charges.
back:
• Healthy: Very low filterability (0.005) due to negative charge repulsion and size restriction.
• Disease: Increased filterability as the absence of negative charges allows anionic albumin to pass freely into the filtrate.

category: Discuss the composition of filtrate
front: Discuss the effect of carbonic anhydrase inhibitors on the solute composition of the filtrate in the proximal tubule.
back:
• Inhibits H+ secretion and HCO3- reabsorption.
• Increases concentrations of Na+, HCO3-, and water in the tubular filtrate.
• Acts as an osmotic diuretic, leading to the excretion of alkaline urine.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: The Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is determined by the product of the net filtration pressure and the [___], which represents the product of glomerular capillary permeability and filtering surface area.
back:
• Capillary filtration coefficient ($K_f$)
• Measures hydraulic conductivity and surface area
• Decreased in diseases like diabetes or chronic hypertension through basement membrane thickening.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: A 55-year-old male presents with acute loin pain. Imaging reveals a large calculus obstructing the proximal ureter. Describe the immediate effect of this obstruction on the physical determinants of GFR.
back:
• Increases Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure ($P_B$)
• Directly opposes filtration across the glomerular membrane
• Results in decreased net filtration pressure and GFR.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: Explain the role of the macula densa in autoregulating GFR when renal perfusion pressure decreases.
back:
• Senses decreased NaCl delivery to the distal tubule
• Triggers afferent arteriolar vasodilation to increase glomerular pressure
• Stimulates renin release, causing efferent arteriolar constriction via Angiotensin II.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: Contrast the biphasic effect of efferent arteriolar constriction on GFR with the effect of afferent arteriolar constriction.
back:
• Afferent: Constriction reduces glomerular hydrostatic pressure ($P_G$), always decreasing GFR.
• Efferent: Moderate constriction increases $P_G$ and GFR; severe constriction reduces GFR as the rise in colloid osmotic pressure overrides $P_G$.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: Describe the specific physiological purpose of Angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction during states of volume depletion.
back:
• Maintains GFR and excretion of metabolic wastes (urea/creatinine)
• Increases glomerular hydrostatic pressure
• Reduces peritubular capillary hydrostatic pressure to increase sodium and water reabsorption.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: In minimal-change nephropathy, the loss of negative charges on the [___] leads to selective proteinuria, specifically albuminuria, despite an otherwise normal-appearing glomerulus under light microscopy.
back:
• Glomerular basement membrane and podocytes
• Loss of electrostatic repulsion allows negatively charged albumin to filter
• Results in a dramatic increase in glomerular permeability to plasma proteins.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: A patient consumes a high-protein meal, leading to a significant increase in renal blood flow and GFR within two hours. Explain the underlying mechanism for this GFR change.
back:
• Increased proximal tubular amino acid and sodium reabsorption
• Decreased NaCl delivery to the macula densa
• Triggers tubuloglomerular feedback to dilate afferent arterioles and increase filtration.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: Explain how a primary reduction in Renal Plasma Flow (RPF) can decrease GFR even if glomerular hydrostatic pressure remains unchanged.
back:
• Increases the filtration fraction ($GFR/RPF$)
• Causes plasma proteins to concentrate more rapidly along the capillary
• Elevates average glomerular colloid osmotic pressure, which opposes filtration.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: Contrast the myogenic mechanism with tubuloglomerular feedback regarding their triggers for GFR autoregulation.
back:
• Myogenic: Direct response of afferent arteriolar smooth muscle to vessel wall stretch/pressure.
• Tubuloglomerular: Mediated by macula densa sensing changes in NaCl concentration at the distal tubule.

category: Describe the determinants of GFR
front: Identify the two primary physiological factors that determine the glomerular capillary colloid osmotic pressure ($\pi_G$).
back:
• Arterial plasma colloid osmotic pressure
• Filtration fraction (the portion of plasma filtered into Bowman's capsule)
• Increases in either factor will decrease GFR.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: The Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is mathematically defined as the product of the [___] and the net filtration pressure.
back:
• Capillary filtration coefficient (Kf)
• Calculated as: GFR = Kf × Net Filtration Pressure
• Kf represents the product of surface area and hydraulic permeability.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
coreConcept: Effect of Urinary Tract Obstruction on GFR
front: A 45-year-old male with a history of recurrent renal calculi presents with severe flank pain. Imaging reveals a stone obstructing the left ureter. The resultant drop in GFR is primarily caused by an increase in [___].
back:
• Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure (Pb)
• Obstruction prevents outflow, raising pressure against glomerular capillaries
• Opposes filtration, reducing the net filtration pressure gradient.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
coreConcept: Biphasic Effect of Efferent Arteriolar Resistance
front: Explain how severe constriction (greater than 3-fold) of the efferent arteriole can paradoxically lead to a decrease in GFR.
back:
• Severe constriction significantly reduces Renal Blood Flow (RBF)
• This increases the Filtration Fraction (FF)
• Higher FF causes a rapid, non-linear rise in Glomerular Colloid Osmotic Pressure (πg)
• Opposes filtration more than the rise in hydrostatic pressure ($P_G$).

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: Contrast the GFR response to a 25% increase in Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) in a healthy kidney versus one where renal autoregulation is entirely absent.
back:
• Healthy Kidney: GFR remains nearly constant (±10%) due to myogenic/feedback mechanisms.
• Impaired Autoregulation: GFR would increase linearly with MAP (~25%).
• Result: Unregulated MAP rises would cause massive urine output and volume depletion.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: Identify the primary autacoids that function to increase GFR by counteracting the vasoconstrictive effects of the sympathetic nervous system and Angiotensin II on the afferent arterioles.
back:
• Prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2)
• Endothelial-derived Nitric Oxide (NO)
• Bradykinin
• Essential for preventing excessive GFR reduction during stress/volume depletion.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: In the tubuloglomerular feedback mechanism, the macula densa cells sense a decrease in [___] concentration to trigger afferent arteriolar dilation.
back:
• Sodium Chloride (NaCl)
• Low NaCl indicates low GFR and slow loop of Henle flow
• Trigger dilates afferent arteriole and increases Renin secretion.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: A patient with bilateral renal artery stenosis is started on an ACE inhibitor for hypertension. They subsequently develop acute renal failure. This occurs because blocking Angiotensin II [___].
back:
• Prevents necessary efferent arteriolar constriction
• Lowers glomerular hydrostatic pressure ($P_G$)
• In stenosis, Ang II-mediated efferent constriction is essential to maintain GFR against low perfusion pressure.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: Describe the mechanism by which a high-protein meal increases both Renal Blood Flow and GFR within 1-2 hours of ingestion.
back:
• Amino acids are reabsorbed with Na+ in the proximal tubule
• This reduces NaCl delivery to the macula densa
• Decreased distal NaCl triggers macula densa feedback
• Results in afferent arteriolar vasodilation and subsequent GFR rise.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: Contrast the effects of strong sympathetic stimulation versus basal Angiotensin II levels on the glomerular Filtration Fraction (FF).
back:
• Sympathetic Activity: Constricts both arterioles; RBF and GFR both fall (FF variable/down).
• Angiotensin II: Preferentially constricts efferent arterioles; RBF falls but GFR is maintained (FF increases).
• Ang II allows waste excretion despite volume depletion.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: Identify the three primary physiological variables that determine the glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure ($P_G$).
back:
• Arterial Pressure (MAP)
• Afferent Arteriolar Resistance ($R_A$)
• Efferent Arteriolar Resistance ($R_E$)
• $P_G$ is the most variable and regulated determinant of GFR.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: In the formula for Glomerular Filtration Rate ($GFR = K_f \times \text{Net Filtration Pressure}$), the [___] represents the product of the capillary surface area and hydraulic conductivity.
back:
• Capillary filtration coefficient ($K_f$)
• Reduced by chronic diseases like diabetes and hypertension
• Reductions lead to decreased overall GFR.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: A 45-year-old male presents with severe renal colic and ultrasound evidence of a large ureteral stone causing hydronephrosis. The resulting decrease in GFR is primarily due to a pathological increase in [___].
back:
• Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure ($P_B$)
• Obstruction increases the pressure opposing filtration
• Net filtration pressure is significantly reduced.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: Explain the biphasic effect of efferent arteriolar constriction on the Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR).
back:
• Moderate constriction: Increases glomerular hydrostatic pressure ($P_G$), slightly raising GFR.
• Severe constriction (>3-fold): Markedly reduces renal blood flow, causing glomerular colloid osmotic pressure ($\pi_G$) to rise rapidly and override the $P_G$ increase, net-decreasing GFR.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: Contrast the physiological consequences of isolated increases in afferent arteriolar resistance ($R_A$) versus efferent arteriolar resistance ($R_E$) on renal hemodynamics.
back:
• Afferent ($R_A$): Always decreases glomerular hydrostatic pressure and GFR.
• Efferent ($R_E$): Increases glomerular hydrostatic pressure; however, both mechanisms decrease renal blood flow regardless of their opposing effects on GFR.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: Describe the impact of administering pharmacological inhibitors of Nitric Oxide (NO) production on the Glomerular Filtration Rate.
back:
• NO normally decreases renal vascular resistance
• Inhibition causes renal vasoconstriction
• Results in decreased GFR and reduced sodium excretion, potentially elevating blood pressure.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: The tubuloglomerular feedback mechanism for GFR autoregulation relies on [___] cells in the distal tubule sensing changes in sodium chloride delivery.
back:
• Macula densa
• Low NaCl delivery triggers afferent vasodilation
• Stimulates renin release to constrict efferent arterioles via Angiotensin II.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: A 60-year-old with heart failure is given high-dose NSAIDs. Explain the mechanism by which this leads to acute GFR reduction.
back:
• NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis ($PGE_2$, $PGI_2$)
• Prostaglandins normally dilate afferent arterioles to maintain GFR
• Inhibition causes unopposed afferent vasoconstriction, especially during low volume/pressure states.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: Describe the physiological pathway through which a high-protein diet increases the GFR via tubuloglomerular feedback.
back:
• Amino acids are co-reabsorbed with sodium in the proximal tubule.
• Decreased sodium delivery to the macula densa triggers feedback.
• Results in afferent arteriolar dilation and a subsequent rise in glomerular hydrostatic pressure and GFR.

category: Discuss the hormones and autocoids that affect GFR
front: The autacoid released by damaged vascular endothelial cells that acts as a powerful vasoconstrictor to decrease GFR is [___].
back:
• Endothelin
• Levels are often increased in toxemia of pregnancy, acute renal failure, and chronic uremia.

category: Discuss the hormones and autocoids that affect GFR
front: A patient with volume depletion takes high-dose aspirin for joint pain and subsequently experiences a significant drop in GFR. Describe the underlying pathophysiology.
back:
• Aspirin inhibits Prostaglandins (PGE2 and PGI2).
• Prostaglandins normally vasodilate afferent arterioles to dampen sympathetic/Angiotensin II constriction.
• Loss of these vasodilators leads to severe reductions in GFR.

category: Discuss the hormones and autocoids that affect GFR
front: Explain the role of Nitric Oxide (NO) in maintaining baseline renal function.
back:
• NO decreases renal vascular resistance.
• It maintains baseline vasodilation, increasing GFR.
• Inhibiting NO production causes renal vasoconstriction, decreased GFR, and hypertension.

category: Discuss the hormones and autocoids that affect GFR
front: Contrast the effects of Norepinephrine and Angiotensin II on the resistance of renal arterioles.
back:
• Norepinephrine: Constricts both afferent and efferent arterioles, sharply reducing GFR.
• Angiotensin II: Preferentially constricts efferent arterioles to maintain glomerular hydrostatic pressure and GFR.

category: Discuss the hormones and autocoids that affect GFR
front: Describe the physiological utility of Angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction during hemorrhage.
back:
• It prevents a severe drop in glomerular hydrostatic pressure.
• It maintains GFR and waste excretion (urea/creatinine).
• It reduces peritubular capillary pressure to increase sodium and water reabsorption.

category: Discuss the hormones and autocoids that affect GFR
front: Blood levels of the hormones [___] and [___] parallel sympathetic nervous system activity and typically only decrease GFR during severe acute disturbances like hemorrhage.
back:
• Norepinephrine
• Epinephrine

category: Discuss the hormones and autocoids that affect GFR
front: A patient presents with renal artery stenosis. Explain why his GFR is maintained near normal despite reduced renal perfusion pressure.
back:
• Reduced pressure activates the Renin-Angiotensin System.
• Angiotensin II increases efferent arteriolar resistance.
• This raises glomerular hydrostatic pressure to compensate for low perfusion.

category: Discuss the hormones and autocoids that affect GFR
front: Describe the biphasic effect of increasing efferent arteriolar constriction on GFR.
back:
• Moderate constriction: Increases GFR by raising glomerular hydrostatic pressure.
• Severe constriction (>3x normal): Decreases GFR because drastic reductions in blood flow cause excessive rise in glomerular colloid osmotic pressure.

category: Explain the factors affecting GFR
front: The product of capillary permeability and effective surface area, known as the [___], is a major determinant of GFR and is significantly reduced in chronic diseases like diabetes mellitus.
back:
• Glomerular capillary filtration coefficient (Kf)
  • Reduction occurs via basement membrane thickening or loss of capillary surface area
