front: A patient survives a severe motor vehicle accident with significant blood loss. Explain the nervous mechanism that immediately increases the effectiveness of renal water and salt retention.
back:
• Activation of arterial baroreceptors and low-pressure stretch receptors.
• Increased renal sympathetic nerve activity.
• Constriction of renal arterioles (reducing GFR).
• Stimulation of the RAAS pathway.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: How does the preferential constriction of efferent arterioles by Angiotensin II maintain the effectiveness of waste product excretion during volume depletion?
back:
• Increases glomerular hydrostatic pressure.
• Prevents drastic falls in GFR despite low renal blood flow.
• Allows continued filtration of urea and creatinine while maximizing tubular reabsorption.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
coreConcept: Angiotensin II and Pressure Natriuresis Sensitivity
front: Contrast the impact of a high-sodium diet on the renal-pressure natriuresis curve in a normal individual versus a patient with an impaired ability to suppress Angiotensin II.
back:
• Normal: Steep curve; sodium balance is maintained with minimal blood pressure increase.
• Impaired: Shallow curve; much greater increases in arterial pressure are required to increase sodium excretion (salt-sensitivity).

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Identify the three specific renal pathways through which Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) acts to minimize extracellular fluid volume expansion.
back:
• Increases GFR slightly.
• Decreases renin secretion and Angiotensin II formation.
• Directly inhibits sodium and water reabsorption in the collecting ducts.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: In the renal–body fluid feedback loop, a slight increase in blood volume causes a large increase in urine output primarily by elevating [___].
back: Arterial pressure.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: A 60-year-old male with an aldosterone-secreting adrenal tumor (Conn Syndrome) presents with mild hypertension but no progressive edema. Explain the physiologic "escape" mechanism involved.
back:
• Initial sodium retention expands ECF volume.
• Arterial pressure rises.
• Pressure natriuresis/diuresis eventually overcomes the sodium-retaining effect of aldosterone.
• Balance is restored at a higher blood pressure.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Explain how an increased distal tubular flow rate increases the effectiveness of potassium secretion despite suppressed aldosterone levels in a high-sodium diet.
back:
• Secreted potassium is rapidly flushed away, maintaining a low luminal concentration.
• Activates high-conductance BK (big potassium) channels.
• Increases the electrochemical gradient favoring diffusion into the lumen.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Contrast the influence of Angiotensin II/Aldosterone versus the ADH-thirst system in the daily regulation of extracellular sodium concentration.
back:
• Ang II/Aldo: Regulate total body sodium content and volume; minimal impact on concentration.
• ADH-Thirst: The primary controllers of sodium concentration and osmolarity by regulating water intake and excretion.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: List the three components of the integrated response that suppress antinatriuretic systems when sodium intake is acutely elevated.
back:
• Activation of low-pressure stretch receptor reflexes.
• Suppression of Angiotensin II and Aldosterone.
• Stimulation of natriuretic peptides (e.g., ANP).

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase in blood volume and ECF volume
front: In the setting of heart failure, the compensatory activation of the [___] system is a primary hormonal driver of the large increase in both blood and ECF volumes.
back:
• Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)
• Increases sodium and water reabsorption to support cardiac output

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase in blood volume and ECF volume
front: A 45-year-old male with chronic alcoholism presents with massive ascites. Explain the dual physical forces causing this localized ECF volume expansion in the peritoneal cavity.
back:
• Decreased plasma protein synthesis (low colloid osmotic pressure)
• Portal venous obstruction (increased portal capillary hydrostatic pressure)

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase in blood volume and ECF volume
front: Explain the role of aldosterone in the development of extracellular fluid volume expansion during primary aldosteronism (Conn syndrome).
back:
• Stimulates principal cells to reabsorb sodium and water
• Expands ECF volume and increases arterial pressure until 'renal escape' occurs

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase in blood volume and ECF volume
front: Contrast the pathogenesis of edema in acute glomerulonephritis with that seen in nephrotic syndrome regarding the primary Starling force involved.
back:
• Glomerulonephritis: Primary increase in capillary hydrostatic pressure (salt/water retention)
• Nephrotic Syndrome: Primary decrease in plasma colloid osmotic pressure (protein loss)

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase in blood volume and ECF volume
front: Identify the primary renal pathology that causes widespread ECF edema in children following a group A beta-streptococcal infection.
back:
• Acute glomerulonephritis
• Characterized by immune complex deposition and reduced GFR

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase in blood volume and ECF volume
front: In patients with nephrotic syndrome, the massive loss of [___] in the urine initiates a sequence of events leading to severe ECF volume expansion.
back:
• Plasma proteins (Albumin)
• Leads to decreased colloid osmotic pressure and fluid transudation

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase in blood volume and ECF volume
front: A patient presents with high blood volume and ECF edema. It is determined this is caused by an increased vascular capacity. Name two physiological or pathological conditions responsible for this.
back:
• Pregnancy (vascular expansion of uterus/placenta)
• Large varicose veins in the lower limbs

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase in blood volume and ECF volume
front: Describe the physiological mechanism of 'mineralocorticoid escape' that prevents infinite ECF expansion during chronic aldosterone excess.
back:
• Retention of Na+/water raises arterial pressure
• Pressure natriuresis and diuresis eventually balance salt/water output with intake

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase in blood volume and ECF volume
front: Distinguish between the effects of excessive ADH versus excessive aldosterone on total extracellular fluid volume expansion.
back:
• Aldosterone: Causes large, persistent ECF expansion and hypertension
• ADH: Causes only small, transient ECF expansion (volume is limited by pressure natriuresis)

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase in blood volume and ECF volume
front: Enlist the three major safety factors that normally prevent the accumulation of excess fluid in the interstitial spaces (edema).
back:
• Low tissue compliance in the negative pressure range
• Ability of lymph flow to increase 10–50 fold
• Washdown of interstitial fluid proteins

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase ECF volume but with normal blood volume
front: In conditions like nephrotic syndrome, the primary mechanism causing ECF expansion with a normal or reduced blood volume is the loss of [___] in the urine.
back:
• Plasma proteins (specifically albumin).
• This reduces plasma colloid osmotic pressure.
• Fluid leaks from capillaries into the interstitium, triggering renal salt and water retention.

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase ECF volume but with normal blood volume
coreConcept: Effective vs Absolute Blood Volume in Cirrhosis
front: A 45-year-old male with chronic liver cirrhosis presents with massive ascites and pedal edema. Despite the obvious fluid overload, explain why his kidneys continue to retain sodium as if he were dehydrated.
back:
• Portal hypertension and low albumin cause fluid to leak into the peritoneal cavity.
• This lowers effective plasma volume.
• The kidneys react to perceived hypovolemia by activating RAAS and sympathetic systems to retain salt.

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase ECF volume but with normal blood volume
front: Describe the physiological role of the tissue interstitial spaces as an 'overflow release valve' when ECF volume rises 30-50% above normal.
back:
• Once interstitial pressure becomes positive, tissue compliance increases massively.
• Large fluid volumes shift into the interstitium (edema).
• This protects the cardiovascular system from dangerous circulatory overload and pulmonary edema.

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase ECF volume but with normal blood volume
coreConcept: Differential Blood Volume Status in Edema
front: Contrast the blood volume status in Congestive Heart Failure versus Nephrotic Syndrome during states of generalized edema.
back:
• Heart Failure: Both ECF volume and blood volume are markedly increased as the body tries to restore cardiac output.
• Nephrotic Syndrome: ECF is expanded (edema), but blood volume is often normal or reduced due to protein loss.

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase ECF volume but with normal blood volume
front: Identify the compensatory renal response triggered when plasma volume leaks into the interstitium during protein-wasting kidney diseases.
back:
• Decreased plasma volume stimulates the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS).
• This causes avid renal sodium and water retention.
• This cycle progressively expands ECF (edema) while only transiently restoring blood volume.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: During acute hemorrhage, reflex activation of the [___] system primarily decreases sodium and water excretion by constricting renal arterioles and stimulating renin release.
back:
* Sympathetic Nervous System
* Decreases GFR (in severe cases)
* Increases tubular reabsorption
* Activates the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: A patient with hypertension shows a failure to suppress Angiotensin II levels despite high dietary salt intake. Explain the impact on the renal pressure-natriuresis relationship.
back:
* Decreases the slope of the pressure-natriuresis curve
* Increases 'salt-sensitivity' of blood pressure
* Higher arterial pressures are required to maintain sodium balance

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Explain the mechanism by which Angiotensin II enhances peritubular capillary reabsorption to increase the effectiveness of volume conservation.
back:
* Constricts efferent arterioles
* Lowers peritubular capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc)
* Increases filtration fraction, which elevates peritubular colloid osmotic pressure (πc)

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Contrast the long-term effects of Aldosterone and ADH on extracellular fluid sodium concentration during volume depletion.
back:
* Aldosterone: Increases Na+ quantity but has little effect on concentration (water follows Na+)
* ADH: Primary regulator of sodium concentration (reabsorbs water independently of sodium)

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Identify the hormonal factor released in response to atrial stretch that directly inhibits collecting duct sodium reabsorption and suppresses renin secretion.
back:
* Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP)
* Opposes Angiotensin II-mediated sodium retention
* Attenuates volume expansion in conditions like heart failure

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: The intrinsic mechanism that serves as the first line of defense to buffer spontaneous changes in GFR by matching proximal tubular reabsorption to the filtered load is [___].
back:
* Glomerulotubular Balance
* Maintains fractional reabsorption (typically ~65%)
* Prevents distal tubule overloading during GFR fluctuations

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: A patient with a renin-secreting tumor develops hypertension but eventually returns to sodium balance despite persistent high aldosterone. Name this physiologic phenomenon.
back:
* Aldosterone Escape
* Mechanism: Rise in arterial pressure triggers pressure natriuresis
* Offsets the hormone-mediated sodium reabsorption

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Explain the nervous reflex initiated by the activation of low-pressure stretch receptors in the right atrium during volume expansion.
back:
* Inhibits renal sympathetic nerve activity
* Increases GFR and decreases tubular reabsorption
* Rapidly facilitates excretion of the excess fluid volume

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Contrast the acute pressure natriuresis response with the chronic response during a sustained increase in arterial pressure.
back:
* Acute: Limited to direct hemodynamic effects on the tubule
* Chronic: Amplified by suppression of Angiotensin II and Aldosterone
* Chronic response is significantly more effective at restoring balance

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Identify the three primary hormonal changes that work synergistically to facilitate sodium excretion when salt intake is elevated.
back:
* Decreased Angiotensin II formation
* Decreased Aldosterone secretion
* Increased Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) release

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase ECF volume but with normal blood volume
front: In Nephrotic Syndrome, the primary factor initiating fluid leakage into the interstitium and subsequent extracellular fluid (ECF) expansion is decreased [___].
back:
● Plasma colloid osmotic pressure
● Due to heavy loss of plasma proteins (albuminuria) in the urine
● Reduces the force retaining fluid within the vascular compartment.

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase ECF volume but with normal blood volume
front: A 55-year-old male with chronic liver cirrhosis presents with massive ascites and pedal edema. Despite the obvious increase in ECF volume, his effective blood volume is normal or reduced. Identify the dual pathophysiological mechanism in the liver responsible for this.
back:
● Decreased protein synthesis (lowered colloid osmotic pressure)
● Portal venous obstruction (increased capillary hydrostatic pressure)
● Leads to fluid transudation and secondary renal salt/water retention.

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase ECF volume but with normal blood volume
front: Explain the renal response to the reduction in plasma volume that occurs during the development of generalized edema in nephrotic syndrome.
back:
● Activation of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)
● Increased sympathetic nervous system activity
● Leads to avid renal sodium and water retention to restore blood volume.

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase ECF volume but with normal blood volume
front: Contrast the blood volume dynamics between Congestive Heart Failure and Nephrotic Syndrome when both present with massive ECF expansion.
back:
● Heart Failure: High ECF volume + High blood volume (renal retention overflows into both).
● Nephrotic Syndrome: High ECF volume + Normal/Low blood volume (fluid leaks out of vessels).

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase ECF volume but with normal blood volume
front: Identify the 'overflow reservoir' that protects the cardiovascular system from overload by accepting excess ECF during renal salt retention.
back:
● The Interstitial Spaces
● Act as a relief valve when extracellular volume rises 30-50% above normal
● Prevents dangerous overload that could lead to pulmonary edema.

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase ECF volume but with normal blood volume
front: Large-scale transudation of fluid and protein into the abdominal cavity specifically seen in cirrhosis is termed [___].
back:
● Ascites
● Caused by high portal capillary pressure and decreased plasma protein concentration.

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase ECF volume but with normal blood volume
front: A 6-year-old child presents with periorbital edema and hypoalbuminemia (<2 g/dl). Clinical diagnosis is minimal-change nephropathy. Why does the child's blood volume remain low despite the kidneys retaining sodium?
back:
● Low plasma colloid osmotic pressure allows retained fluid to leak into tissues.
● The vascular compartment cannot hold the retained salt/water effectively.

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase ECF volume but with normal blood volume
front: Explain how the compliance of the interstitial spaces changes once edema begins to develop, facilitating a massive increase in ECF volume.
back:
● Interstitial fluid pressure shifts from negative to positive.
● Tissues lose their low-compliance safety factor.
● Spaces become highly compliant, allowing large fluid accumulation with minimal pressure rise.

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase ECF volume but with normal blood volume
front: Contrast the initiating vascular trigger of ECF expansion in Nephrotic Syndrome vs. Liver Cirrhosis.
back:
● Nephrotic Syndrome: Primarily decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure (systemic capillaries).
● Liver Cirrhosis: Combined decreased colloid pressure AND increased portal capillary hydrostatic pressure.

category: Explain the conditions that cause large increase ECF volume but with normal blood volume
front: Which specific hormonal activation occurs in both cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome to prevent circulatory collapse despite ECF expansion?
back:
● Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)
● Triggered by decreased effective arterial blood volume
● Causes the kidneys to retain sodium and water indefinitely.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Sympathetic nervous system activation increases the effectiveness of fluid retention during hemorrhage by stimulating the release of [___] from the juxtaglomerular cells.
back:
* Renin.
* This initiates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).
* It significantly increases sodium and water reabsorption in the renal tubules to restore blood volume.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: A patient with congestive heart failure presents with generalized edema and persistent sodium retention. Explain the underlying feedback failure despite the expanded extracellular fluid volume.
back:
* Low cardiac output and arterial pressure are sensed as a "volume deficit."
* This activates sympathetic nerves and the RAAS.
* These signals override volume expansion sensors, causing the kidneys to continue retaining salt and water.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Contrast the effects of Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) and Aldosterone on the osmolarity and volume of excreted urine.
back:
* ADH: Increases water reabsorption independently of solutes, resulting in highly concentrated urine (high osmolarity).
* Aldosterone: Increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion, primarily regulating the total quantity of sodium and urine volume.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Contrast the renal-pressure natriuresis response to a high-sodium diet in a healthy individual versus a patient with an impaired ability to suppress Angiotensin II formation.
back:
* Healthy: Angiotensin II is suppressed, allowing the kidneys to excrete excess sodium with minimal blood pressure rise.
* Impaired: High Angiotensin II levels persist, requiring a dramatic increase in arterial pressure to drive sodium excretion via pressure natriuresis.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Identify the primary mechanism by which Angiotensin II increases the physical reabsorptive force within the peritubular capillaries.
back:
* Constriction of efferent arterioles.
* Lowers peritubular capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc).
* Increases filtration fraction, which raises peritubular colloid osmotic pressure (πc).
* Both changes facilitate bulk flow of fluid into the capillaries.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: In the renal-body fluid feedback system, the primary hormonal effector that regulates water reabsorption independently of solute excretion rate is [___].
back:
* Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) / Vasopressin.
* It acts on V2 receptors to increase water permeability in the late distal tubules and collecting ducts.
* This allows precise control of extracellular fluid osmolarity.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: A patient with primary aldosteronism (Conn Syndrome) exhibits hypertension but experiences an 'escape' from continuous sodium retention. Explain the physiological mechanism involved.
back:
* Initial sodium retention expands ECF volume and increases arterial pressure.
* Elevated pressure triggers pressure natriuresis and diuresis.
* Sodium output eventually matches intake at a higher blood pressure, preventing further volume expansion.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Explain why a renin-secreting tumor typically leads to severe hypertension but only minimal increases in total extracellular fluid volume.
back:
* Excessive Angiotensin II initially retains sodium.
* Resultant hypertension rapidly activates pressure natriuresis.
* The high pressure overrides the salt-retaining hormonal effect, establishing balance at an elevated pressure with near-normal volume.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Describe the negative feedback physiological loop initiated by a water deficit that results in increased extracellular fluid (ECF) osmolarity.
back:
* Hyperosmolarity causes hypothalamic osmoreceptors to shrink.
* Stimulates ADH release from the posterior pituitary.
* ADH increases water permeability in distal nephron segments.
* Increased water reabsorption dilutes ECF toward normal.

category: Explain the nervous and hormonal factors that increase the effectiveness of renal body fluid feedback control
front: Name the specific magnocellular neurons in the hypothalamus where the majority of Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) is synthesized.
back:
* Supraoptic nuclei (approx. 5/6ths).
* Paraventricular nuclei (approx. 1/6th).
* ADH is then transported down axons for storage and release in the posterior pituitary.

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
coreConcept: Carbonic Anhydrase Role in Acid-Base Balance
front: The enzyme [___] is essential in the proximal tubular epithelial cells for the rapid conversion of CO2 and water into carbonic acid to facilitate H+ secretion.
back:
• Carbonic anhydrase
• Facilitates dissociation of H2CO3 into H+ and HCO3-
• Present in both the tubular cell cytoplasm and the brush border.

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: A 5-year-old child presents with severe diarrhea and signs of metabolic acidosis. Describe the specific renal tubular response to restore pH.
back:
• Increased H+ secretion across all tubular segments.
• Complete reabsorption of filtered HCO3-.
• Generation of 'new' HCO3- via increased ammonia and phosphate buffering.

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Explain the mechanism of secondary active H+ secretion in the proximal tubule.
back:
• Mediated by the Sodium-Hydrogen Exchanger (NHE3) in the luminal membrane.
• Driven by the Na+ gradient established by the basolateral Na+-K+ ATPase.
• Accounts for roughly 90-95% of total H+ secretion.

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
coreConcept: Primary vs Secondary Active H+ Secretion
front: Contrast the H+ secretion mechanism of the early tubular segments (proximal tubule) with that of the late distal segments (collecting ducts).
back:
• Proximal: Secondary active transport (Na+/H+ counter-transport).
• Distal: Primary active transport (H+-ATPase and H+/K+-ATPase).
• Distal segments can secrete H+ against a much larger concentration gradient (900-fold).

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Identify the primary amino acid precursor used by the kidneys to generate ammonium (NH4+) and describe the byproduct generated for the blood.
back:
• Precursor: Glutamine (metabolized in proximal tubular cells).
• Byproduct: Two 'new' HCO3- ions are returned to the peritubular blood for every glutamine molecule.
• Helps replenish extracellular bicarbonate stores during acidosis.

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: In the late distal and collecting tubules, primary active secretion of hydrogen ions is specifically performed by [___] cells.
back:
• Type A Intercalated cells.
• These cells use H+-ATPase and H+-K+ ATPase pumps.
• Responsible for establishing the minimum urine pH of approximately 4.5.

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: A patient with primary aldosteronism (Conn Syndrome) presents with metabolic alkalosis. Explain the underlying renal H+ handling mechanism.
back:
• Aldosterone stimulates H+ secretion by Type A intercalated cells.
• Increased H+ secretion leads to excessive reabsorption and generation of HCO3-.
• The net result is an increase in extracellular fluid pH.

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Describe the 'ammonia trapping' mechanism in the medullary collecting ducts during chronic acidosis.
back:
• NH3 (ammonia) diffuses from cells into the tubular lumen.
• Secreted H+ reacts with NH3 to form NH4+ (ammonium).
• Luminal membrane is impermeable to NH4+, trapping it for urinary excretion.

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Contrast the net effect on blood HCO3- levels when H+ is titrated against filtered HCO3- versus when it is titrated against HPO4(2-) (phosphate buffer).
back:
• Filtered HCO3-: Results in simple reabsorption (net replacement).
• Phosphate Buffer: Results in the generation of 'new' HCO3- added to the blood.
• Titration against non-bicarbonate buffers is essential for correcting acid deficits.

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: State the minimum urinary pH achievable by the human kidneys and identify why H+ cannot be excreted purely as free ions.
back:
• Minimum pH: Approximately 4.5.
• Limit: Secretion against a 1000:1 gradient is the biological maximum.
• Buffers (ammonia/phosphate) are required to excrete the daily non-volatile acid load.

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: The secondary active secretion of hydrogen ions in the proximal tubule is primarily mediated by the [___] protein in the luminal membrane.
back:
• Sodium-hydrogen exchanger (NHE)
• Uses the sodium gradient (Na+-K+ ATPase) to drive H+ secretion
• Accounts for ~95% of bicarbonate reabsorption

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: A patient with severe diabetic ketoacidosis exhibits a massive increase in renal acid excretion. Identify the primary inducible buffer system utilized by the kidneys to excrete these excess H+ ions during chronic acidosis.
back:
• Ammonium (NH4+) buffer system
• Generated from glutamine metabolism
• Excretion of each NH4+ adds one 'new' HCO3- to the blood

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Explain the step-by-step mechanism of bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, given that the luminal membrane is impermeable to HCO3-.
back:
• Secreted H+ reacts with filtered HCO3- to form H2CO3
• Carbonic anhydrase converts H2CO3 to CO2 and H2O
• CO2 diffuses into cells, reforms H2CO3, which dissociates into reabsorbed HCO3- and H+

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
coreConcept: Primary vs. Secondary Active H+ Secretion
front: Contrast the hydrogen ion secretion mechanisms of the proximal tubule versus the Type A intercalated cells of the collecting duct.
back:
• Proximal: Secondary active transport (Na+/H+ exchanger); low gradient (pH ~6.7)
• Distal (Type A): Primary active transport (H+-ATPase/H+-K+ ATPase); high gradient (pH ~4.5)

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Identify the hormonal stimulus that directly activates H+-ATPase in Type A intercalated cells, and explain the resulting acid-base effect of its excess.
back:
• Aldosterone
• Stimulates H+ secretion and HCO3- reabsorption
• Excess causes metabolic alkalosis (e.g., Conn syndrome)

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: The [___] buffer system serves as the major titratable acid in the urine because its pK of 6.8 is close to the average tubular fluid pH.
back:
• Phosphate buffer system (HPO4=)
• Combines with H+ to form H2PO4-
• Capacity is limited by the amount of filtered phosphate

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
coreConcept: PCO2 Influence on Renal H+ Secretion
front: A patient presents with a plasma pH of 7.20 and a PCO2 of 60 mmHg. How does the increase in arterial CO2 directly stimulate the renal tubular cells to correct this condition?
back:
• High PCO2 increases intracellular CO2 in tubular cells
• Stimulates increased H+ formation and secretion
• Results in complete HCO3- reabsorption and 'new' HCO3- generation

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Describe the mathematical components used to calculate Net Acid Excretion (NAE) by the kidneys.
back:
• NAE = (NH4+ Excretion + Urinary Titratable Acid) - HCO3- Excretion
• NAE must equal nonvolatile acid production for balance
• In alkalosis, NAE becomes negative

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Contrast the functions of Type A and Type B intercalated cells regarding hydrogen and bicarbonate handling.
back:
• Type A: Secretes H+ and reabsorbs HCO3- (active in acidosis)
• Type B: Secretes HCO3- and reabsorbs H+ (active in alkalosis)
• Type B uses 'pendrin' for luminal HCO3- secretion

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: What is the minimum urinary pH achievable by the primary active H+ pumps in the distal nephron?
back:
• pH 4.5
• Represents a 900-fold concentration gradient of H+ ions
• Limit is essential for preventing tubular damage

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: In the proximal tubule, hydrogen ions are secreted into the tubular lumen primarily via the [___] secondary active transport protein.
back:
• Sodium-Hydrogen Exchanger (NHE)
• Couples Na+ reabsorption down its concentration gradient with H+ secretion
• Powered indirectly by the basolateral Na+-K+ ATPase pump

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: A patient with chronic metabolic acidosis shows a significant increase in urinary ammonium ($NH_4^+$) excretion. Identify the primary precursor metabolized by the renal tubules to produce this ammonium.
back:
• Glutamine
• Metabolized in proximal tubules to produce two NH4+ ions and two "new" HCO3- molecules
• Serves as the dominant mechanism for acid elimination during chronic acidosis

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Explain the cellular mechanism of bicarbonate "reabsorption" in the proximal tubule, noting why it is considered an indirect process.
back:
• Secreted H+ reacts with filtered HCO3- to form H2CO3, which dissociates into CO2 and H2O
• CO2 diffuses into the cell and reforms HCO3- via carbonic anhydrase
• One HCO3- enters the blood for every H+ secreted, though the original filtered molecule is not the one reabsorbed

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Contrast the $H^+$ secretory capacity and mechanisms of the proximal tubule versus the type A intercalated cells of the collecting duct.
back:
• Proximal Tubule: High capacity; uses secondary active transport (NHE); lowers pH to ~6.7
• Type A Intercalated Cells: Lower capacity but higher gradient; uses primary active transport (H+-ATPase); lowers pH to its minimum of ~4.5

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Explain how the secretion of hydrogen ions into the tubular lumen can result in the generation of "new" bicarbonate rather than simple reabsorption.
back:
• Occurs when secreted H+ combines with non-bicarbonate buffers (Phosphate or Ammonia)
• The HCO3- generated within the tubular cell enters the peritubular capillary as a net gain
• This replaces HCO3- stores lost during systemic buffering of non-volatile acids

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
coreConcept: Carbonic Anhydrase in Renal Acid-Base Handling
front: The enzyme [___], located in the brush border and cytoplasm of renal tubular cells, is essential for the rapid interconversion of $CO_2$ and $H_2O$ to $H_2CO_3$.
back:
• Carbonic Anhydrase
• Essential for both H+ secretion and HCO3- reabsorption
• Target of diuretics like acetazolamide, which causes metabolic acidosis

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: A patient presents with severe metabolic acidosis due to diabetic ketoacidosis. Describe the renal response regarding $H^+$ secretion and $NH_4^+$ production.
back:
• Increased H+ secretion ensures complete reabsorption of all filtered HCO3-
• Increased glutamine uptake and metabolism in the proximal tubule
• Massive increase in NH4+ excretion to carry excess H+ out of the body

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Explain the role of the phosphate buffer system in renal $H^+$ handling and its primary limitation.
back:
• Secreted H+ reacts with filtered HPO4(2-) to form H2PO4-
• Generates new HCO3- for the blood while excreting H+ as titratable acid
• Limitation: Capacity is strictly limited by the amount of filtered phosphate remaining after reabsorption

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Contrast the functions of Type A and Type B intercalated cells in the collecting tubule during acid-base disturbances.
back:
• Type A: Secretes H+ (luminal H+-ATPase) and reabsorbs HCO3- (basolateral Cl-/HCO3- exchanger); active in acidosis
• Type B: Secretes HCO3- (luminal pendrin) and reabsorbs H+ (basolateral H+-ATPase); active in alkalosis

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Define the term "titratable acid" and state why it does not include ammonium.
back:
• The amount of strong base (NaOH) needed to return urine pH to 7.4
• Represents H+ buffered by phosphate and organic acids
• Excludes NH4+ because the pK of ammonia (9.2) is too high for titration at pH 7.4

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: In the proximal tubule, the secondary active transport mechanism responsible for secreting hydrogen ions into the lumen in exchange for sodium is the [___].
back:
* Sodium-Hydrogen Exchanger (NHE3)
* Driven by the sodium gradient established by Na+-K+ ATPase
* Accounts for approximately 80-90% of total renal H+ secretion

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: A patient with Conn syndrome (primary aldosteronism) presents with hypertension and metabolic alkalosis. Explain the renal mechanism contributing to the high serum pH in this patient.
back:
* Aldosterone stimulates H+-ATPase in Type A intercalated cells
* Excess H+ secretion leads to over-reabsorption of HCO3-
* Generates "new" bicarbonate added to extracellular fluid

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Explain the role of carbonic anhydrase in the tubular reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate ions.
back:
* Catalyzes H2CO3 dissociation into CO2 and H2O in lumen
* CO2 diffuses into cells and recombines with H2O
* Intracellular H2CO3 dissociates to regenerate HCO3- for blood entry

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
coreConcept: Primary vs Secondary Active H+ Secretion
front: Contrast the hydrogen ion secretory power of the proximal tubule with that of the type A intercalated cells in the collecting duct.
back:
* Proximal Tubule: High capacity but low gradient; minimum pH ~6.7
* Type A Cells: Primary active transport (H+-ATPase)
* Can secrete H+ against 1000-fold gradient; minimum pH ~4.5

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Identify the primary source of hydrogen ion buffering in the tubular fluid once all filtered bicarbonate has been reabsorbed.
back:
* Phosphate buffer system (HPO4=)
* Ammonia buffer system (NH3)
* Combination with these buffers generates "new" bicarbonate for the blood

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: The amino acid primarily extracted from the blood to synthesize ammonium (NH4+) and "new" bicarbonate in the proximal tubular cells is [___].
back:
* Glutamine
* Each molecule yields two NH4+ ions and two HCO3- ions
* Synthesis is upregulated during chronic metabolic acidosis

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: A patient presents with severe diabetic ketoacidosis. Describe the renal response regarding the handling of ammonium during this chronic state.
back:
* Markedly increased glutamine metabolism
* Dominant mechanism for H+ elimination (up to 500 mEq/day)
* Provides the majority of new bicarbonate to replenish extracellular stores

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Describe the mechanism of "Ammonia Trapping" in the medullary collecting ducts.
back:
* NH3 diffuses freely into the tubular lumen
* Reacts with actively secreted H+ to form NH4+
* Luminal membrane is impermeable to NH4+, trapping it for excretion

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Contrast the renal handling of hydrogen ions during metabolic alkalosis versus metabolic acidosis.
back:
* Alkalosis: Incomplete H+ titration; excess HCO3- excreted in urine
* Acidosis: Excess H+ secretion; complete HCO3- reabsorption plus new HCO3- generation
* Acidosis involves NH4+ and titratable acid excretion

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Provide the formula used to quantify the net renal excretion of acid into the urine.
back:
* Net Acid Excretion = (NH4+ excretion + Titratable acid) - HCO3- excretion
* Measures the net addition of HCO3- to the blood
* Negative value indicates net loss of base (alkalosis)

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: In the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, the pH of extracellular fluid is primarily determined by the ratio of [___] to dissolved carbon dioxide.
back: Bicarbonate (HCO3⁻). An increase in this ratio raises pH (alkalosis), while a decrease in HCO3⁻ relative to PCO2 lowers pH (acidosis).

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: A 3-year-old child presents with severe watery diarrhea. Lab results show a pH of 7.25 and HCO3⁻ of 15 mEq/L. Identify the primary acid-base disturbance.
back: Metabolic Acidosis. Loss of bicarbonate-rich intestinal secretions leads to a primary decrease in plasma HCO3⁻, resulting in a state of acidemia.

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: Explain the renal compensatory mechanism during chronic respiratory acidosis characterized by persistently elevated PCO2.
back: The kidneys increase hydrogen ion secretion and generate 'new' bicarbonate via the ammonia and phosphate buffer systems, raising plasma HCO3⁻ to return pH toward normal.

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: Contrast the plasma electrolyte findings in metabolic acidosis caused by severe diarrhea versus diabetic ketoacidosis.
back: Diarrhea causes a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis as Cl⁻ replaces lost HCO3⁻. DKA causes a high anion gap due to the accumulation of unmeasured ketoanions.

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: Describe the primary acid-base disturbance and compensatory response in a person ascending rapidly to high altitude.
back: Disturbance: Respiratory Alkalosis due to hyperventilation-induced PCO2 loss. Compensation: Renal excretion of HCO3⁻ to decrease plasma base levels and return pH toward normal.

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: The condition characterized by a primary decrease in PCO2 due to excessive pulmonary ventilation is termed [___].
back: Respiratory Alkalosis. This results in an increased pH and triggers a compensatory renal response to decrease HCO3⁻ reabsorption and increase its excretion.

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: An infant with pyloric stenosis presents with projectile vomiting. Labs show pH 7.55 and HCO3⁻ 34 mEq/L. Identify the disturbance and expected respiratory compensation.
back: Disturbance: Metabolic Alkalosis from loss of gastric HCl. Compensation: Alveolar hypoventilation to retain CO2, thereby increasing H2CO3 and lowering the pH toward normal.

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: Analyze the 'titration' principle between filtered HCO3⁻ and secreted H⁺ in the renal tubules during metabolic alkalosis.
back: Secreted H⁺ is insufficient to react with all filtered HCO3⁻. The excess HCO3⁻ is not reabsorbed and is excreted in urine, effectively removing base from extracellular fluid.

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: Distinguish between an uncompensated and a fully compensated respiratory acidosis based on blood pH and HCO3⁻ levels.
back: Uncompensated: pH is low (<7.35) with normal HCO3⁻. Fully Compensated: pH returns to low-normal (7.35-7.40) while HCO3⁻ is significantly elevated above 24 mEq/L.

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: Specify the clinical formula used to estimate the plasma anion gap for diagnosing metabolic acidosis.
back: Anion Gap = [Na⁺] - ([Cl⁻] + [HCO3⁻]). Normal range is 8–16 mEq/L, representing unmeasured anions like albumin, phosphates, and sulfates.

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: Metabolic acidosis is primarily characterized by a decrease in the plasma concentration of [___].
back:
• Bicarbonate ($HCO_3^-$)
• Leads to a drop in pH (< 7.4)
• Triggers respiratory compensation (hyperventilation) to lower $PCO_2$

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: A 65-year-old male with severe emphysema presents with pH 7.30 and $PCO_2$ 60 mm Hg. Identify the primary disturbance.
back:
• Respiratory Acidosis
• Caused by decreased alveolar ventilation (CO2 retention)
• Renal compensation gradually increases $HCO_3^-$ to raise pH

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: Explain the respiratory center's response to an increase in extracellular fluid hydrogen ion concentration.
back:
• Stimulates alveolar ventilation (hyperventilation)
• Increases $CO_2$ removal from the lungs
• Reduces $PCO_2$ and $H_2CO_3$ levels
• Returns pH toward normal (7.4)

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: Contrast the serum $HCO_3^-$ levels in acute versus chronic respiratory acidosis.
back:
• Acute: Minimal rise in $HCO_3^-$ (primary chemical buffering only)
• Chronic: Significant rise in $HCO_3^-$ (renal compensation via new bicarbonate generation and increased ammonia excretion)

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: Specify the clinical formula used to estimate the plasma anion gap in metabolic acidosis.
back:
• $[Na^+] - ([Cl^-] + [HCO_3^-])$
• Normal range: 8–16 mEq/L
• High Gap: Excess non-volatile acids (e.g., lactate, ketoacids)
• Normal Gap: $HCO_3^-$ loss (e.g., diarrhea)

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: The normal physiological range for arterial blood pH is [___] to [___].
back:
• 7.35 to 7.45
• Average arterial value: 7.40
• Venous blood/interstitial fluid: ~7.35 (due to higher $CO_2$)

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: A patient with persistent gastric vomiting presents with a pH of 7.55 and $HCO_3^-$ of 36 mEq/L. Identify the pathophysiology.
back:
• Metabolic Alkalosis
• Caused by loss of gastric HCl
• Compensation involves hypoventilation (retaining $CO_2$) and increased renal $HCO_3^-$ excretion

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: Describe the three renal mechanisms used to correct extracellular fluid acidosis.
back:
• Secretion of excess $H^+$
• Reabsorption of all filtered $HCO_3^-$
• Production of "new" $HCO_3^-$ (via phosphate and ammonia buffering systems)

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: Contrast the primary chemical markers of Respiratory Alkalosis versus Metabolic Alkalosis.
back:
• Respiratory: Low $PCO_2$ (primary), low $HCO_3^-$ (compensation)
• Metabolic: High $HCO_3^-$ (primary), high $PCO_2$ (compensation)

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: State the isohydric principle's implication for body fluid buffer systems.
back:
• All buffers in a common solution are in equilibrium with the same $H^+$ concentration
• A shift in one buffer system causes a parallel shift in all others

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: In a patient suffering from severe emphysema, the primary acid-base disturbance is respiratory acidosis, which is chemically defined by a decrease in pH and an increase in arterial [___].
back:
• PCO2 (partial pressure of carbon dioxide).
• Caused by decreased alveolar ventilation and CO2 retention.
• Leads to increased H2CO3 and H+ concentrations.

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: A 3-year-old child presents with severe watery diarrhea. Laboratory findings show a pH of 7.25 and HCO3- of 15 mEq/L. Identify the disturbance and the expected respiratory compensatory response.
back:
• Metabolic acidosis.
• Respiratory compensation: Hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing) to reduce PCO2.
• Caused by excessive loss of sodium bicarbonate in the feces.

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: Explain the cellular mechanism by which a rise in extracellular PCO2 directly stimulates renal H+ secretion in the proximal tubule.
back:
• CO2 diffuses into tubular cells and forms H2CO3 via carbonic anhydrase.
• H2CO3 dissociates into H+ and HCO3-.
• Increased intracellular H+ stimulates the Na+-H+ counter-transporter to secrete H+ into the lumen.

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
front: Contrast the primary laboratory abnormalities and compensatory limits in respiratory alkalosis versus metabolic alkalosis.
back:
• Respiratory Alkalosis: Primary ↓PCO2; Compensation is renal HCO3- excretion.
• Metabolic Alkalosis: Primary ↑HCO3-; Compensation is hypoventilation (↑PCO2).
• Limitation: Respiratory compensation for metabolic alkalosis is limited by the stimulus of hypoxemia.

category: Analyze the acid base disturbances on the basis of pH, HCO3 and CO2
coreConcept: Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibition and Acid-Base Status
front: Describe the physiological effect of acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) on urinary HCO3- excretion and its subsequent impact on blood pH.
back:
• Inhibits HCO3- reabsorption in the proximal tubule.
• Increases urinary HCO3- excretion (alkaline urine).
• Causes metabolic acidosis in the blood due to loss of the primary extracellular buffer.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Severe diarrhea leads to metabolic acidosis primarily due to the excessive loss of [___] in the feces.
back:
• Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3)
• Gastrointestinal secretions are rich in bicarbonate
• Loss of base shifts the Henderson-Hasselbalch ratio towards acidosis

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: A 15-year-old male with type 1 diabetes presents with deep, labored breathing and a blood pH of 7.1. Identify the specific respiratory pattern and its purpose.
back:
• Kussmaul breathing
• Represents respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis
• Increases alveolar ventilation to blow off CO2 and raise pH

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Explain the respiratory feedback mechanism triggered by a significant decrease in extracellular fluid pH.
back:
• Low pH stimulates peripheral and central chemoreceptors
• Triggers increased alveolar ventilation rate
• Reduces PCO2, which decreases H2CO3 and H+ concentrations

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Contrast the typical causes of High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (HAGMA) with those of Normal Anion Gap (Hyperchloremic) Acidosis.
back:
• HAGMA: Diabetes (ketoacids), lactic acidosis, renal failure, salicylate poisoning
• Normal Gap: Diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis (RTA), carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
• Differentiated by the presence of unmeasured anions

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Identify the primary amino acid substrate utilized by the kidneys to generate ammonium (NH4+) and 'new' bicarbonate during chronic acidosis.
back:
• Glutamine
• Metabolized in proximal tubular cells into two NH4+ and two HCO3-
• NH4+ is secreted; HCO3- enters blood as 'new' buffer

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: In metabolic acidosis, the kidneys contribute 'new' bicarbonate to the blood when secreted H+ combines with [___] instead of filtered HCO3-.
back:
• Non-bicarbonate buffers
• Primarily phosphate (HPO4=) and ammonia (NH3)
• This process replenishes extracellular bicarbonate stores

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: A patient presents with metabolic acidosis after ingesting ethylene glycol (antifreeze). Describe the expected effect on the plasma anion gap.
back:
• Increased Anion Gap
• Ethylene glycol metabolizes into glycolic and oxalic acids
• These unmeasured anions replace bicarbonate in the plasma

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Describe the cellular mechanism by which the phosphate buffer system generates new bicarbonate during acidosis.
back:
• Secreted H+ combines with filtered HPO4=
• Forms H2PO4- which is excreted as titratable acid
• The cellular HCO3- generated during H+ production enters peritubular blood

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Contrast the speed and efficiency of the respiratory versus renal systems in compensating for metabolic acidosis.
back:
• Respiratory: Rapid (minutes), but only 50–75% effective in returning pH to normal
• Renal: Slow (hours to days), but the most powerful and complete compensation

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Provide the clinical formula used to estimate the plasma anion gap during the workup of metabolic acidosis.
back:
• [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-])
• Normal range is typically 8–16 mEq/L
• Represents unmeasured anions like albumin, phosphate, and organic acids

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Metabolic acidosis is fundamentally characterized by a primary decrease in the extracellular fluid concentration of [___].
back:
• Bicarbonate (HCO3−)
• Leads to a decreased HCO3−/CO2 ratio
• Results in a drop in blood pH below 7.4

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
coreConcept: Metabolic Acidosis in Chronic Renal Failure
front: A patient with end-stage renal disease presents with a blood pH of 7.15 and low bicarbonate. Describe the primary renal pathophysiology contributing to this acid-base imbalance.
back:
• Failure to excrete nonvolatile metabolic acids
• Decreased filtration of phosphate buffers
• Impaired ammonium (NH4+) synthesis and excretion
• Resultant inability to generate sufficient "new" bicarbonate

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Explain the physiological mechanism by which the respiratory system compensates for a sudden drop in plasma pH during metabolic acidosis.
back:
• Increased [H+] stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors
• Alveolar ventilation rate increases (hyperventilation)
• Rapidly reduces extracellular PCO2
• Returns the HCO3−/PCO2 ratio toward normal to raise pH

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Contrast the effects on the plasma anion gap in a patient with severe diarrhea versus a patient with uncontrolled type 1 diabetes mellitus.
back:
• Diarrhea: Normal Anion Gap (Hyperchloremic) due to direct HCO3− loss replaced by Cl−
• Diabetes: Increased Anion Gap due to accumulation of unmeasured ketoacid anions (acetoacetate/beta-hydroxybutyrate)

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Identify the primary renal buffer system responsible for the majority of "new" bicarbonate generation during chronic metabolic acidosis.
back:
• Ammonia-Ammonium (NH3/NH4+) buffer system
• Renal glutamine metabolism produces 2 NH4+ and 2 new HCO3−
• NH4+ is trapped in the lumen and excreted

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: The primary mechanism for hydrogen ion secretion in the proximal tubule and thick ascending limb is [___] counter-transport.
back:
• Sodium-hydrogen counter-transport (NHE)
• Energy derived from the sodium gradient established by Na+-K+ ATPase
• Responsible for ~95% of total bicarbonate reabsorption

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: A patient presents with persistent vomiting leading to metabolic alkalosis. Describe the renal response regarding the filtered bicarbonate load and H+ titration.
back:
• Tubular H+ secretion decreases
• Bicarbonate/H+ ratio in tubular fluid increases
• Excess filtered bicarbonate is not titrated by H+ and is excreted in urine

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Explain the role of carbonic anhydrase in the luminal reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate.
back:
• Catalyzes CO2 + H2O into H2CO3 in the lumen (from filtered HCO3- and secreted H+)
• H2CO3 dissociates to CO2 and H2O, which diffuse into tubular cells
• Reconstitutes HCO3- inside the cell for basolateral transport

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
coreConcept: Primary vs Secondary Active H+ Secretion
front: Contrast the hydrogen ion secretion systems of the early tubular segments with those of the late distal and collecting tubules.
back:
• Early (Proximal/TAL): Secondary active transport via Na+-H+ counter-transport
• Late (Collecting Ducts): Primary active transport via H+-ATPase and H+-K+ ATPase
• Late segments can secrete H+ against a 900-fold gradient

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Identify the non-bicarbonate urinary buffer system that utilizes sodium salts to excrete excess H+ as 'titratable acid.'
back:
• Phosphate buffer system (HPO4=)
• Combines with excess secreted H+ to form H2PO4-
• Excreted as NaH2PO4, resulting in the addition of one 'new' HCO3- to blood

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: For each molecule of [___] metabolized in the proximal tubule epithelial cells, two ammonium ions are secreted and two 'new' bicarbonate ions are reabsorbed into the blood.
back:
• Glutamine
• Metabolism occurs during acidosis
• Key source of NH4+ in early tubular segments

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: A patient develops chronic metabolic acidosis. Explain why the ammonia buffer system eventually dominates over the phosphate system in H+ elimination.
back:
• Chronic acidosis stimulates hepatic glutamine production and renal glutamine metabolism
• Ammonia production is physiologically upregulated (up to 500 mEq/day)
• Unlike phosphate, ammonia supply is not limited by filtered load

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Explain the mechanism of 'ammonia trapping' in the medullary collecting ducts during states of excess H+ secretion.
back:
• NH3 (gas) diffuses from interstitium into the tubular lumen
• Combines with actively secreted H+ to form NH4+
• Luminal membrane is impermeable to NH4+, trapping it for excretion

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Contrast the function of Type A and Type B intercalated cells in the cortical collecting tubule regarding H+ handling.
back:
• Type A: Secretes H+ and reabsorbs HCO3-/K+ (Active in Acidosis)
• Type B: Reabsorbs H+ and secretes HCO3-/K+ via Pendrin (Active in Alkalosis)
• Have transporters on opposite membrane sides

category: Explain the renal handling of H + ion
front: Provide the clinical formula used to quantify 'Net Acid Excretion' (NAE) by the kidneys.
back:
• NAE = NH4+ excretion + Titratable acid - HCO3- excretion
• Represents total H+ removed from body fluids
• Equals the rate of net HCO3- addition to the blood

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Metabolic acidosis is primarily defined by a decrease in the extracellular fluid concentration of [___].
back: Bicarbonate ($HCO_3^-$). This reduction decreases the $HCO_3^-/Pco_2$ ratio, lowering the blood pH.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: A 5-year-old presenting with severe watery diarrhea for 3 days has a blood pH of 7.2. Explain the underlying acid-base pathophysiology.
back: Metabolic acidosis caused by the loss of large amounts of sodium bicarbonate ($NaHCO_3$) in the feces.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Explain the respiratory center's feedback response to a decrease in arterial blood pH during metabolic acidosis.
back: Low pH stimulates chemoreceptors to increase alveolar ventilation (hyperventilation); this 'blows off' $CO_2$, reducing $Pco_2$ to return pH toward normal.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Contrast the plasma anion gap findings in metabolic acidosis caused by renal tubular acidosis versus diabetic ketoacidosis.
back: Renal tubular acidosis: Normal anion gap (Hyperchloremic). Diabetic ketoacidosis: Increased anion gap due to unmeasured ketoanions (acetoacetate).

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Identify the primary source and metabolic pathway used by the kidneys to generate 'new' bicarbonate during chronic metabolic acidosis.
back: Glutamine metabolism in the proximal tubules; it produces two $NH_4^+$ ions (excreted) and two 'new' $HCO_3^-$ ions (added to blood).

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: In the renal correction of metabolic acidosis, the minimum urine pH that can be achieved in the collecting tubules is [___].
back: 4.5. This allows for a maximum $H^+$ concentration gradient of about 900-fold compared to plasma.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: A patient with chronic renal failure presents with a high plasma anion gap. Explain why the kidneys fail to maintain acid-base balance in this condition.
back: Failure to excrete metabolic acid anions and reduced production of $NH_4^+$, preventing the generation of sufficient 'new' $HCO_3^-$.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Explain the mechanism by which 'new' bicarbonate is added to the blood when secreted $H^+$ reacts with filtered phosphate buffers.
back: Once filtered $HCO_3^-$ is fully reabsorbed, excess $H^+$ combines with $HPO_4^{2-}$; the $HCO_3^-$ simultaneously generated in the tubular cell enters the blood as a net gain.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Contrast the efficiency and onset of respiratory compensation versus renal compensation in metabolic acidosis.
back: Respiratory: Rapid onset (minutes), 50-75% effective. Renal: Slow onset (hours to days), more powerful and can return pH to near-normal.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic acidosis
front: Identify three non-volatile acids or their precursors that cause metabolic acidosis when ingested in toxic amounts.
back: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid), Methyl alcohol (formic acid), and Ethylene glycol (glycolic acid).

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: In response to metabolic alkalosis, Type B intercalated cells in the collecting tubule secrete bicarbonate into the lumen via the apical [___] counter-transporter.
back:
• Pendrin (Cl-/HCO3- exchanger).
• This mechanism actively eliminates excess base from the extracellular fluid while reabsorbing hydrogen ions via basolateral H+-ATPases.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: A 3-week-old infant presents with projectile, non-bilious vomiting and dehydration. Labs show pH 7.55 and HCO3- 34 mEq/L. Identify the primary acid-base disturbance and the initial renal compensatory goal.
back:
• Metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of HCl).
• Renal Goal: Excretion of excess filtered HCO3-.
• Mechanism: Reduced H+ secretion leads to incomplete titration and failure of bicarbonate reabsorption.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: Explain the respiratory compensatory mechanism initiated by a primary increase in extracellular bicarbonate concentration.
back:
• Increased pH inhibits medullary cheoreceptors.
• Alveolar ventilation rate decreases (hypoventilation).
• Arterial PCO2 rises (hypercapnia).
• The resulting respiratory acidosis shifts the pH back toward the normal range (7.4).

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: Contrast the saline responsiveness of metabolic alkalosis caused by chronic vomiting versus that caused by primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn Syndrome).
back:
• Vomiting: Saline-responsive; volume depletion sustains alkalosis via Ang II/Aldosterone; corrected by NaCl infusion.
• Conn Syndrome: Saline-resistant; alkalosis is driven by direct hormonal stimulation of H+ secretion; not corrected by volume expansion.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: Outline why extracellular fluid volume depletion (Contraction Alkalosis) prevents the kidneys from correcting metabolic alkalosis.
back:
• Low volume activates the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS).
• Angiotensin II stimulates apical Na+/H+ exchange.
• Aldosterone stimulates H+ secretion in intercalated cells.
• Both prioritize Na+ reabsorption over pH normalization, causing inappropriate HCO3- retention.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: Metabolic alkalosis is characterized by an arterial pH above 7.4 and a primary increase in the extracellular fluid concentration of [___].
back:
• Bicarbonate (HCO3-).
• Occurs through excessive gain of base or loss of hydrogen ions (H+).
• Usually involves a failure of the kidneys to excrete excess bicarbonate.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: A neonate with pyloric stenosis presents with persistent vomiting of gastric contents. Explain the resulting acid-base disturbance and the specific ion loss involved.
back:
• Diagnosis: Metabolic alkalosis.
• Pathophysiology: Loss of hydrochloric acid (HCl) from the stomach.
• Result: Net loss of H+ ions leads to an increase in plasma bicarbonate concentration.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: Explain how the respiratory system carries out its biological function to compensate for a primary increase in plasma bicarbonate.
back:
• Step 1: Inhibition of hypothalamic respiratory centers.
• Step 2: Decreased rate of alveolar ventilation.
• Step 3: Elevation of extracellular Pco2, which shifts the pH back toward normal.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: Contrast the renal handling of bicarbonate during metabolic alkalosis versus metabolic acidosis.
back:
• Alkalosis: Filtered HCO3- exceeds secreted H+; excess HCO3- is excreted in urine.
• Acidosis: Secreted H+ exceeds filtered HCO3-; all HCO3- is reabsorbed and new HCO3- is generated via NH4+ excretion.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: Identify the hormonal step by which extracellular fluid volume depletion maintains a state of metabolic alkalosis.
back:
• Activation of Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System.
• Angiotensin II stimulates apical Na+-H+ exchange.
• Aldosterone stimulates H+ secretion by intercalated cells, driving excessive bicarbonate reabsorption.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: During alkalosis, the [___] intercalated cells of the collecting tubules secrete bicarbonate into the lumen while reabsorbing hydrogen ions.
back:
• Type B.
• Utilize the chloride-bicarbonate counter-transporter (pendrin) on the apical membrane.
• Move H+ into the blood via basolateral H+-ATPase.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: A patient with heart failure taking loop diuretics develops a high plasma pH and elevated HCO3-. Outline the underlying pathophysiology.
back:
• Mechanism: Diuretics cause volume depletion and increased distal flow.
• Effect: Stimulation of Ang II and Aldosterone.
• Result: Enhanced renal H+ secretion and HCO3- reabsorption leads to metabolic alkalosis.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: Describe the physiological mechanism that limits the effectiveness of respiratory compensation during severe metabolic alkalosis.
back:
• Inhibition of ventilation raises Pco2 but simultaneously lowers arterial Po2 (hypoxemia).
• Low Po2 stimulates oxygen-sensitive chemoreceptors.
• This force opposes the respiratory depression, preventing complete pH normalization.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: Contrast the primary chemical changes in the 'physiological loop' of respiratory alkalosis versus metabolic alkalosis.
back:
• Respiratory Alkalosis: Primary decrease in Pco2 (hyperventilation); compensated by renal HCO3- excretion.
• Metabolic Alkalosis: Primary increase in HCO3- (acid loss); compensated by respiratory CO2 retention (increased Pco2).

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: How does excessive aldosterone secretion in Conn syndrome directly influence urine pH and blood bicarbonate?
back:
• Stimulates H+ secretion in collecting ducts.
• Leads to the formation of acidic urine.
• Causes excessive addition of new HCO3- to blood, resulting in metabolic alkalosis.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: Metabolic alkalosis is defined by a primary increase in extracellular [___] concentration, leading to an arterial pH above 7.4.
back:
• Bicarbonate (HCO3-)
• Results in a decreased hydrogen ion (H+) concentration
• Often associated with a secondary increase in PCO2 via respiratory compensation.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: A neonate with persistent projectile vomiting due to pyloric stenosis presents with lethargy. ABG shows pH 7.55 and elevated HCO3-. Identify the ionic loss responsible for this acid-base state.
back:
• Metabolic alkalosis
• Caused by loss of Hydrogen (H+) and Chloride (Cl-) ions as Hydrochloric acid (HCl)
• Results in increased plasma bicarbonate levels as H+ is lost.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: Explain the role of the respiratory center in compensating for an increased plasma bicarbonate concentration.
back:
• High pH inhibits peripheral and central chemoreceptors
• Leads to decreased alveolar ventilation (hypoventilation)
• Causes CO2 retention, increasing PCO2 to shift pH back toward normal.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: A patient with hypertension has pH 7.54 and high HCO3-. Contrast the expected urinary chloride findings in Chloride-Responsive versus Chloride-Resistant metabolic alkalosis.
back:
• Chloride-Responsive (e.g., diuretics/vomiting): Urine Cl- < 20 mEq/L; corrected by saline.
• Chloride-Resistant (e.g., Conn’s syndrome): Urine Cl- > 20 mEq/L; associated with mineralocorticoid excess.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: Describe how excessive aldosterone secretion (e.g., Conn syndrome) causes the development of metabolic alkalosis.
back:
• Stimulates H+ secretion by Type A intercalated cells in collecting ducts
• Increases new HCO3- generation and reabsorption into blood
• Associated hypokalemia further stimulates renal H+ secretion.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
coreConcept: Hypokalemia in the maintenance of alkalosis
front: In metabolic alkalosis, hypokalemia maintains the disturbance because [___] ions shift into the intracellular fluid in exchange for potassium, further raising extracellular pH.
back:
• Hydrogen (H+)
• This shift reduces extracellular H+ concentration
• Intracellular acidosis in renal cells also stimulates tubular H+ secretion and HCO3- reabsorption.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: A patient using high-dose Furosemide (loop diuretic) presents with metabolic alkalosis. Explain the mechanism known as "Contraction Alkalosis" in this context.
back:
• Loss of extracellular fluid volume (isotonic NaCl/H2O)
• Bicarbonate remains in a smaller total fluid volume
• Increases the concentration of existing HCO3- in the plasma.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: Describe the specific cellular mechanism in the cortical collecting duct used to excrete excess bicarbonate during alkalosis.
back:
• Activation of Type B intercalated cells
• Pendrin (Cl-/HCO3- exchanger) on the apical membrane secretes HCO3- into the lumen
• H+-ATPase on the basolateral membrane pumps H+ back into the blood.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: Contrast the renal handling of filtered bicarbonate (HCO3-) in metabolic acidosis versus metabolic alkalosis.
back:
• Acidosis: Secreted H+ exceeds filtered HCO3-; all HCO3- is reabsorbed.
• Alkalosis: Filtered HCO3- exceeds secreted H+; excess HCO3- is excreted in urine to lower pH.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of metabolic alkalosis
front: Identify the primary pharmacological treatment to neutralize excess base in severe metabolic alkalosis when immediate correction is needed.
back:
• Ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) administration
• Liver converts NH4Cl into urea, releasing HCl
• HCl reacts with bicarbonate buffers to shift pH in the acidic direction.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: Respiratory acidosis is primarily initiated by a pathological decrease in alveolar ventilation, which leads to a primary increase in extracellular fluid [___].
back:
• PCO2 (partial pressure of carbon dioxide).
• Resultant increase in H2CO3 and H+ concentration.
• Commonly termed hypercapnia.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
coreConcept: Clinical Presentation of Chronic Respiratory Acidosis
front: A 65-year-old heavy smoker with a barrel chest presents with lethargy and disorientation. Arterial blood gas (ABG) shows a pH of 7.28 and PCO2 of 65 mmHg. Identify the acid-base disturbance and the most likely underlying condition.
back:
• Respiratory Acidosis.
• Likely caused by Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) or Emphysema.
• Impaired gas exchange leads to CO2 retention.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: Explain the kidneys' immediate versus long-term response to sustained elevation of arterial PCO2.
back:
• Immediate: Chemical buffering by intracellular proteins and hemoglobin.
• Long-term (3-5 days): Kidneys increase H+ secretion, reabsorb all filtered HCO3-, and generate new HCO3- via ammonium excretion.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: Contrast the renal handling of bicarbonate (HCO3-) in respiratory acidosis versus metabolic alkalosis.
back:
• Respiratory Acidosis: Decreased HCO3-/H+ ratio in tubules; all filtered HCO3- is reabsorbed.
• Metabolic Alkalosis: Increased HCO3-/H+ ratio in tubules; excess HCO3- is excreted in the urine.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
coreConcept: Ammonia Buffering and New Bicarbonate Generation
front: Explain the role of the ammonium (NH4+) buffer system in compensating for chronic respiratory acidosis.
back:
• Dominant mechanism for eliminating excess H+.
• Glutamine metabolism in proximal tubules increases NH4+ production.
• For every NH4+ excreted, a 'new' HCO3- is added to the blood.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: During renal compensation for acidosis, the [___] cells of the late distal and collecting tubules perform primary active secretion of H+ via the H+-ATPase pump.
back:
• Type A intercalated cells.
• These cells can secrete H+ against a large concentration gradient.
• Enables urine pH to drop as low as 4.5.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: A patient with severe pneumonia exhibits a PCO2 of 55 mmHg and a pH of 7.32. Their plasma HCO3- is 28 mEq/L. Determine if this represents acute or chronic compensation.
back:
• Chronic (partially compensated) Respiratory Acidosis.
• Plasma HCO3- has risen above the normal 24 mEq/L.
• Indicates the kidneys have had several days to generate and reabsorb additional bicarbonate.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
coreConcept: Direct CO2 Effect on Tubular Secretion
front: Detail the cellular mechanism by which increased extracellular PCO2 directly stimulates tubular H+ secretion.
back:
• Elevated CO2 diffuses into tubular epithelial cells.
• Carbonic anhydrase converts CO2 + H2O into H2CO3.
• H2CO3 dissociates into H+ (secreted) and HCO3- (reabsorbed into blood).

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: Contrast the respiratory compensation seen in metabolic acidosis with the 'respiratory' status in primary respiratory acidosis.
back:
• Metabolic Acidosis: Lungs increase ventilation to decrease PCO2 (compensation).
• Respiratory Acidosis: Lungs are the source of pathology (hypoventilation); they cannot compensate for themselves.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: Identify three non-pulmonary causes that can trigger respiratory acidosis by suppressing the respiratory center.
back:
• Damage to the medulla oblongata (trauma).
• Narcotic or opioid overdose.
• Severe anesthesia or sedative use.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Respiratory alkalosis is primarily initiated by a decrease in arterial [___] due to alveolar hyperventilation.
back:
- PCO2 (Partial pressure of carbon dioxide).
- A reduction in PCO2 increases the HCO3- / PCO2 ratio, thereby raising blood pH.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: A 19-year-old medical student presents with rapid breathing, perioral numbness, and carpopedal spasms during a viva exam. Identify the underlying acid-base disturbance.
back:
- Respiratory alkalosis.
- Hyperventilation causes perioral numbness and spasms because alkalosis increases calcium binding to plasma proteins, reducing ionized calcium levels.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Explain the renal compensatory mechanism for chronic respiratory alkalosis.
back:
- Decreased PCO2 reduces H+ secretion by tubular cells.
- Filtered HCO3- is not fully titrated, increasing its urinary excretion.
- This lowers plasma bicarbonate concentration to return pH toward normal.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Contrast the magnitude of bicarbonate reduction in acute versus chronic respiratory alkalosis.
back:
- Acute: HCO3- falls ~2 mEq/L for every 10 mmHg drop in PCO2 (via chemical buffering).
- Chronic: HCO3- falls ~5 mEq/L for every 10 mmHg drop in PCO2 (via renal compensation).

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Identify the specific trigger for respiratory alkalosis observed when a person ascends to high altitudes.
back:
- Low atmospheric PO2 stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors.
- This activates the respiratory center to increase ventilation rate.
- Excess CO2 is "blown off," lowering PCO2 and raising pH.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: In respiratory alkalosis, the Henderson-Hasselbalch ratio of [HCO3-] / (0.03 ! PCO2) [___] as a direct consequence of hyperventilation.
back:
- Increases.
- This increased ratio mathematically results in alkalemia (pH > 7.4).

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: A patient with severe pneumonia and hypoxemia develops a PCO2 of 25 mmHg and pH of 7.52. Explain why this patient has alkalosis despite pulmonary pathology.
back:
- Hypoxemia stimulates oxygen-sensitive chemoreceptors to drive hyperventilation.
- This hyperventilation overrides the metabolic CO2 production rate, resulting in low arterial PCO2 and high pH.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Explain how the "isohydric principle" ensures that all buffer systems respond simultaneously to a drop in PCO2.
back:
- All buffer systems share a common H+ pool.
