- A shift in the bicarbonate system equilibrium immediately forces parallel shifts in protein and phosphate buffers to maintain chemical balance.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Distinguish between metabolic alkalosis and respiratory alkalosis using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.
back:
- Metabolic: Primary increase in the numerator (plasma [HCO3-]).
- Respiratory: Primary decrease in the denominator (arterial PCO2).

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Identify the timeframe required for maximal renal compensation to be achieved in sustained respiratory alkalosis.
back:
- 2 to 5 days.
- Renal adjustments involving H+ secretion and HCO3- excretion are significantly slower than immediate chemical buffering or respiratory changes.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: In respiratory alkalosis, the primary physiological disturbance is an excessive loss of CO₂ from the extracellular fluid resulting from [___].
back:
• Alveolar hyperventilation
• Characterized by decreased arterial PCO₂ (<40 mmHg)
• Results in an increased plasma pH (>7.45) due to a higher HCO₃⁻/CO₂ ratio.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: A trekker ascending K2 experiences rapid breathing and dizziness. Blood gas analysis reveals pH 7.51, PCO₂ 26 mmHg, and HCO₃⁻ 21 mEq/L. Identify the primary disturbance and the physiological stimulus for this change.
back:
• Respiratory Alkalosis
• Stimulus: Low PO₂ at high altitude
• Mechanism: Hypoxia activates peripheral chemoreceptors, triggering hyperventilation to increase oxygen uptake, which washes out CO₂.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Explain the renal mechanism responsible for achieving chronic compensation during persistent respiratory alkalosis.
back:
• Reduced PCO₂ decreases tubular H⁺ secretion
• Decreased H⁺ availability prevents complete reabsorption of filtered HCO₃⁻
• Increased urinary excretion of HCO₃⁻ lowers plasma bicarbonate concentration back toward a normal pH ratio.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Contrast the compensatory plasma bicarbonate shifts between acute and chronic respiratory alkalosis.
back:
• Acute: Minimal change (~2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg fall in PCO₂) via chemical buffering and intracellular shifts.
• Chronic: Significant change (~4-5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg fall in PCO₂) via renal HCO₃⁻ excretion.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Describe the initial acid-base disturbance seen in salicylate (aspirin) toxicity and its underlying cause.
back:
• Primary Respiratory Alkalosis
• Cause: Salicylates directly stimulate the medullary respiratory center
• Effect: Increased alveolar ventilation leads to rapid CO₂ depletion before metabolic acidosis typically develops.

category: Enlist the factors which increase and decrease the release of ADH
front: The most sensitive physiological stimulus for the release of antidiuretic hormone is a 1% increase in [___].
back: * Plasma osmolarity. * Sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors in the AV3V region. * Triggers rapid secretion from the posterior pituitary to increase renal water conservation.

category: Enlist the factors which increase and decrease the release of ADH
front: A 45-year-old trauma victim experiences a 15% reduction in blood volume due to hemorrhage. Describe the primary baroreceptor-mediated response regarding ADH secretion.
back: * Decreased stretch in arterial baroreceptors and cardiopulmonary receptors. * Leads to reflex stimulation of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei. * Results in massive ADH release to conserve water and restore blood pressure.

category: Enlist the factors which increase and decrease the release of ADH
coreConcept: Nausea as a Potent ADH Stimulant
front: Explain how severe nausea or vomiting influences the secretion of antidiuretic hormone.
back: * Nausea acts as an extremely potent non-osmotic stimulus for release. * ADH levels can increase up to 100 times the normal range. * Occurs via neural pathways independent of osmolarity or blood pressure status.

category: Enlist the factors which increase and decrease the release of ADH
front: Contrast the effects of Angiotensin II and Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis for ADH regulation.
back: * Angiotensin II: Stimulates the subfornical organ and lamina terminalis to increase ADH release during volume depletion. * ANP: Released during atrial stretch; directly inhibits ADH secretion to promote diuresis and reduce fluid overload.

category: Enlist the factors which increase and decrease the release of ADH
front: Enlist three common pharmacological agents or substances that act as potent inhibitors of ADH release from the posterior pituitary.
back: * Alcohol (Ethanol). * Clonidine (antihypertensive). * Haloperidol (dopamine blocker). * These substances decrease water reabsorption by suppressing central ADH secretion regardless of plasma osmolarity.

category: Enlist the factors which increase and decrease the release of ADH
front: In response to [___], the firing rate of magnocellular neurons in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei decreases, leading to water diuresis.
back: * Decreased plasma osmolarity (hypo-osmolarity). * This causes osmoreceptor swelling and subsequent inhibition of ADH release. * Results in decreased water permeability in collecting ducts and excretion of dilute urine.

category: Enlist the factors which increase and decrease the release of ADH
front: A patient with advanced liver cirrhosis presents with significant ascites and decreased effective arterial blood volume. Explain the expected effect on ADH release.
back: * Decreased effective volume is sensed by arterial baroreceptors. * This triggers non-osmotic stimulation of hypothalamic nuclei. * ADH release increases despite low plasma osmolarity, contributing to hyponatremia and water retention.

category: Enlist the factors which increase and decrease the release of ADH
front: Describe the baroreceptor-mediated mechanism that decreases ADH release when a patient moves from a standing to a supine position.
back: * Supine position increases venous return and cardiac filling. * This stretches low-pressure atrial baroreceptors, increasing their firing rate. * Signals to the hypothalamus inhibit ADH secretion, promoting diuresis to normalize circulating volume.

category: Enlist the factors which increase and decrease the release of ADH
front: Contrast the responsiveness of ADH secretion to changes in plasma osmolarity versus changes in extracellular fluid volume.
back: * Osmolarity: Highly sensitive; a 1% increase triggers release via hypothalamic osmoreceptors. * Volume: Less sensitive; requires a 10% decrease (hypovolemia) to stimulate significant secretion via baroreceptor reflexes.

category: Enlist the factors which increase and decrease the release of ADH
front: List four stimuli that non-osmotically increase the release of ADH during acute stress or physiological disturbances.
back: * Hypovolemia (decreased blood volume). * Hypotension (decreased blood pressure). * Severe nausea/vomiting. * Acute arterial hypoxia. * These stimuli override osmotic control to prioritize restoration of blood volume and hemodynamic stability.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: Respiratory acidosis is characterized by a decrease in the ratio of [___] in the renal tubular fluid, resulting in excess hydrogen ion availability.
back:
• HCO3- / H+ (Bicarbonate to Hydrogen ion ratio)
• A decrease in this ratio leads to complete reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate.
• Remaining excess hydrogen ions are excreted via urinary buffers.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
coreConcept: Causes and Compensation of Respiratory Acidosis
front: A 70-year-old male with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with a pH of 7.28 and a PaCO2 of 65 mmHg. Identify the primary cause of this acid-base disorder and the role of the renal system in this patient.
back:
• Diagnosis: Respiratory Acidosis.
• Cause: Hypoventilation leading to CO2 retention.
• Renal Role: Increased secretion of H+ and generation of new HCO3- to elevate plasma bicarbonate levels.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: Explain the cellular mechanism by which increased PCO2 in the blood stimulates renal hydrogen ion secretion in the proximal tubule.
back:
• High blood PCO2 raises PCO2 inside tubular cells.
• Intracellular CO2 and H2O form H2CO3, which dissociates into H+ and HCO3-.
• Increased H+ availability directly stimulates the Na+-H+ counter-transport mechanism to secrete protons into the lumen.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: Contrast the effectiveness of chemical buffering versus renal compensation in a patient who has suddenly stopped breathing (respiratory arrest).
back:
• Chemical Buffering: Occurs within seconds; prevents extreme pH shifts but cannot eliminate the excess CO2.
• Renal Compensation: Most powerful but slow; takes 3–5 days to reach maximum effectiveness in generating new bicarbonate.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: Explain why administration of Acetazolamide (a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) is contraindicated in a patient already suffering from respiratory acidosis.
back:
• Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule.
• This blocks the reabsorption of filtered HCO3- and prevents the secretion of H+.
• Consequently, it prevents renal compensation, causing a further drop in blood pH.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Respiratory alkalosis is primarily initiated by [___], which causes excessive elimination of carbon dioxide and a subsequent increase in extracellular pH.
back:
• Alveolar hyperventilation
• Results in decreased arterial PCO2 (hypocapnia)
• Shifs the Henderson-Hasselbalch ratio in favor of alkalosis

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: A 22-year-old medical student presents with rapid breathing, lightheadedness, and perioral numbness during a viva. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.52 and PCO2 25 mmHg. Identify the acid-base disturbance.
back:
• Acute Respiratory Alkalosis
• Caused by psychogenic hyperventilation (anxiety)
• PCO2 is below the normal 40 mmHg range

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Explain the renal mechanism responsible for compensating for a chronic reduction in arterial PCO2.
back:
• Reduction in tubular H+ secretion
• Incomplete reabsorption of filtered HCO3-
• Increased urinary excretion of HCO3-
• Result: Decreased plasma [HCO3-] to return pH toward normal

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Contrast the primary compensatory mechanism in metabolic acidosis with that of respiratory alkalosis.
back:
• Metabolic Acidosis: Respiratory compensation (increased ventilation to lower PCO2)
• Respiratory Alkalosis: Renal compensation (decreased HCO3- reabsorption/increased excretion)

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Identify the specific physiological stimulus encountered at high altitudes that triggers respiratory alkalosis.
back:
• Low atmospheric PO2 (Hypoxia)
• Stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors
• Triggers reflex hyperventilation and excessive CO2 washout

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: In the chronic phase of respiratory alkalosis, the net acid excretion by the kidneys becomes [___].
back:
• Negative
• Indicates a net loss of HCO3- from the blood
• Titratable acid and ammonium excretion drop to near zero

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: A patient with salicylate poisoning initially presents with hyperpnea and a pH of 7.50. Predict the PCO2 finding and the underlying cause of this early phase.
back:
• Low PCO2 (<35 mmHg)
• Direct stimulation of the medullary respiratory center by salicylates
• Leads to primary respiratory alkalosis

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Explain why acute respiratory alkalosis often manifests with carpopedal spasm and a positive Chvostek sign despite normal total serum calcium.
back:
• Low H+ concentration causes H+ to dissociate from albumin
• More calcium ions bind to the newly available negative sites on albumin
• Decreases ionized (free) calcium, causing hypocalcemic tetany

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: Contrast the time course required for respiratory vs. renal compensation in acid-base disturbances.
back:
• Respiratory: Rapid (starts in minutes; maximal in 12-24 hours)
• Renal: Slow (starts in hours; requires 3-5 days for maximal effect)

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory alkalosis
front: State the effect on the HCO3-/H+ ratio in the renal tubular fluid during an episode of hyperventilation.
back:
• The ratio increases
• Filtered HCO3- load exceeds the amount of secreted H+
• Leads to HCO3- spillage into the urine

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: Respiratory acidosis is characterized by a primary increase in extracellular fluid [___], which leads to a decrease in pH.
back:
• PCO2 (Partial pressure of carbon dioxide)
• Result of decreased alveolar ventilation (hypercapnia)
• Normal arterial PCO2 is ~40 mmHg; values >40 mmHg indicate acidosis

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
coreConcept: COPD as a Cause of Respiratory Acidosis
front: A 65-year-old male with severe emphysema presents with disorientation. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.25 and PCO2 60 mmHg. Explain the primary pathophysiology.
back:
• Respiratory acidosis
• Impaired alveolar gas exchange prevents CO2 elimination
• CO2 reacts with H2O to form H2CO3, which dissociates into excess H+ and HCO3-

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: Describe how the kidneys generate "new" bicarbonate to compensate for chronic respiratory acidosis.
back:
• Excess H+ is secreted into the tubular lumen
• H+ combines with non-bicarbonate buffers (Ammonia and Phosphate)
• For every H+ excreted with these buffers, one new HCO3- is returned to the blood

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: Contrast the plasma bicarbonate levels in acute versus chronic respiratory acidosis.
back:
• Acute: Minimal rise (~1 mEq/L per 10 mmHg PCO2 rise) due to immediate chemical buffering
• Chronic: Significant rise (~3.5-4 mEq/L per 10 mmHg PCO2 rise) due to renal compensation taking 3-5 days

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
coreConcept: Direct PCO2 Effect on Tubular Secretion
front: Identify the direct effect of increased plasma PCO2 on the renal tubular epithelial cells regarding hydrogen ion handling.
back:
• Stimulates H+ secretion
• CO2 diffuses into cells, forming H2CO3 via carbonic anhydrase
• Yields H+ for luminal secretion and HCO3- for basolateral reabsorption

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: In the presence of chronic respiratory acidosis, the most important renal buffer system for excreting excess hydrogen ions is the [___] system.
back:
• Ammonia (NH3/NH4+) system
• Derived from glutamine metabolism in proximal tubules
• Increases up to 10-fold (500 mEq/day) during chronic acidotic states

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: A patient with a morphine overdose exhibits shallow, infrequent breathing. Predict the immediate effect on the extracellular fluid HCO3- to CO2 ratio.
back:
• The ratio decreases
• PCO2 increases (denominator) due to depression of the medullary respiratory center
• Resultant decrease in pH according to the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: How does the Type A intercalated cell carry out its biological function to correct respiratory acidosis?
back:
• Active H+ secretion via luminal H+-ATPase and H+-K+-ATPase pumps
• Reabsorption of HCO3- across the basolateral membrane via Cl-/HCO3- exchangers
• Capable of secreting H+ against gradients up to 1000:1

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: Distinguish between the "titration" process in normal states versus respiratory acidosis within the renal tubules.
back:
• Normal: Filtered HCO3- and secreted H+ are roughly equal (~4320-4400 mEq)
• Acidosis: Secreted H+ greatly exceeds filtered HCO3-
• Excess H+ is excreted via non-bicarbonate buffers

category: Explain the causes and compensation of respiratory acidosis
front: State the lower limit of urine pH that can be achieved by the kidneys during maximal compensation for respiratory acidosis.
back:
• pH 4.5
• Corresponds to an H+ concentration of 0.03 mEq/L
• Occurs primarily in the medullary collecting ducts

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: A patient with a blood pH of 7.40, significantly elevated PCO2, and elevated HCO3- most likely has a [___] acid-base disorder.
back:
• Mixed acid-base disorder
• Specifically, a combination of Respiratory Acidosis and Metabolic Alkalosis
• The pH appears normal because the two primary disturbances cancel each other out.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
coreConcept: Mixed Respiratory Acidosis and Metabolic Alkalosis
front: A 65-year-old male with chronic emphysema (COPD) is administered high-dose loop diuretics for heart failure. Identify the likely resulting mixed acid-base disorder.
back:
• Chronic Respiratory Acidosis (from COPD hypoventilation)
• Metabolic Alkalosis (from diuretic-induced volume depletion/H+ secretion)
• Results in an elevated PCO2 and significantly elevated HCO3-.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: Explain the role of the medulla oblongata in the mixed acid-base disorder resulting from salicylate (aspirin) poisoning.
back:
• Direct stimulation of the medullary respiratory center causes hyperventilation.
• This induces primary Respiratory Alkalosis.
• Occurs simultaneously with primary Metabolic Acidosis due to interference with oxidative phosphorylation.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: Contrast the measured PCO2 in simple metabolic acidosis with its value in a mixed metabolic acidosis and respiratory acidosis condition.
back:
• Simple Metabolic Acidosis: PCO2 is low (respiratory compensation).
• Mixed Disorder: PCO2 is higher than predicted by Winter’s formula.
• Suggests an additional failure to ventilate appropriately.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: Identify the diagnostic significance of a patient's acid-base values falling outside the shaded 95% confidence limits on a standard nomogram.
back:
• Indicates a Mixed Acid-Base Disorder.
• Suggests the compensation is either inadequate or excessive for a single primary disturbance.
• Requires investigation of multiple underlying etiologies.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: In metabolic acidosis, if the measured PCO2 is significantly lower than the value calculated by [___], a concomitant respiratory alkalosis is present.
back:
• Winter's Formula
• Expected PCO2 = (1.5 × [HCO3-]) + 8 ± 2
• Indicates the patient is hyperventilating more than necessary for simple compensation.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: A patient with pyloric stenosis experiences persistent vomiting but also develops severe diarrhea from a hospital-acquired infection. Predict the mixed acid-base finding.
back:
• Mixed Metabolic Alkalosis (from vomiting/HCl loss)
• Metabolic Acidosis (from diarrhea/HCO3- loss)
• The pH may be near 7.4, but electrolytes will show abnormal HCO3- and Cl- levels.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: Describe how renal compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis results in the generation of 'new' bicarbonate.
back:
• Increased H+ secretion by type A intercalated cells.
• H+ combines with ammonia (NH3) or phosphate (HPO4=) in the lumen.
• For every H+ excreted with these non-bicarbonate buffers, one new HCO3- enters the blood.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: Contrast the physiological onset and timeframe of respiratory vs. renal compensation for acid-base disturbances.
back:
• Respiratory: Rapid onset (minutes); peaks within 3–12 hours.
• Renal: Slow onset (hours); peaks within 3–5 days.
• Mixed disorders often occur if an acute insult happens before renal compensation completes.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: Identify the primary source of nonvolatile acid production that requires renal excretion to prevent metabolic acidosis.
back:
• Metabolism of proteins.
• Produces approximately 80 mEq/day of nonvolatile acids (e.g., sulfuric, phosphoric acid).
• These cannot be excreted by the lungs and require renal H+ secretion.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: A clinical condition where lab values fail to show predicted compensatory responses because two or more primary pathologies are present simultaneously is termed a [___].
back:
Mixed acid-base disorder
- Identified when blood gas values fall outside shaded areas of an acid-base nomogram.
- Example: Simultaneous metabolic acidosis (diarrhea) and respiratory acidosis (emphysema).

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
coreConcept: Identifying Mixed Acidosis from Clinical Data
front: A patient with severe emphysema presents with acute diarrhea. Labs show a drastically reduced pH, low plasma [HCO3-], and an elevated Pco2. Identify the specific complex disorder.
back:
Mixed Acidosis
- Diarrhea causes primary metabolic acidosis (HCO3- loss).
- Emphysema causes primary respiratory acidosis (CO2 retention).
- The pH drops more severely because both systems fail to compensate.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
coreConcept: Synergistic pH Shifts in Mixed Disorders
front: Explain why arterial pH values in mixed acid-base disorders are typically more extreme than those seen in simple acid-base disturbances.
back:
Loss of antagonistic compensation
- In simple disorders, one system moves pH back toward 7.4.
- In mixed disorders, both primary metabolic and respiratory components move pH in the same direction.
- This results in a synergistic pH shift.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: Contrast the expected Pco2 level in simple metabolic acidosis with that seen in a mixed acidosis consisting of metabolic and respiratory components.
back:
Pco2 Comparison
- Simple Metabolic Acidosis: Pco2 is low (respiratory compensation via hyperventilation).
- Mixed Acidosis: Pco2 is high or normal (indicates concurrent respiratory failure or independent respiratory acidosis).

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: State the significance of arterial pH, HCO3-, and Pco2 values plotting outside the 95% confidence limits on a standard acid-base nomogram.
back:
Suggests a Mixed Acid-Base Disorder
- Values in shaded areas indicate simple disorders with normal compensation.
- Values outside shaded areas imply an inadequate or inappropriate compensatory response.
- Indicates two primary underlying causes.

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: A mixed acid-base disorder is characterized by the simultaneous presence of two or more [___] acid-base disturbances.
back:
• Primary
  • Occurs when independent processes coexist (e.g., renal failure plus vomiting)
  • pH depends on the direction and severity of each disturbance

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: A patient with chronic emphysema develops severe diarrhea. Identify the resulting mixed acid-base disorder and its effect on pH.
back:
• Mixed Respiratory Acidosis and Metabolic Acidosis
  • Emphysema causes CO2 retention; diarrhea causes bicarbonate loss
  • pH decreases severely as both processes shift it downward

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: Explain why a patient with salicylate (aspirin) poisoning typically exhibits a mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis.
back:
• Direct stimulation of the medullary respiratory center causes hyperventilation (Resp Alk)
  • Interference with mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation leads to organic acid buildup (Met Acid)

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: Contrast the arterial blood pH in simple metabolic acidosis versus a mixed disorder where metabolic acidosis is combined with respiratory alkalosis.
back:
• Simple: pH is always abnormal (acidic)
  • Mixed Opposing: pH may appear near-normal because the two primary processes pull pH in opposite directions
  • Requires evaluation of PCO2 and Anion Gap

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: In a patient with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, how does a measured PCO2 higher than the value predicted by Winter's Formula indicate a mixed disorder?
back:
• Indicates a superimposed primary respiratory acidosis
  • The lungs are failing to provide the expected compensatory hyperventilation
  • Commonly seen in sepsis with concomitant respiratory failure

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: To detect a superimposed metabolic alkalosis in a patient with high anion gap metabolic acidosis, clinicians utilize the [___] ratio.
back:
• Delta-Delta (ΔAG / ΔHCO3)
  • A ratio > 2.0 suggests a mixed disorder with metabolic alkalosis
  • A ratio < 1.0 suggests a mixed hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: A patient with heart failure on chronic loop diuretics develops acute pneumonia. Identify the mixed acid-base disorder likely to be present.
back:
• Metabolic Alkalosis and Respiratory Acidosis
  • Diuretics cause bicarbonate retention/contraction alkalosis
  • Pneumonia causes impaired gas exchange and CO2 retention

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: Describe the physiological outcome when a patient experiences simultaneous respiratory alkalosis and metabolic alkalosis.
back:
• Additive pH increase leading to extreme alkalemia
  • Common in pregnancy with severe vomiting or liver failure with hyperventilation
  • Can cause cardiac arrhythmias and neuromuscular excitability

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: Contrast the expected bicarbonate level in simple respiratory acidosis versus a mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis.
back:
• Simple: HCO3 increases as a renal compensation for CO2 retention
  • Mixed: HCO3 is lower than expected (or even low) because the metabolic component consumes bicarbonate

category: Explain the causes and compensation of mixed acid base disorder
front: Identify the primary danger of a mixed acidosis (Metabolic + Respiratory) compared to a simple acid-base disorder.
back:
• Loss of compensatory mechanisms
  • Both the renal and respiratory systems are primary drivers of the pathology
  • Results in rapid, profound drops in pH that are often fatal

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: The clinical estimation of the plasma anion gap involves subtracting the sum of [___] and bicarbonate concentrations from the plasma sodium concentration.
back:
• Chloride ([Cl⁻])
• It targets the anions routinely measured in clinical laboratories.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: A patient presents with metabolic acidosis following severe diarrhea. Lab results show decreased [HCO3⁻] and an appropriately elevated [Cl⁻]. Identify the anion gap classification.
back:
• Normal Anion Gap
• Also known as hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: How does the accumulation of nonvolatile acids, such as lactic acid or ketoacids, lead to an increased anion gap?
back:
• These acids release H⁺ which is buffered by HCO3⁻.
• The remaining acid anions (lactate/ketoacids) are unmeasured.
• Sodium is balanced by these unmeasured anions instead of chloride.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Contrast the primary unmeasured anions versus unmeasured cations that clinically define the theoretical gap in plasma electroneutrality.
back:
• Unmeasured Anions: Albumin, phosphate, sulfate, and organic acids.
• Unmeasured Cations: Calcium, magnesium, and potassium.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Identify the primary reason the 'anion gap' is used as a diagnostic concept despite the physical reality of plasma electroneutrality.
back:
• It identifies changes in unmeasured ions.
• In reality, total anions and cations are always equal.
• It accounts for ions not routinely measured in standard labs.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: The normal clinical range for the calculated plasma anion gap, representing the difference between unmeasured anions and cations, is [___] mEq/L.
back:
• 8 to 16 mEq/L
• Values outside this range suggest specific acid-base disturbances.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: A patient with chronic renal failure presents with metabolic acidosis and a high anion gap. Specify the ions responsible for this increase.
back:
• Retention of phosphates and sulfates.
• Accumulation of other unmeasured organic anions.
• Failure of the kidneys to excrete these weak acid anions.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Describe the mechanism by which carbonic anhydrase inhibitors lead to a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.
back:
• They cause primary loss of HCO3⁻ in urine.
• This is matched by a proportional rise in plasma Cl⁻.
• No addition of unmeasured organic anions occurs.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Distinguish between the effect of methanol poisoning and Addison's disease on the calculated anion gap.
back:
• Methanol: Increased anion gap (due to unmeasured formic acid).
• Addison's: Normal anion gap (due to hyperchloremia).

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: List the three routinely measured ions used in the standard clinical formula to estimate the anion gap.
back:
• Sodium (Na⁺)
• Chloride (Cl⁻)
• Bicarbonate (HCO3⁻)

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: The plasma anion gap is mathematically calculated using the formula: [Na⁺] – ([Cl⁻] + [___]).
back:
• [HCO₃⁻]
• Represents the difference between unmeasured anions and unmeasured cations.
• Normal range is typically 8–16 mEq/L.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: A 22-year-old male with type 1 diabetes presents with pH 7.1, Na⁺ 140 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 100 mEq/L, and HCO₃⁻ 10 mEq/L. This patient's specific metabolic disturbance is [___].
back:
• High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (HAGMA)
• Calculated gap: 140 - (100 + 10) = 30 mEq/L (High)
• Pathophysiology: Accumulation of unmeasured acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Explain the role of plasma albumin as the primary component of the normal anion gap.
back:
• Albumin carries a net negative charge, acting as the largest "unmeasured anion."
• It accounts for nearly 75% of the normal gap value.
• Maintains the gap despite the law of electroneutrality.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: A patient with metabolic acidosis shows an anion gap of 11 mEq/L. Contrast the expected serum chloride level in this case versus a case of ethylene glycol poisoning.
back:
• Case (11 mEq/L): Hyperchloremic (Normal Anion Gap); Cl⁻ is elevated to replace lost HCO₃⁻.
• Ethylene Glycol: High Anion Gap; Cl⁻ remains normal as glycolate/oxalate anions accumulate.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Explain the necessary adjustment for the anion gap in a patient with severe hypoalbuminemia.
back:
• The "normal" AG decreases by 2.5 mEq/L for every 1 g/dL drop in albumin below 4 g/dL.
• Failure to adjust masks high anion gap acidosis in malnourished patients.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: In metabolic acidosis resulting from Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA), the anion gap is typically [___].
back:
• Normal (8-16 mEq/L)
• Also known as hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.
• HCO₃⁻ loss is balanced by chloride retention by the kidneys.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: A patient presents with a plasma gap of 22 mEq/L following excessive aspirin ingestion. Identify the unmeasured anions contributing to this finding.
back:
• Salicylates
• Lactate (due to uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation)
• Ketoacids (due to altered lipid metabolism)

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Contrast the mechanism of anion gap elevation in Chronic Renal Failure versus Lactic Acidosis.
back:
• Renal Failure: Accumulation of inorganic acids (phosphates, sulfates) due to reduced GFR.
• Lactic Acidosis: Accumulation of organic lactate due to tissue hypoxia or anaerobic glycolysis.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Contrast the diagnostic utility of the anion gap in diarrhea versus DKA-related acidosis.
back:
• Diarrhea: Normal AG; loss of NaHCO₃ causes compensatory Cl⁻ rise.
• DKA: Increased AG; ketoanions accumulate, keeping Cl⁻ levels relatively stable while consuming HCO₃⁻.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Name the three primary electrolytes routinely measured to calculate the clinical anion gap.
back:
• Sodium (Na⁺)
• Chloride (Cl⁻)
• Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: The plasma anion gap is a diagnostic tool calculated by subtracting the concentrations of [___] and bicarbonate from the concentration of sodium.
back:
• Chloride (Cl-)
• It estimates the concentration of unmeasured anions in the plasma to narrow the differential diagnosis of metabolic acidosis.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: A patient with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes presents with a blood pH of 7.1 and elevated acetoacetic acid levels. Predict the state of the anion gap in this condition.
back:
• Increased (High) Anion Gap
• Caused by the accumulation of unmeasured ketoacid anions which replace lost bicarbonate without increasing chloride levels.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Explain the mechanism by which chronic renal failure leads to an increased plasma anion gap.
back:
• Decreased GFR leads to reduced excretion of anions from weak acids
• Accumulation of unmeasured anions like phosphates, sulfates, and urates increases the gap.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Contrast the mechanism of 'hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis' with high-anion gap metabolic acidosis regarding plasma chloride levels.
back:
• Hyperchloremic: Chloride increases proportionally as bicarbonate falls, keeping the gap normal (e.g., diarrhea).
• High-Anion Gap: Chloride remains normal while bicarbonate is replaced by unmeasured organic anions.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Identify the three primary unmeasured cations that must be theoretically accounted for when calculating the anion gap.
back:
• Calcium (Ca2+)
• Magnesium (Mg2+)
• Potassium (K+)

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Under normal physiological conditions, the plasma anion gap typically ranges between [___] mEq/L.
back:
• 8 to 16 mEq/L
• This range represents the normal excess of unmeasured anions over unmeasured cations.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: A child presents with severe metabolic acidosis following a week of heavy diarrhea. Identify the expected anion gap status and the rationale.
back:
• Normal Anion Gap (Hyperchloremic)
• Diarrhea involves massive loss of sodium bicarbonate; the kidneys retain chloride to maintain electroneutrality, preventing a gap increase.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Describe how the ingestion of methyl alcohol or ethylene glycol alters the biochemical composition of the anion gap.
back:
• Metabolism produces unmeasured organic acids (formic or oxalic acid)
• These anions consume bicarbonate, leading to an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Contrast the effect of Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA) and Lactic Acidosis on the calculated plasma anion gap.
back:
• RTA: Normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) due to failed H+ secretion or HCO3- reabsorption.
• Lactic Acidosis: Increased anion gap due to the accumulation of unmeasured lactate anions.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Identify the major unmeasured anions that contribute to the normal 8-16 mEq/L gap in healthy individuals.
back:
• Albumin (most significant)
• Phosphate
• Sulfate
• Organic anions

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Clinically, the anion gap is calculated by subtracting the sum of measured chloride and bicarbonate concentrations from the plasma concentration of [___].
back:
• Sodium ([Na+])
• Formula: AG = [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-])
• Represents the concentration of unmeasured anions in the plasma.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: A 25-year-old known diabetic presents with Kussmaul breathing and fruity breath. Lab results show pH 7.2 and an anion gap of 22 mEq/L. Identify the primary physiological mechanism for this elevated gap.
back:
• Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
• Accumulation of unmeasured fixed ketoacids (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate)
• Consumption of bicarbonate buffer by H+ ions released from ketoacids.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Explain the mechanism by which severe diarrhea leads to a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.
back:
• Direct gastrointestinal loss of bicarbonate (HCO3-)
• To maintain electroneutrality, the kidneys retain Chloride (Cl-)
• The rise in measured Cl- balances the fall in HCO3-, preserving the gap.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Contrast the diagnostic implications of a High Anion Gap metabolic acidosis with a Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.
back:
• High AG: Indicates addition of fixed/organic acids (e.g., Lactic acid, Toxins, Ketoacids)
• Hyperchloremic (Normal AG): Indicates primary loss of base (Diarrhea) or renal tubular defects (RTA).

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: In patients with severe hypoalbuminemia, the calculated anion gap may be misleadingly low. State the standard clinical correction factor for this condition.
back:
• Albumin is the primary unmeasured anion
• Correction: Increase calculated AG by ~2.5 mEq/L for every 1 g/dL drop in serum albumin below 4 g/dL.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: The common mnemonic 'MUDPILES' is used to remember causes of metabolic acidosis associated with an [___] anion gap.
back:
• Increased (or High)
• Includes Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Propylene glycol, Iron/Isoniazid, Lactic acid, Ethylene glycol, and Salicylates.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: A patient with chronic renal failure presents with metabolic acidosis and a high anion gap. Identify the specific unmeasured anions responsible for this laboratory finding.
back:
• Failure of GFR leads to retention of metabolic waste anions
• Predominantly sulfates, phosphates, urates, and organic acids
• These replace lost bicarbonate while Na+ remains constant.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Explain why the body maintains a clinical 'Anion Gap' despite the Law of Electroneutrality stating total cations must equal total anions.
back:
• Clinically, we only measure common electrolytes (Na+, Cl-, HCO3-)
• The 'gap' represents unmeasured anions (Albumin, PO4, SO4) exceeding unmeasured cations (K+, Ca++, Mg++).

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Contrast the effects of Lactic Acidosis and Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA) on the measured plasma chloride levels.
back:
• Lactic Acidosis: Normal Cl- (High AG as lactate replaces HCO3-)
• RTA: Increased Cl- (Normal AG as kidneys retain Cl- to compensate for HCO3- loss).

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: State the normal range for the serum anion gap in a healthy individual.
back:
• 8 to 16 mEq/L
• Values consistently above this range signify the presence of an unmeasured fixed acid.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: The clinical anion gap is calculated by subtracting the sum of [___] and bicarbonate from the plasma sodium concentration.
back:
• Chloride ([Cl⁻])
• Formula: AG = [Na⁺] – ([Cl⁻] + [HCO₃⁻])
• Represents unmeasured anions like albumin, phosphate, and sulfate.

category: Define and explain anion gap
coreConcept: Calculation and Interpretation of Anion Gap
front: A patient with chronic renal failure presents with pH 7.2, sodium 140 mEq/L, chloride 104 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 12 mEq/L. Identify the calculated anion gap and the specific acid-base state.
back:
• Anion Gap: 24 mEq/L (140 - 116)
• Diagnosis: High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (HAGMA)
• Cause: Accumulation of unmeasured fixed acids (sulfates/phosphates) due to renal failure.

category: Define and explain anion gap
coreConcept: Mechanism of High Anion Gap Acidosis
front: Explain the mechanism by which the addition of lactic acid to the extracellular fluid increases the anion gap.
back:
• Lactate consumes HCO₃⁻ to form H₂CO₃ (H₂O + CO₂)
• Lactate anions are 'unmeasured' in standard electrolytes
• Bicarbonate is replaced by lactate, widening the gap between measured cations and anions.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Contrast the pathogenesis of hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with that of high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
back:
• Hyperchloremic (Normal AG): HCO₃⁻ loss (e.g., diarrhea) is matched by Cl⁻ increase to maintain electroneutrality.
• High AG: Fixed acids (e.g., ketones) add new unmeasured anions that replace HCO₃⁻, while Cl⁻ remains normal.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Identify the standard clinical correction required for the anion gap in a patient with significantly reduced plasma albumin levels.
back:
• Albumin is the primary unmeasured anion
• Low albumin falsely lowers the calculated AG
• Correction: Add ~2.5 mEq/L to the AG for every 1 g/dL decrease in albumin below normal.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Metabolic acidosis caused by severe diarrhea is characterized by a [___] anion gap.
back:
• Normal (Hyperchloremic)
• Mechanism: Massive gastrointestinal loss of NaHCO₃ is compensated by renal retention of Chloride to maintain charge balance.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: A type 1 diabetic patient presents with Kussmaul breathing. Lab results: Na⁺ 136, Cl⁻ 96, HCO₃⁻ 10. Identify the unmeasured anions contributing to this gap.
back:
• Anion Gap: 30 mEq/L
• Unmeasured Anions: Ketoacids (Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate)
• Diagnosis: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA).

category: Define and explain anion gap
coreConcept: Physiological Basis of the Anion Gap
front: Describe the physiological 'electroneutrality principle' and how it explains the clinical existence of an anion gap.
back:
• Plasma is always neutral (cations = anions)
• The 'gap' is an artifact of measuring only three ions (Na⁺, Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻)
• It equals the difference between unmeasured anions (e.g., proteins) and unmeasured cations (e.g., Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺).

category: Define and explain anion gap
coreConcept: Differential Diagnosis of Acidosis via Anion Gap
front: Contrast the expected anion gap findings in Type 1 Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA) versus Salicylate poisoning.
back:
• Type 1 RTA: Normal Anion Gap (Hyperchloremic) due to H⁺ secretion failure.
• Salicylate Poisoning: High Anion Gap due to accumulation of salicylic acid and interference with oxidative phosphorylation.

category: Define and explain anion gap
front: Identify the two most common 'unmeasured' cations that are excluded from the standard anion gap calculation.
back:
• Potassium (K⁺)
• Calcium (Ca²⁺)
• Magnesium (Mg²⁺) is also frequently excluded.
• Normal AG range: 8–16 mEq/L.
